News.title: How to save exhausted bumble bees and four other ways to help creatures in your garden suffering in the heatwave
News.content:
BEE KIND How to save exhausted bumble bees and four other ways to help creatures in your garden suffering in the heatwave

WHILE we battle through heatwaves by jumping into paddling pools and stocking up on ice lollies, the country’s wildlife has no such luxury.

As our gardens bake, experts warn that birds, hedgehogs and other wildlife are being left exhausted, dehydrated and struggling to find food.



The RSPCA says that rescue centres are “fit to bursting” and it is facing a growing hedgehog crisis after seeing a sharp rise in admissions so far this summer.

In June alone, shortly after the first heatwave of 2026 hit, more than 315 hedgehogs were treated at the charity’s four wildlife centres – that is up 56 per cent from the same month last year.



Experts say making a few simple changes in your garden can provide a vital lifeline to Britain’s wildlife. From leaving out fresh water to resisting the urge to mow every inch of lawn, we reveal how you can help.

SPOT THE WARNING SIGNS: If you see a hedgehog out and about during the day, you may think it’s really cute — but it could actually be a cry for help.



Rebecca Machin, scientific and policy officer at RSPCA Wildlife, says: “People need to be aware of the warning signs that animals might be in danger.

“If you see hedgehogs out in the day, that is unusual in itself but if they are staggering, they may need help. It’s the same if you see a bird panting.”

Rebecca reveals there are lots of things people can do to give wild animals a helping hand.

“If a bee is exhausted and can’t move, you can help by putting them back on to a flower,” she explains.



“Or, if you see small frogs emerging from a pond on to concrete, there is a risk of them sticking, so usher them back in.”

FOOD FOR THOUGHT: Just like humans, animals get thirsty in hot weather but sustenance is often harder to come by.

Forget fancy feeders, though — you might already have the perfect wildlife treat sitting in your cupboard.

After one of the driest summers on record, many animals are struggling to dig worms — their primary source of food — out of the hard soil.



But pet food makes an excellent substitute.

Rebecca says: “Regular wet cat or dog food can be great for badgers and hedgehogs, but make sure you leave it out at night so the neighbors’ pets don’t steal it.”

DOWN TOOLS: Leaving your lawnmower in the shed could be the key to helping wildlife this summer.

Beccy Speight, chief executive of the RSPB, says: “From birds taking refuge in hedges and dense shrubs, to longer grass giving butterflies and insects shelter from the heat, overgrown areas in the garden can provide respite.



Letting the lawn grow a little longer or allowing leaf piles to build up will also provide invertebrates and amphibians with cool, damp areas.”

Experts also recommend creating some shady areas with pebbles or logs in the corner of your garden.

DRINK IT IN: As temperatures soar, we won’t be the only ones searching for the nearest watering hole this summer.

Birds, hedgehogs, bees and butterflies all need access to fresh water to stay hydrated.

Beccy says: “Providing clean water for drinking and bathing all year round is one of the simplest ways to help garden wildlife.



“During the summer, it’s even more of a lifeline, especially with the heatwaves and the likelihood of more dry weather ahead.”

It is not as simple as sticking a bowl of water out in the garden, though.

Beccy explains: “People are being encouraged to provide clean water in a bird bath, pond or shallow dish.

“Adding a few stones around the edge can help butterflies and insects perch safely while drinking, while also making it easier for species such as hedgehogs, frogs and toads to access the water.

“However, hygiene is essential.



“Bird baths should be emptied and refilled daily and cleaned and disinfected every week to help prevent disease spreading between birds.”

DON’T SPARK TROUBLE: Experts warn that many animals’ natural habitats are in danger this summer after months of no significant rain.

Zoe Quiroz Cullen, head of climate and international policy at The Wildlife Trusts, says: “With many of our landscapes already dry, there is a real risk of wildfire across the UK.

“Remember to clear away all your rubbish, leave your barbecue at home in favour of packing a picnic, and carefully discard any cigarette butts to avoid starting an accidental fire.”

News.title: Schoolboy, 14, reels in record-breaking catch on his first time cast fishing after two-hour battle with monster skate
News.content:
HOLY CARP Schoolboy, 14, reels in record-breaking catch on his first time cast fishing after two-hour battle with monster skate

A SCHOOLBOY has broken the UK record for the biggest fish caught by a child.

Henry Ralph, 14, caught a massive 195lb skate fish at a beach near at Oban in Argyll & Bute, Scotland.



During his very first time cast fishing, Henry caught the mega fish with huge wings, a thrashing tale and rough, thorny skin.

At first, he thought his line was snagged on a heavy clump of kelp – but when the scaly titan started splashing around, he knew he’d caught something big.



The supersized fish took Henry two hours to reel in, and nearly pulled him into the murky sea as he played tug of war with the mammoth skate.

Once he’d got hold of it, the determined teen realised that the slippery skate was twice his size.

Michael Hannah, Henry’s fishing guide, helped measure the creature which was 81 inches long and 69 inches wide.

Henry said: “It was really hard to reel in and was like the fight of a lifetime. It took about two hours but I am quite determined and I wasn’t going to let it go.



“When I saw it flailing around about 20 yards from the shore, that’s when I realised how big it was. I was just shocked at the size of it.

“I did feel tired afterwards and had to sit down but after a while I was ready to catch another one.”

Henry, who lives in Moray, has been fishing since he was eight.

Michael works with the Moray Skate Guide watched in awe as the lad battled the marine monster single-handed.

Michael said: “He is only a wee boy but didn’t need my help. He didn’t want to give it up, it was phenomenal to watch.



“I know grown men who would have handed the rod over. It was the fish of a lifetime for Henry and he is only 14!”

The guide confirmed that the fish was safely returned to the waters.

This comes after a boy from the UK caught a 152lb catfish during a holiday in Spain.

In 2023, Joshua Davenport, who was 11 at the time, broke the European record for the largest freshwater caught with a net by a child.

Joshua had been fishing with his parents when he snagged the mega catfish with his bait, fighting for 25 minutes to secure the catch.



The catfish was 9ft long and took three adults to lift it onto the scales.

News.title: Knifeman who stabbed Salman Rushdie 15 times in front of stunned audience convicted of terrorism charges
News.content:
THE knifeman who stabbed Salman Rushdie 15 times in front of a horrifed audience in 2022 has been convicted of federal terrorism charges.

Matar was accused of doing the Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah’s deadly dirty work by carrying out his decades-old death sentence on Rushdie.



A jury found Hadi Matar, 28, guilty of all the charges against him, including engaging in an act of transnational terrorism.

He now faces the terrifying prospect of life behind bars over the savage 2022 attack at a packed amphitheatre.



Matar is already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence after being convicted of attempted murder over the shocking assault.

The federal conviction could now see his punishment stretch to life in prison.

The Indian-born British and American novelist was preparing to speak about writers’ safety when Matar stormed the stage and launched his frenzied attack.

The celebrated author was repeatedly slashed in front of a stunned audience, suffering devastating injuries that left him blind in his right eye.

Matar’s lawyers had argued there was no proof of what was going through his mind when he attacked the literary giant.

Defence lawyer Nathaniel Barone claimed prosecutors had no evidence proving Matar’s state of mind.



But prosecutors painted a chilling picture of an attacker allegedly obsessed with a decades-old death sentence against Rushdie.

They said Matar was driven by late Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini’s 1989 call for Rushdie’s death over his controversial novel The Satanic Verses.

The attacker refused to testify during the explosive trial.



Rushdie, however, took the stand and confronted the man accused of trying to kill him.

He told jurors: “I cant say what his ambitions or his aim was, but the wounds were dispersed across my body.”

Prosecutors claimed Matar had repeatedly discussed the fatwa with contacts on messaging apps in the years before the attack.

Court exhibits allegedly showed him raging that Rushdie had attacked Islam and had emboldened others to insult the faith by surviving.

Matar also allegedly referred to a 2006 comment by the late Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah.



The US-born attacker also holds Lebanese citizenship, while Hezbollah is based in Lebanon.

Prosecutors said photographs found in Matar’s New Jersey bedroom and on his computer showed his support for Hezbollah, which the US has designated a terrorist organisation.

Assistant US Attorney Timothy Lynch told jurors in his opening statement on July 22: “Matar aimed to fulfill the fatwa and wanted everyone to know he was doing this for Hezbollah.”

The prosecution claimed Matar’s messages revealed a terrifying escalation from wanting to expose Rushdie to allegedly plotting to kill him.

In a private note to himself, Matar allegedly wrote: “We need to kill him ASAP,” according to Lynch.



Prosecutors said Matar framed the planned killing as part of what he considered a jihad, or holy war.

By spring 2022, investigators calimed Matar had worked out where Rushdie lived and was tacking his public appearances.

He allegedly homed in on Rushdie’s scheduled appearance at the Chautauqua Institution in western New York.



As Rushdie was being introduced, his attacker climbed onto the stage behind him.

Matar then stabbed the author 15 times as horrified spectators gasped.

Audience members and another speaker, Henry Reese, desperately scrambled to help the gravely wounded writer.

Law enforcement officers assigned to the event arrested Matar after civilians managed to restrain him.

Rushdie had spent years living under the shadow of a death threat after The Satanic Verses was published in 1988.



The novel triggered furious protests across parts of the Muslim world over what some believers viewed as blasphemous suggestions about the Prophet Muhammad.

The shocking fallout was deadly, with at least 45 people killed in riots linked to the book.

A Japanese translator was stabbed to death, an Italian translator was attacked and survived, while the book’s Norwegian publisher survived a shooting.

Rushdie, who was born into a Muslim family, has maintained that the controversial dream sequence in the novel was simply fiction.

He was forced into hiding for years before gradually returning to public life after Iran’s government distanced itself from Khomeini’s fatwa in 1998.



Rushdie told the trial in Buffalo, New York: “For two decades or more, I led a public life without a hint of trouble.”

But the threat never fully disappeared.

The fatwa was never rescinded, while Khomeini’s successor, the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, indicated in 2017 that it remained in effect.

An Iranian foundation has also offered a bounty of more than $3million for Rushdie’s killing.

Rushdie went on to publish a memoir about the horrific attack in 2024 before returning to fiction with last year’s The Eleventh Hour.



The acclaimed author won Britain’s prestigious Booker Prize for his 1981 novel Midnight’s Children, which explored his native India.

He was later knighted by the late Queen Elizabeth II and received a Dayton Literary Peace Prize lifetime achievement award in November.

News.title: Killer husband who murdered wife & took his own life had strangled her in Scots home just weeks before
News.content:
A BRUTE throttled his estranged wife in her home — three weeks before returning to murder her, we can reveal.

Stacy Mair called police after Jim Mair, 44, left her “struggling to breathe” in the horror attack at the ­cottage they once shared.



The thug was taken into cells — but was freed on bail the next day after a court appearance.

He ignored orders to stay away from the mum, 35, and on Sunday night launched the fatal attack on her at the rural pad near Houston, Renfrewshire, before taking his own life.



It came after the tree removal business boss appeared at Paisley Sheriff Court on July 6 accused of compressing Stacy’s neck.

Mair had appeared on petition — reserved for the most serious cases — and was charged under domestic abuse laws.



Officers said Mair’s death was being treated as unexplained pending a post-mortem.

Cops locked down the property at the end of a single-track on Tuesday as they continued to probe the murder.

Stacy, originally of Falkland, Fife, was the second woman killed by her ex in the space of six days — sparking calls for stricter sentences to protect abuse victims.

We told how Lee Greenan stabbed to death beauty clinic boss Vikki Soloman, 44, at her home in East Craigs, Edinburgh, ten days ago.

The coward, 46, was arrested following a manhunt after he sparked alarm by walking into the nearby Mid Yoken pub ­covered in blood.

He is thought to have died by suicide to avoid facing justice after his body was found in his cell at HMP Edinburgh.



Tory justice spokesman Stephen Kerr said both cases were a “devastating reminder that domestic abuse remains one of the gravest threats” facing women.

He called for “tougher sentencing, better protection for victims and a justice system that prioritises the safety of women above the needs of criminals.”

Labour counterpart Pauline McNeill warned: “Action is needed to confront rising levels of violence against women and ensure our justice system tackles misogyny and protects women.”

Victims minister Kirsten Oswald said: “My deepest condolences go to Vikki Soloman and Stacy Mair’s families.

“We have taken action to tackle domestic abuse, including legislation to strengthen confidence in the system and ensure police, prosecutors and courts have the powers they need to bring perpetrators to justice.



“Violent men need to change their behaviour and be held accountable for coercive control, abuse and violence.”

News.title: Gormless French cops watch on as 1,000 illegal migrants head for UK hours after PM claimed small boats plan was working
News.content:
A FLOTILLA of up to 1,000 migrants headed for Britain as French cops watched on despite getting more than £1billion from UK taxpayers to stop them.

The fresh influx came a day after PM Andy Burnham insisted Labour’s plan to clamp down on illegal migration was working.



The gormless French cops who watched the illegal migrants set sail for Britain said: “Our order is to let them go.”

On one of the busiest days for Channel crossings this year, The Sun witnessed chaos unfold as asylum seekers repeatedly stormed beaches.



Astonishing scenes saw violence erupt among the migrants fighting for space on crammed dinghies.

Tory Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp was on the beach and posted videos of the chaos.

He said: “The most shocking thing was the complete inaction by the Gendarmes — they just stood there and watched the migrants launching.

“It was extraordinary.”

One French officer was filmed saying: “Our order is to let them go.

“We just have to say to them ‘don’t do that, it’s dangerous’.”



While the official numbers will be released today, provisional estimates last night were that more than 1,000 migrants could have made the perilous journey.

The last time the daily tally hit four figures was last October, when 1,075 migrants crossed.

Reform’s Nigel Farage said: “The invasion continues.



“Yet Burnham said ‘the plan is working’.

“What planet is he on?”

We watched as an hour of mayhem unfolded from midday at Neufchâtel-Hardelot, south of Calais, after a dinghy carrying around 60 migrants, including toddlers and what appeared to be a baby, got stranded yards from shore.

Fighting broke out as desperate passengers tried to push the boat into deeper water.

The Sun watched men pull each other’s hair while one stripped off his belt and whipped fellow migrants.



Several became aggressive towards journalists and the public.

Around ten to 12 gendarmes watched on.

Reporters pointed out the violence to them but they did not enter the shallow water to intervene.

One cop said it would be “too dangerous”.

Labour ministers have previously claimed to have convinced the French government to relax laws to let officers snare migrants in the shallows.



Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has bunged them millions more based on the promise to deploy ­cutting-edge tactics.

But one wetsuit-wearing officer was seen pottering around one of the boats on a paddleboard.

Under the new deal, the UK will withhold cash if the French police are failing to deliver value for money.

After almost an hour, the migrants succeeded in pushing the dinghy out to sea.



Before it left, two men who appeared to be directing other passengers climbed ashore.

One man onboard blew kisses to the pair, while others cheered.

When asked whether the pair were suspected of helping organise the crossing, gendarmes said there was “no evidence”.

The men were later seen walking away from the beach and speaking with volunteers from non-governmental organisations.



French sources told The Sun there had been intense activity along the Opal Coast from 1am as calm seas and light winds created ideal conditions.

More than 13,007 migrants have crossed the Channel this year — down 45 per cent on 2025.

But the heatwave has triggered a stampede and poses a fresh challenge to Mr Burnham, who name-checked immigration as a top public priority.

The Sun earlier witnessed dramatic scenes at nearby Wimereux.

Arriving shortly after 5.30am, reporters found around 100 migrants attempting to board a larger boat waiting offshore after being ferried out in smaller RIBs.



Around 80 squeezed aboard but the rest were forced back including two women and three children.

A boy, aged four or five, was shivering after reaching shore.

Firefighters carried him to medics.

Three migrants from Punjab told The Sun they had each paid between £500 and £1,500 for repeated attempts to reach Britain.



'THE BOATS LEFT ALL NIGHT LONG' By Louis Wood, Sun photographer I’VE been covering migrant crossings on the French coast for the past 15 years and I can honestly say this was probably the busiest day I’ve witnessed. I have never seen anything like it. Boats left throughout the night and the crossings kept going until after 3pm. There seemed to be another launch or group preparing to leave everywhere we went. The scenes on Hardelot beach were extraordinary. There were around 60 people crammed on a dinghy that became stranded just offshore and for almost an hour complete chaos unfolded. People were pulling each other off the dinghy to push it to get the engine working. Journalists covering the event were threatened. Throughout this, the gendarmes stayed on the beach. Even as disorder continued and we were abused simply for trying to report what was happening, they didn’t step in. I’ve never seen crossings on this scale. It felt like the smugglers were operating almost continuously, launching boats from different beaches throughout the day. When we left there were still crossing attempts taking place.

One said he had tried 20 times, losing his money on every failed attempt but insisted he would continue until he reached the UK.

Further north in Gravelines 100 migrants scrambled along the sand to board a dinghy.

French authorities in a rescue lifeboat appeared to be handing them life jackets.

The crossings came days after a Sudanese migrant was stabbed to death at nearby Berck-sur-Mer before a dinghy carrying a record 165 people set sail for Kent.

Workers overlooking the beach told The Sun gendarmes said the victim was attacked following a dispute over space aboard the boat.



French prosecutors have not confirmed a motive and a murder investigation continues.

The Sun returned to Berck.

Within minutes of arriving, we saw another attempted crossing.

Only a small number appeared to get aboard, leaving many stranded on the sand wearing life jackets.

Berck is becoming one of the north’s busiest launch sites as smugglers try to circumvent a crackdown in Calais and Dunkirk.



It is about an hour from Calais’ main camps and migrants are taken there by minibus or “sea taxi” to hide in the dunes.

The alleged pilot of the record Berck crossing, Chan Mathok Atak, 19, has since been charged with facilitating illegal immigration and the Government’s new offence of endangering others at sea.

He denies the allegations.

According to the UN refugee agency, almost 35,000 Sudanese are now living in France after fleeing civil war and famine.

Many settle in Paris before moving to camps near Calais, Boulogne and the Opal Coast.



A French border police source told The Sun: “They are an insular group who tend to live and operate together.

“Like any other group they fight themselves.

“Knife attacks have become all too common.”

In response to Mr Philp’s video, the Home Office said: “We are aware of posts circulating online that claim French law enforcement are failing to prevent small boat Channel crossings.

“UK-French co-operation has already stopped over 46,000 attempted crossings since the election.



“In May alone, 65 per cent of all small boat events were stopped despite soaring temperatures, which have historically led to increased crossings.

“But we know there is more to do.

“That is why the Home Secretary has signed a landmark new ­payment-by-results deal with France to boost enforcement action on beaches and put people smugglers behind bars.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“On top of the 46,000 crossing attempts prevented, removals of small boat migrants are at record levels and asylum claims are down by 12 per cent.

“We have also removed or deported almost 70,000 people who were here illegally — an increase of 41 per cent — and are going further to remove the incentives that draw illegal migrants to this country.”

News.title: Fifa’s Gianni Infantino is drunk on power and behaving like a Mafia Don – but football doesn’t belong to him
News.content:
The Wadfather

DRUNK on power and swimming in cash extracted from footie fans, Fifa’s Gianni Infantino is behaving like a Mafia Don.

His plan to sell off shares in the World Cup for £15billion has rightly led to global shock and outrage.



Condemnation from the FA and Uefa was swift and absolute.

Fifa, they warned, was gambling with “the soul” of the people’s sport.



Scheming Infantino is unlikely to be easily deterred in his relentless pursuit of money.

He is bribing less powerful federations with £30million each if they sign up to his sell-off. The weak men at the Czech FA have already folded.



Other administrations, especially from poorer nations in Africa and Asia, are being blackmailed with a loss of future funding unless they agree to sign up within just 53 days.

Like a Thunderbirds puppet playing Don Corleone, Infantino clearly thinks he is making an offer they can’t refuse.

But his shameless attempts to turn the one true global game into a Godfather movie sequel must be fought off.

After all Infantino is forgetting one fact: football doesn’t belong to him.



Our Beautiful Game will never be defeated by one man’s megalomania.

No easy fix

QUITE how Andy Burnham will fix social care remains as much a mystery after his big speech as it was before.

The PM is the latest occupant of No10 in the last three decades to offer cross-party talks, launch a “national conversation” and vow to end the shameful treatment of the elderly and vulnerable.

But how exactly will he do it?

We won’t get any answers for at least a year while Burnham waits for Dame Louise Casey’s report into the system.



Whatever recommendations she ultimately makes will likely cost billions and see taxes going up. Burnham did, however, sensibly shut down the debate on assisted dying.

Campaigners, who have made their case with great determination, will be disappointed. But Burnham is right that a badly drafted law sanctioning state killing is the last thing an already overwhelmed NHS needs.

The priority must be to deliver proper palliative care.

What’s le plan?

DURING the weeks when high winds across the Channel kept illegal migrants at bay, Labour MPs were quick to boast that the small boats were being stopped.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

They’re not crowing now. Calm waters saw more than 900 arrive last week and as many as 1,000 as French cops largely stood by and watched.



How many more unvetted young men must arrive before Andy Burnham realises that Labour’s “plan” isn’t working?

News.title: Clicky Ponting reaction would be the same in any match, going against Brits’ sense of fair play is why we abhor cheats
News.content:
WELL, it’s simply not cricket.

The “gentleman’s game” that spread the notion of fair play across the British Empire is mired in an alleged cheating scandal centred on a portly bloke from Saltburn.



The grave accusation facing auction house company secretary Brian Devine is that he clicked his fingers to trick umpires into thinking that batsmen had edged the ball.

It led him to be christened Clicky Ponting after former Australia skipper Ricky Ponting.



After all, the win-at-all-costs Aussies have their own brazen and ignoble tradition of shredding the rule book.

Devine, 38, who has been suspended by Saltburn Cricket Club, is alleged to have used the shabby con trick on the North Yorkshire circuit “for years”.



If proven, this skullduggery has blossomed in a sport that prides itself on being played within the Spirit of Cricket.

Respect for opponents and umpires has long been trumpeted by its lawmakers, the MCC, in this ancient pastime that was birthed on the village greens of Britain.

Today, cricket is the second most popular sport in the world with a fanbase of 2.5billion, most of them from the Indian subcontinent.

Yet England remains the cradle of the game and, some would like to think, its moral heartbeat.



It makes Devine’s alleged deception — which has made headlines across the globe — so galling to many.

Asked if there was any other explanation, apart from cheating, for his finger clicks, Devine said: “Naturally, I cannot comment on that.”

The opening batsman has now been dropped by his official sponsor, a Saltburn Indian restaurant called Spices.

Its proprietor Akmol Hussain said he was “very shocked and disgusted” and that the player had “damaged the reputation of cricket and my restaurant”.



Others weighed in too.

Piers Morgan, a keen fan of Britain’s national summer sport, insisted: “Unbelievable. Clicky Ponting must be the biggest cheat in cricket history.”

While Georgina Vaughn, the mother of Devine’s partner Clare, insisted: “It was only a little village cricket match and now it’s become this thing that’s all over the news and social media.

“It has got totally out of hand and there is nothing any of us want to say.”



Devine’s alleged clicking was spotted when Saltburn’s second XI took on Norton in Division Two of the North Yorkshire and South Durham League on Saturday.

Saltburn confirmed they have suspended the player for the “foreseeable future”, adding that they are treating the allegations “with the utmost seriousness”.

For many, it won’t matter a jot that this was a lowly amateur contest rather than a high-octane Ashes clash at Lord’s.

The principles of British decency and fairness should remain sacrosanct.

We are a country — at all levels of society — that plays by the rules.



It’s woven into our fabric, from forming orderly queues to paying taxes.

Our international reputation as a land that zealously upholds our democratic freedoms rests on it.

And our ingrained sense of fair play is why many of us abhor cheats.

When the Argentinians were using the full range of their dark arts to try to rattle England’s players in the World Cup semi-final, Three Lions fans were rightly aggrieved.

Diego Maradona’s Hand of God was regarded here not as some crafty piece of gamesmanship, but as a disgusting act of duplicity.



When “Coughing Major” Charles Ingram was convicted of cheating on a 2001 episode of Who Wants to be a Millionaire?, it led to public vilification.

People taunted him with cries of “cough” and “cheat” because they felt they’d been conned.

If the accusations against Saltburn’s Devine stack up, how will it compare to other sporting con jobs?



Marathon runner Fred Lorz pulled a fast one at the 1904 Olympics in St Louis, Missouri.

In 32C heat, and cloying humidity on a hilly course, American Lorz decided to hitch a lift in a car for 11 miles before rejoining the race.

Flashing across the winning line in a time of 3hrs 13mins, he was found out shortly before the gold medal was hung around his neck.

Golf, which prides itself on self-regulation by its players, isn’t immune to those trying to scam a result.

At the 1985 Open in Deal, Kent, Scottish golfer David Robertson was caught repeatedly marking where his ball was on the green, putting it in his pocket, then placing it back down as much as 20 feet closer to the hole.



He was banned for 20 years from playing as a pro.

Cricket has also had its share of rule breakers.

In 1771, Thomas White walked in to bat at a match in Surrey with a bat “fully as wide as the wicket itself”.

The rules were changed two days later limiting the size.

The infamous Bodyline Ashes series of 1932 saw England’s bowlers aim at the body and head of Australian batsmen in an attempt to nullify their star player Don Bradman.



Former England cricket captain Mike Brearley quipped years later of the then skipper: “Jardine won the Ashes but nearly lost an Empire.”

Again, laws of the game were changed.

In 1981, Australian Trevor Chappell famously bowled the last ball underarm to prevent New Zealand potentially hitting the six they needed to draw the game.

Australia won the match, and it led to another rule change.

The Aussies were up to it again in 2018, when captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner were caught using sandpaper to rough up one side of the ball to make it swing more in the air in a Test against South Africa.



Smith later broke down in tears as he apologised at a press conference.

Now Saltburn’s Devine faces a possible reckoning.

The North Yorkshire and South Durham League has launched an investigation.

If the English cricketer now as famous as Ben Stokes is found to have hoodwinked umpires, the rulebook must be thrown at him.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A points deduction and ban must follow.



For cheats must never be allowed to prosper, whether it’s in the cauldron of international sport or Yorkshire village cricket.

News.title: Shocking moment serial killer spars in street with teens just hours before he killed man & chopped up his body
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment serial killer James Desborough is filmed fighting teens in the street – just hours before he murdered his second victim.

Footage shows the psycho ex-builder, convicted of sadistically killing three men, sparring with teenagers in Truro, Cornwall.



The videos were taken on June 3 last year – the last day victim Daniel Coleman was seen alive – while the pair were on a pub crawl in the city.

Desborough, 40 – fan of serial killer TV show Dexter – is seen with a moustache scrapping with two young men and a young woman in the cobbled Boscawen Street in the city centre.



Wearing black shorts and a jumper he is seen flailing as he parrys blows and throws slaps at the teens.

He takes on a young woman with black hair with his hands behind his back as he tries to dodge but is slapped in the face.



Just hours later he took Coleman back to his lair in the woods in the Cornish hamlet Sticker where he killed him, chopped up his body, cremated it and buried it in a shallow grave.

Winchester Crown Court heard how Desborough had three “explosions of fatal violence” towards vulnerable and weaker men.



The muscly and intimidating dad-of-one was staying at a centre for recovering addicts in Newquay early last year where he met Coleman, 43, and Claudio Aquilino, 57.

While living at the centre Desborough slept with Mr Coleman’s wife, though the two remained friends and after they left the centre they both lived at Desborough’s cabin in Paramoor Woods in Sticker, Cornwall, in spring 2025.

They were joined by a number of other residents, including Mr Aquilino, who would intermittently stay on the land.

But Desborough became angry with the people staying with him and on May 30, he sent a text saying he was “bloodthirsty” and “real hostile” to one of his friends.

Chillingly, a week earlier, Desborough had told Daniel he was a “fing r*d” and warned him: “Don’t take me for a mug, boy.”



That was the same date Mr Aquilino became a missing person.

Desborough killed Mr Coleman in the early hours of June 4 after getting him drunk on the pub crawl in Truro.

Police searched Desborough’s land after the men were declared missing and they found 1,900 burnt bone fragments belonging to Mr Aquilino at the stream.



A shallow grave was also found in which Mr Coleman’s burnt and dismembered body was found next to a can of petrol.

Desborough smiled in court as the jury gave their guilty verdict.

While in jail awaiting trial for the murders, Desborough strangled his third victim, cell mate Steven Kempster, because he was irritated by his snoring.

Mr Justice Saini, who sentenced James Desborough, 40, at Winchester crown court, said the circumstances of the case were unique.

Handing Desborough a rare whole-life order, he said the killer was a highly dangerous person who had considered his victims “worthless”.



The judge said Desborough killed his two friends because they were vulnerable, homeless, physically slight individuals who he considered would not necessarily be missed given their chaotic personal lives.

“I also find you did not consider them to be worthy of respect as humans,” the judge said.

Saini added that a whole-life order was a “last resort”, used only when the seriousness of a case was “exceptionally high”.



During the sentencing hearing, emotional victim statements were read out that made clear the men who were killed were loved and did have worthwhile lives.

Coleman’s 14-year-old daughter said: “I love him. I was a daddy’s girl; now I can’t be. It hurts to see I’ll never see him smile again.”

She said it terrified her to think her father would have been frightened when he was killed and told Desborough he was a “miscreant killer”.

More than 700 officers and scientists were involved in the 175-day search of the woods, with Devon and Cornwall police drawing on resources from five other forces.

The weather was very hot and the nature of the terrain jungle-like and boggy.



Cops sometimes had to wade through water up to their chests as they searched.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Aquilino’s family said he had been a talented artist and a good cook, although addiction problems had made his life very difficult.

Aquilino and Coleman, who suffered from long-term addictions, had previously lived with Desborough at a homeless hostel in the Cornish surfing hotspot of Newquay.

News.title: Man convicted on terrorism charges for 2022 stabbing attack on author Salman Rushdie
News.content:
Man convicted on terrorism charges for 2022 stabbing attack on author Salman Rushdie

A jury has found Hadi Matar guilty of all the charges against him, including engaging in an act of transnational terrorism - he is already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence on an attempted murder conviction

View 4 Images Salman Rushdie lost sight in one of his eye following the attack (Image: Getty Images for PEN America)

A man has been convicted of federal terrorism charges in connection to the 2022 stabbing of author Salman Rushdie.

A jury found Hadi Matar guilty of all the charges against him, including engaging in an act of transnational terrorism.

Matar, 28, is already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence on an attempted murder conviction in the August 2022 attack on an amphitheatre stage.

View 4 Images The writer said he has struggled since the attack to write again (Image: Getty Images)

The federal conviction carries a potential life sentence.

Rushdie has faced a decades-old death threat over one of his books.

In August 2022, before he was was about to speak on writers' safety, Rushdie was slashed 15 times in front of a stunned audience.

He was gravely wounded and lost the sight in his right eye.

View 4 Images Rushdie was airlifted to hospital where he spent 6 weeks (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

In 2025, Rushdie detailed the horrific attack in which he was repeatedly stabbed by the masked man on a stage.

Rushdie testified that he initially thought the perpetrator was going to punch him.

"I only saw him at the last minute," Rushdie said.

"I was aware of someone wearing black clothes, or dark clothes and a black face mask.

"I was very struck by his eyes, which were dark and seemed very ferocious."

View 4 Images Medics and doctors rushed to the stage (Image: Twitter)

Article continues below

Rushdie only realised that the attacker was wielding a knife when saw blood on his clothes.

He recalled lying on stage in "an enormous quantity of blood" that led to a "sense of great pain and shock."

He testified, "It occurred to me that I was dying. That was my predominant thought."

News.title: Morrisons message to customers as 100 stores could shut over 'cost pressures'
News.content:
Morrisons message to customers as 100 stores could shut over 'cost pressures'

Morrisons is planning to shut about 100 lossmaking convenience stores as the supermarket faces cost pressures it says have been worsened by “Government policy”

View Image Around 100 Morrisons stores are set to close (Image: Getty Images)

Shoppers told which Morrisons supermarkets are "subject to review" as two are to close.

‌



Morrisons is planning to shut about 100 lossmaking convenience stores as the supermarket faces cost pressures it says have been worsened by “Government policy”.

‌



And the supermarket chain has now confirmed the closure of two of two stores in Blackpool, the one on Central Drive shut first on July 12 followed by another located on Lytham Road.

‌



Free apples in Tesco for next few weeks for certain customers at 800 stores READ MORE :

"The performance of all company owned stores across our Convenience business is subject to continuous review, a Morrisons spokesperson told the Blackpool Gazette.

"This process has identified a number of stores, which were part of the McColl’s acquisition, whose performance has been challenged for a number of years and which are loss making, despite remedial action.

"Having completed the review, we are now proposing to take the tough but necessary decision to close a number of these stores over the next few months."

‌



In May, Morrisons said that the proposals would see stores closed over the following months and hundreds of shop workers were understood to be at risk of redundancy.

The particular Government policy choices, the supermarket claimed had worsened cost pressures were also not detailed, but it comes at a time when many retailers have faced rising business costs including higher minimum wages and last year’s national insurance rate hike.

A Morrisons spokesperson said at the time: "This situation has been exacerbated in more recent years by significant cost increases resulting from Government policy choices, which have made returning these stores to profitability even more difficult.

‌



“Having completed the review, we are now proposing to take the tough but necessary decision to close a number of these stores over the next few months.”

Morrisons has around 1,700 convenience shops as well as about 500 supermarkets, and employs some 95,000 staff.

Alongside the fresh closure plans, however, Morrisons stressed that it was still spotting opportunities to open hundreds more franchise convenience stores in the years ahead. It also insisted that the planned closures and the targeting of new shops will be “improving the quality of our convenience estate and making it stronger overall”.

Article continues below

Recently, the retailer has also shut some of its cafes, convenience stores, florists, and fresh food counters as part of a shake-up which led to the loss of hundreds of jobs.

The Mirror has contacted Morrisons for comment.

News.title: Major Hollywood producer arrested over alleged $100 million Ponzi scheme
News.content:
Major Hollywood producer arrested over alleged $100 million Ponzi scheme

Jason Cloth is accused of defrauding investors out of more than $100 million by using false promises to lure them into funding film projects and a gaming platform

View 2 Images Jason Cloth (Image: Max Cisotti/Dave Benett/WireImage)

A Hollywood film producer behind the Oscar-winning hit Joker is accused of masterminding a Ponzi scheme that defrauded clients out of more than $100 million (£75 million).

‌



Jason Cloth, 60, is accused of using his Canadian company, Creative Wealth Media Finance Corp, to lure investors into backing film projects and a gaming platform with false promises about the value and performance of their investments.

‌



Federal prosecutors allege the scheme ran from 2019 until this year, with Cloth fraudulently obtaining more than $100 million from an Illinois-based investment adviser, the adviser's clients and other investors.

‌



It is claimed the operation worked as a Ponzi scheme, with money from newer investors allegedly being used to repay earlier ones, according to the US Attorney Office for the Northern District of Illinois.

View 2 Images Cloth at the UK Premiere of Babylon in 2023 (Image: Max Cisotti/Dave Benett/WireImage)

Prosecutors also alleged some of the cash was diverted towards other ventures, including a real estate development in Canada.

‌



Cloth, of Beverly Hills, has been charged with seven counts of wire fraud in Chicago, authorities said on Wednesday. He was arrested Tuesday and made his initial court appearance in Los Angeles.

If convicted, he could face up to 20 years behind bars on each count. Prosecutors are also seeking the forfeiture of at least $12.25 million (£9.2 million).

The arrest comes two years after Cloth was ordered to pay $19.6 million in a separate civil fraud case in Florida, according to Variety.

‌



He failed to appear for the trial, where a jury found he had defrauded an investor in The Pathway - a TNT documentary series about the NDA draft - out of $6.6 million.

The jury also awarded an extra $13 million in punitive damages.

Alongside Joker, starring Joaquin Phoenix, IMDb credits Cloth as a producer on several other major films, including Babylon, Longlegs, Ghostbusters: Afterlife and The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare.

Article continues below

In addition to his work on Joker, Cloth has also been involved in films such as Longlegs, Babylon, and Ghostbusters: Afterlife.

News.title: France wildfires live: Three firefighters dead after scorching heatwave threatens nuclear plant
News.content:
A scorching heatwave threatens to force the closure of the Golfech nuclear power plant in south-west France just days after operations at the site resumed following a 17-day shutdown

Three firefighters have died tackling wildfires in Greece as high winds have seen blazes spread across Crete and mainland Greece after days of devastation in France and Spain.

Two firefighters perished after becoming trapped in a blaze near the village of Krya Vrysi in Crete, while another died fighting a separate wildfire in the Peloponnese region, local media reports.

“The wind is unbelievable – you can’t stand sometimes. The flames were huge, it was really scary," resident Chrissa Gioukaki told reporters.

Meanwhile, a scorching 42C heatwave threatens to worsen wildfires and force the closure of a nuclear power plant in south-west France just days after it came back online.

The Golfech nuclear power plant was shut down for 17 days after temperatures in the River Garonne, from which the plant draws water to cool its reactors, approached the regulatory limit of 28C. But France's latest heatwave - its hottest one so far - once again forced state-owned electricity company EDF to shut the plant down again.

Meanwhile, astonishing arrests have been made as firefighters continue to battle wildfires that have ravaged 42,000 hectares of south-west France and spread into parts of the Bordeaux metropolitan area. More than 220,000 people in the Gironde region have been evacuated over the past week in what has been France's largest peacetime evacuation.

Two men were arrested several days ago on suspicion of "stealing food and supplies" intended for those affected by the wildfires, the broadcaster reported. Officers have been standing outside evacuation centres and fire-ravaged areas to keep people safe and ensure restricted zones are protected.
