News.title: Moment people run in terror from Japanese mall after it explodes in 7.1 magnitude quake 'bomb'
News.content:
Moment people run in terror from Japanese mall after it explodes in 7.1 magnitude quake 'bomb'

The new footage captured by a car dashcam as the vehicle passed the Aeon Mall in Kumamoto, Japan, shows debris being flung into the road following a suspected gas explosion

Shoppers Flee Mall That Partially Collapsed After Japanese Earthquake

Horror new footage has captured the moment people ran in terror following a 7.1 magnitude earthquake in Japan.

‌



Three mall workers have died and a further three remain unaccounted for at the Aeon Mall Kumamoto, in Kashima City, Kyushu prefecture, Japan, after the strong earthquake struck on Tuesday morning. Video taken by a passing car dashcam showed the shopping centre bursting outwards and towards the street, leaving a massive hole in the building's frontage.

‌



Harrowing clips taken by people inside the building at the time captured the panic as they fled for safety during the early morning incident ahead of an emergency search and rescue operation.

‌



Japan earthquake death toll at 13 as rescuers scramble to reach people trapped READ MORE :

View 4 Images People ran in fear following a quake 'explosion' on Tuesday (Image: Daily Mirror/@yuto4388/Fumika Ono)

Another video, taken from inside the Aeon mall, showed panicked locals running for safety after the earthquake reportedly triggered an explosive gas leak. People could be heard audibly terrified as they ran for safety, with debris seen scattered inside as a cameraman's shaky hands panned around the scene.

According to local reports, rescuers entering the mall to carry out an urgent operation noted smelling gas inside the building.

‌



And a TV correspondent reporting from the site said an emergency vehicle had repeatedly urged people not to go near the site due to a potential leak.

View 4 Images Debris from the quake could be seen scattered inside the mall (Image: Daily Mirror/@yuto4388/Fumika Ono)

Minoru Kihara, Japan's top government spokesperson, said however that the cause of the incident has not yet been confirmed, with investigations still ongoing. Mr Kihara said the mall was using liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), transported in large canisters instead of a pipeline.

‌



Piped and LPG gas systems are designed to shut down during strong earthquakes or suspected leaks. Aeon's leadership said a gas explosion could not have been foreseen.

After it opened more than 20 years ago, spokespeople for the mall said it sustained damage in the 2016 Kumamoto earthquake, and was then renovated in line with Japanese updated seismic standards. Around 3,000 people were evacuated to one of the mall's parking lots before the suspected gas explosion took place in a part of the mall where some people were working.

View 4 Images The shopping mall collapsed following a serious 7.1 magnitude earthquake

‌



Three people who remain missing following the earthquake and explosion are also believed to have been employees. Soldiers and emergency workers are still combing through the badly damaged mall and badly damaged homes in southwestern Japan following the earthquake.

It has killed 18 people so far, among them a foreigner. At least 62 people have been injured, six of them seriously, the prefectural government of Kyushu said.

The tally has been steadily growing, and there are fears that it will only continue to rise given the earthquake hit at a time the mall was bustling with thousands of people. Nearly 34,900 homes were still without electricity and some 15,000 homes without running water, Kumamoto officials said.

Article continues below

View 4 Images Rescue workers continue searching at the damaged AEON Mall (Image: undefined/Kyodo News via AP)

More than 8,800 people left their homes to stay in over 400 shelters, where power sources were being added to provide air conditioning.

Aerial police footage showed some homes in residential areas were completely flattened, including a few that crumbled into a nearby river. Japan’s Self Defense Forces joined rescue workers in the search and rescue operations. Hundreds of professionals were helping with the effort, including firefighters from Taiwan.

News.title: Donald Trump piles pressure on Andy Burnham before unleashing racist diatribe about UK
News.content:
Donald Trump piles pressure on Andy Burnham before unleashing racist diatribe about UK

Trump has seized upon reports that Burnham is considering granting new licences for North Sea drilling - an issue the US President has long been vocal about - but then his comments took a much darker turn

View Image Trump invoked language used by white supremacists (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Donald Trump piled more pressure on Andy Burnham to open up the North Sea for oil and gas drilling, before launching into a racist diatribe about the UK.

‌



Trump has seized upon reports that Burnham is considering granting new licences for drilling - an issue the US President has long been vocal about.

‌



Asked for his impressions of the new Prime Minister, Trump said: "He did say one good thing, he said he's going to open up the North Sea. If he does that, you're going to be a wealthy country, if he does that reasonably."

‌



Trump's desire to see more drilling in the North Sea stems from a decades old feud with the Scottish government, after they approved a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course.

Later in the Oval Office Q&A Trump was asked if he and Burnham had discussed immigration during their phone call last week.

"I did, briefly," he said. "He's going to have to mention it because it's killing your country."

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

He then went on to repeatedly describe immigration to the UK as an "invasion", a narrative that has long been a staple of far right, Neo-nazi propaganda.

He has frequently used language related to the "great replacement", a conspiracy theory that was once a fringe idea, but is becoming the mainstream view of the Republican Party. It claims white populations and western culture are being deliberately diluted and replaced through migration. This is frequently described in terms of "invasion."

‌



In the Oval Office, Trump said: "They're coming from Africa, they're coming from South America, they're coming from different parts of Asia, and they're invading Europe. They're invading Europe! It's an invasion. And the UK is a prime suspect."

Last month during a speech in Normandy to commemorate the anniversary of D-Day, Trump's 'Secretary of War' Pete Hegseth used similar language, comparing migrant boat crossings to the invasion of the Nazis.

"Sadly, today different European beaches are stormed by different dangerous ideologies," he said. "Beaches in Spain, in Italy, in Greece, and Bulgaria, boats and men arrive. When will European capitals do something about that invasion? Or is it too late?"

‌



How Trump's administration flirts with white nationalist imagery and slogans

His administration has long flirted with white supremacist and neo nazi imagery and rhetoric. It started with the Department of Homeland Security, but has spread to several departments - and even the White House itself.

At first glance, this looks like an alarmist - even conspiratorial - thing to suggest. And to begin with, it was all a little ambiguous. In his first term, photos would emerge of members of his administration making the "OK" hand gesture - which was seen by many as code for "White Power". Then there was the rally on the day of Trump's inauguration, where Elon Musk stood in front of thousands of his fans and made a gesture which he insisted meant "my heart goes out to you", but looked to many like something much more sinister. And in his first year since being unexpectedly returned to office, there have been too many dogwhistles, nods, coded signs and outright lifts from the rhetoric of historical racists to discount it.

Last August, the Department for Homeland Security (DHS) Twitter account posted a recruitment tweet for ICE agents. The text read: "Which way, American man?" It accompanied a painting of Uncle Sam at a crossroads, with the different destinations marked as "cultural decline", "homeland", "service", "invasion", "opportunity" and "law and order".

Article continues below

The phrase "Which way, American man?" is a pretty clear reference to "Which way, western man", the title of a 1978 book by neo-Nazi William Gayley Simpson. The book contains passages arguing Hitler was right, and calling for violence against Jews in order to "break their grip" on "the White man's world".

In October, the DHS Twitter account posted a tweet that read: "America for Americans. We are asleep no longer." The phrase has long been linked to what could charitably be referred to as America's "nativist" movement. From the 1920s it started to be used by white supremacist groups, chiefly, the Ku Klux Klan.

In another ICE recruitment ad posted by DHS, the phrase "We'll have our home again" appears prominently. The phrase is the title of an anthem, popular among the "Mannerbund", a white separatist, white nationalist men's movement. The phrase, and song, has also been used by the Proud Boys and UK based racist group Patriotic Alternative.

News.title: Major UK homeware brand launches 'everything must go' sale as 23 stores closing
News.content:
Major UK homeware brand launches 'everything must go' sale as 23 stores closing

Topps Tiles has slashed prices at its Cheam store ahead of its final day with the company closing 23 of its shops around the country due "consumer sentiment" and the economy

View Image Topps Tiles is closing 23 stores (Image: PA Media)

A much-loved homeware retailer is set to close a London outlet within days as part of 23 UK closures.

‌



Topps Tiles has slashed prices at its Cheam store ahead of its final day on August 7, as it looks to make savings across the board with a broader closure programme.

‌



Locals have reported "everything must go" signs popping up in the windows of the popular branch, which was praised as "great" with "helpful" staff. This closure forms part of a wider list of 23 due to shut this year.

‌



In April, the brand confirmed it would close an additional 15 stores this year, on top of eight previously announced, representing 7% of its estate.

Free apples in Tesco for next few weeks for certain customers at 800 stores READ MORE :

Topps Tiles chief executive Alex Jensen stated the closures were being implemented to "support year-on-year growth and provide a stronger financial platform for 2027 and beyond", reports the Express.

He said: "In light of subdued consumer sentiment and geopolitical uncertainty, as well as the cumulative impact of cost inflation, the management team is implementing a targeted programme of self-help measures weighted towards the second half."

‌



In April the company said the stores that have been selected for closure are under-performing with all those due to shut, closing their doors before the end of October.

The retailer has not disclosed which sites will be closed. Topps Tiles said the closures would help slash costs as part of “significant self-help measures”.

The group, headquartered in Enderby, Leicestershire, revealed sales dipped 0.1% to £142.7million in the six months to March 28, with revenues hit by a "lengthy" competition process and disposal programme following its acquisition of rival CTD Tiles in 2024.

Article continues below

It had purchased competitor CTD out of administration in 2024, but a Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) investigation compelled Topps Tiles to offload several branches due to competition worries. The firm also acquired rival Fired Earth out of administration in December 2025 for £3million.

Numerous major retailers have downsized their high street presence over the past few years, with stalwarts like WHSmith concentrating on airports and travel locations rather than the high street.

Major banks, such as Santander and Lloyds, have also closed physical locations as customers shift towards online banking.

News.title: More than half of England in drought, Environment Agency declares
News.content:
Drought has been declared across more than half of England as hot, dry weather takes its toll on the country's water supplies.

The Environment Agency (EA) announcement covers much of central, eastern and southern England, and is a public sign that further restrictions on water use might follow.

It added that the impacts are already being felt, including low river flows, early harvests and high risk of wildfires. More than 20 million people are already under hosepipe bans.

North Wales and the Upper Severn river basin entered drought conditions last week, Natural Resources Wales said.

Scotland does not declare drought but monitors "water scarcity". Some parts of eastern Scotland are in the most extreme category of "significant scarcity", according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.

Northern Ireland is not currently in drought.

News.title: Moment police officers set foot in 'horror scene' funeral home
News.content:
This story contains details some might find distressing

Boxes of tissues sit on a coffee table in a front room at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors. There are opulent chairs, upholstered in pale yellow; a black and white print of a trawler that nods to Hull's fishing heritage.

It feels like an attempt to put customers at ease, painting the picture of a caring, community-led business.

But on the other side of a partition wall - an area Legacy's director Robert Bush ordered an employee to keep hidden from others in the industry - is a labyrinth of dimly-lit corridors.

A police officer shines her torch into messy side rooms, strewn with rubbish and in total disorder.

"It's strange, innit?" she remarks.

News.title: Police to take no further action against Polanski over guillotine re-post
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has said it will take no further action against Green Party leader Zack Polanski after he re-posted a photo of a man wearing a T-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel".

In a statement, the force said it did not believe sharing the picture constituted an offence.

A Green Party spokesperson said it was "obvious from the start" that no crime had been committed, and said Reform UK was "using this as a political football for their own cynical purposes" as a distraction.

In response to the Met's decision, a Reform UK spokesman said: "Once again we see that we are living in two-tier Britain."

"Zack Polanski is allowed to get away with inciting murder whilst ordinary people up and down the country get a knock at the door for making a joke online."

The Met said after careful review it had concluded it was unlikely the sharing of the image online would constitute a criminal offence.

It said the post has been shared by about 130 accounts and the police should not treat individuals differently based on their public profile, meaning any investigation would have to consider all those accounts too.

"Given it is unlikely their actions would have ultimately constituted an offence, such an extensive investigation was deemed to do be disproportionate and not a reasonable use of police resources."

While the Met Police said it would not be taking further action over the sharing of the image, it said it had determined that a crime should be recorded in relation to the wearing of the T-shirt and had referred a crime report to Avon and Somerset Police, who cover Bristol where the photo was taken.

Shortly after the Met Police's statement, Avon and Somerset Police said "the threshold for a criminal offence has not been met".

Setting out its decision, the Avon and Somerset Police said: "Particular consideration has been given to the context around the image; its use of song lyrics, and the marketing of the T-shirt as a satirical piece.

"No complaints were received from people at the event at which it was worn and there is no evidence the wearer of the T-shirt intended to threaten any individual, or encourage anyone else to do so."

The force added they it took the safety of elected politicians "extremely seriously" and it would continue to take action "wherever a threat is identified".

News.title: Limiting sugar before age two linked to better brain health
News.content:
"They may be onto something," said Rachel Richardson, the methods support unit lead for evidence production and methods directorate at Cochrane, an independent non-profit network that gathers and summarises medical research.

However, she said this "does not represent a smoking gun" linking early sugar intake to dementia.

One big issue is, it is impossible to know how much sugar each of the people in the study were actually eating, merely when they were born relative to sugar rationing.

"This evidence relates to people born in the 1940s and 1950s and so its applicability to young children today is limited - for example, weaning took place earlier and this would have a large impact on the early nutrition of babies and children," said Richardson.

Prof Ian Maidment, professor of clinical pharmacy at Aston University, said: "It is an interesting idea, it helps inform debate, but in my opinion we need more evidence."

He said connecting "something that happened 80 years ago" and projecting that onto health now meant there were "loads" of other factors that could be playing a role.

Dr Sara Rodrigues, from Alzheimer's Research UK, said: "It's important to remember that this was an observational study.

"This means it can identify links between diet and dementia risk, but it cannot prove that eating less sugar directly prevents dementia.

"Eating a healthy, balanced diet is one of the best ways to support your brain health and it's never too late to make positive changes."

News.title: Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care
News.content:
In an emotional speech he praised those caring for his father, who has Alzheimer's, and said he wanted to deliver changes to help "my dad and the millions like him".

Speaking to reporters afterwards, he said he wanted to extract more from existing budgets to fund the reforms.

"I think we owe it to the public before we talk about tax rises.. you first have to look the public in the eye and say 'Are we doing everything we can do from within what we've got?'"

For example, he said his announcements on improving pay and training for the social care workforce "will be fully funded".

But he added that fuller reforms "will require difficult decisions" and these "would be put before the country at the right time, and we will hopefully proceed with people's consent".

Burnham said in "an ideal world" he would not want anyone to have to sell their home to pay for care, describing it as a "really awful process".

He added proposals he previously put forward, when he was health secretary in 2009, were intended to stop that, saying: "If everybody on the NHS principle contributed a little, it would mean everybody could protect the majority of what they'd worked for."

He later held talks with Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey and Conservative shadow health secretary Stuart Andrew as part of efforts to get cross-party backing for any changes. Tory leader Kemi Badenoch was unavailable.

The Conservatives have previously urged the prime minister to rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to pay for social care changes.

Speaking to the BBC's Radio 4 PM, Andrew said it had been important to set "red lines" around funding.

He acknowledged finding funding would be a "challenge" but added that there was "a significant amount of money in the system - it's just sometime it is not in the right place".

Burnham did not invite the leaders of Reform UK or the Green Party of England and Wales to the talks. Both parties have expressed disappointment at this.

The PM said there was a feeling at Westminster that social care was "too big a political risk" to deal with, adding he wants to take on the challenge as the "risks of failing to act are too great".

Burnham highlighted the financial impact of care costs on people and spoke of how fixing issues in social care could ease the pressure on the NHS and make savings.

The PM said Baroness Casey's review should consider how to pay for a national care service, adding there needs to a system that becomes "highly integrated" with the NHS.

Burnham said he wants to "immediately" focus on the social care workforce, noting a fair pay agreement is due to come into force from 2028/29 and described it as a "massive building block of a national care service".

News.title: Body of Scottish woman found inside suitcase in Greece
News.content:
The body of a Scottish woman has been found inside a suitcase in an abandoned building in Greece, prompting a multi-agency investigation.

Police Scotland confirmed they are liaising with authorities after the woman was reportedly discovered by a homeless man in the Kypseli district in Athens on 18 July.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, is thought to have travelled to Greece from Cyprus last month, state broadcaster ERT reports. She is believed to have died between five and seven days before she was found.

Greek police told BBC Scotland News the body of a British woman was found and fingerprint data from Interpol matched a woman born in 1988. Investigations are ongoing.

News.title: The athlete who has never held her Olympic medal
News.content:
Ngake was born in Douala, the largest city in Cameroon, around 200 miles to the west of the nation's capital Yaounde.

She is reluctant to reflect too much on that time, having distanced herself from thoughts of her homeland for more than a decade, but it is clear that childhood brought "challenges", many, many challenges. It is also clear that through sport, specifically weightlifting, she found a talent which could elevate her.

Ngake dreamed of not only personal success, but profound change. She aimed to help influence a shift in perceptions around female sport by showcasing the power of strong women in Cameroon.

At the Delhi 2010 Commonwealth Games, the then 18-year-old gave a glimpse of that potential. She placed fourth, achieving the same total as India's bronze medallist Laishram Devi but losing out on a podium place by virtue of weighing more than her rival.

Not that it was of immediate concern. Ngake left that contest on a stretcher, having passed out moments after a successful 121kg lift. It was a disappointing end to her Commonwealth debut, but there was still plenty of pride.

"Not just anybody can qualify for a Commonwealth Games," she smiles. "It means you're strong and, can I say, special?"

With resources limited, a situation not helped by the widely reported corruption scandals within several international federations in Cameroon, attending international competitions was extremely challenging.

As a result, she entered London 2012 with relatively low rank, which meant she was assigned to the B Final, with other athletes not considered to have realistic medal prospects.

However, she not only won the B Final, but lifted considerably more than many in the 'elite' division, securing an overall ranking of sixth. It was an achievement she considered to be "amazing" at the time, long before the results and placements were revised.

There was not time to celebrate that achievement, though. She needed to act quickly.

Exactly how the situation transpired is something, even 14 years on, Ngake is reluctant to discuss, but she is open about the impact of absconding.

"When I decided to stay, sometimes I would sleep on the bus, but when the bus stopped [for the night], I would sleep outside," she recalls with a shrug. "When I wanted to have a shower, I would maybe find a place outside, in public, so to change myself was not too easy."

That period lasted for around two months before she officially applied for asylum and was offered temporary accommodation while her case was reviewed.

Neither the Olympic Games nor any form of sport were in her mind. She was just focused on finding a way to make the UK her home.

Few around the weightlifter knew of her elite performance background and few would have even suspected it as the Olympian settled in to a more low-key existence.

Nearly five years passed before she was able to attain the correct paperwork to take on permanent paid employment. It meant starting at the bottom, but she was happy just to have the opportunity to build.

"At first, I was an office cleaner and yes, that was my full-time job for nine years," the now 34-year-old says. "I was in Leeds, then I moved to Nottingham."

She did not think about the sport she once loved for all that time.

But that changed four years ago.

With Durban stripped of the rights to host the 2022 Commonwealth Games after failing to meet key milestones or provide financial guarantees, Birmingham stepped in.

It meant some of Ngake's former team-mates and coaches from Cameroon would return to the UK themselves and for the first time in a decade she allowed her mind to dwell on weightlifting.

"One of my coaches was still with the team, travelling over for Birmingham 2022 and after he came to stay with me and kept pushing me to start again," she says.

"I'd stopped everything, but he encouraged me and when I did lift a bar again, yes, it felt so natural, it felt right and that was very exciting."

The following year she won gold at the British International and within a further 12 months she not only returned to the international stage, but landed a major career-first, with silver in the snatch discipline at the 2024 World Championships for Great Britain.

As a naturalised athlete, with proven major event medal-winning potential, she was now eligible for UK Sport funding, which soon arrived, enabling Ngake to give up her job as a cleaner and focus on being a full-time athlete.

European honours have followed and she headed into a second Commonwealth Games, 16 years on from her debut in India, as the top seed in the women's 86kg division.

News.title: Pictures show scale of drought across England as rivers dry up
News.content:
Drought has been declared across more than half of England as hot, dry weather takes its toll on the country's water supplies.

The announcement means there have been three droughts in the past five years - 2022, 2025 and now 2026.

Photos from across the country have captured some of the dry conditions - including receding rivers, parched parks and sportspeople trying to play on.

News.title: Serial killer given whole life orders for murders of two men as police investigate four more deaths
News.content:
Serial killer James Desborough has been given two whole life prison sentences with no chance of parole - as police revealed they are looking into four unexplained deaths at the homeless shelter that housed him.

Desborough, already serving a minimum of 19 years for the murder of his prison cellmate, was given the whole life tariffs for killing 57-year-old Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman, 43, in Cornwall.

Aquilino and Coleman met Desborough at Newquay's Sandy Lodge homeless shelter, where police are now reviewing the unexplained deaths of two other men and two women.

Sentencing, Mr Justice Pushpinder Saini described Desborough, 40, as "a highly dangerous individual who had no regard for the life of those you think are worthless".

Desborough befriended the two vulnerable men and used "extreme violence" on both of them, before dismembering and concealing their bodies, the judge said.

He said the former builder used their bank cards and made journeys to give the impression they were still alive.

News.title: Fix palliative care before assisted dying debate, says PM
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that before assisted dying is considered in England and Wales, the funding of palliative and social care should be "fixed".

It is the first time Burnham has set out his position on the issue since becoming prime minister, as MPs prepare to debate it again when Parliament returns in September.

The government is likely to remain officially neutral, but Burnham's remarks suggest he personally will not back a bill being proposed by Labour MP Lauren Edwards.

The position is a shift from that of former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, who voted in favour of the previous attempt to legalise assisted dying and gave time for the issue to be debated in Parliament.

Sir Keir's support was privately cited by some Labour MPs as a reason they backed the bill last time.

Burnham told reporters: "I take the view that that debate - and I don't say that there shouldn't be a debate at some point about those issues - personally, I think there's something that needs to happen first.

"That is the fixing of the funding of palliative care and social care.

"I think it is very challenging to introduce that wider debate in a context of people not receiving that care and having the peace of mind about that care."

In 2025, MPs voted in favour of a bill proposed by Labour MP Kim Leadbeater to legalise assisted dying.

But the bill was not passed by the House of Lords, after an unprecedented number of suggested amendments delayed its progress until it ran out of time in April this year.

Its opponents argued it had substantial flaws that risked vulnerable people being pressured into ending their lives early.

The proposed law - known as the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill - would have allowed people over the age of 18 who were expected to die within six months to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

Labour MP Lauren Edwards plans to bring forward an identical bill in order to "finish the job" started by Leadbeater.

Following Burnham's comments, she said improving social care and legalising assisted dying was "not a case of either/or" and that the two things "can and must go hand in hand".

"The bill that has been before Parliament and thoroughly debated since October 2024 provides for a four-year implementation period - that means if my current bill becomes law next year, we would have until 2031 to fix the status quo that Andy Burnham rightly says is broken."

Jess Asato - a Labour MP and opponent of the bill - said MPs had "a responsibility to consider the safety of introducing such a flawed bill into a broken and failing care system".

"There can be no meaningful choice and no dignity at the end of life if we don't have a palliative care system that provides basic support for the vulnerable and an affordable social care system that gives everyone dignity at the end of their lives."

Burnham was asked about his views on assisted dying after he had announced plans to reform the social care system, with the view to create a national care service and to reach a political consensus on how to fund it.

In 2024, just before the first Commons vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, Burnham told BBC Manchester he would "probably vote in favour of it" if he was in Parliament.

When he was previously an MP he abstained from a 2015 vote on another bill to legalise assisted dying because of concerns over safeguards and people feeling under pressure.

But he told the BBC in 2024 that he had had "family experience in the nine years since that has changed my view".

He said: "I think we do allow people to suffer and families to suffer too much."

He caveated his support as being for the principle of assisted dying and insisted he would want a requirement before any new law was implemented that hospices would be "properly funded and sorted out".

News.title: Peppa Pig owners win copyright battle against 'impostor' Wolfoo
News.content:
In a ruling this week, the judge said "all videos featuring Wolfoo" must be taken down before 16:00 BST on Monday.

Hasbro and Peppa Pig's creators Astley Baker Davies Ltd originally took court action in London in 2022.

They claimed SConnect had attempted "to deceive the young Wolfoo viewership, most aged between two and five, into believing that Wolfoo is the same character as Peppa Pig" or connected to Peppa, the judge wrote.

The companies initially complained about Wolfoo's appearance and artwork, but focused their legal case on the audio because they believed it would be easier to prove that sound clips were directly copied.

The evidence of "copying of the audio clips is compelling", the judge decided.

"That copying was extensive, seemingly endemic at least so far as the English language Wolfoo videos are concerned."

SConnect denied the copyright infringement claim but accepted that some Wolfoo videos made before mid-2020 included audio from Peppa Pig because an independent third-party contractor had used the clips without the company's knowledge.

SConnect said all infringing videos were removed, and that Wolfoo animations made after mid-2020 used only voices and sounds that were created in-house.

However, the judge said the fact the sounds were supplied by a third party was "irrelevant"; that while many infringing videos were removed, some were simply moved to other channels; and that the claim that all new sounds were recorded in-house "can be disproved".

BBC News has asked SConnect for comment.

The judge said clips from Peppa Pig were found in all 92 English-language Wolfoo videos that were examined, and about 75% of the foreign-language videos.

News.title: Libel claim against Matt Hancock thrown out
News.content:
In April last year at the High Court, Mrs Justice Collins Rice said she believed there were "compelling reasons for further investigation at trial" and refused Hancock's attempt to have the claim thrown out.

Earlier this year, Hancock appealed against that decision and Lord Justice Warby, sitting with Lady Justice King and Lady Justice Whipple at the Court of Appeal, said in a judgment on Wednesday that Mrs Justice Collins Rice had "erred in law".

"The Holocaust was a deliberate genocidal campaign to eradicate an entire people for motives of ethnic or religious prejudice. The Covid vaccine rollout was not," the judge said.

"On the undisputed facts it was, at least in part, a benevolent public health programme with the aim of saving lives."

He added that Bridgen's post "did not suggest that the vaccine rollout was worse than the Holocaust, but it did expressly suggest some form of comparability" and that it suggested the vaccines were a "crime against humanity".

Hancock was granted a summary judgment â a legal step which ends the claim in his favour without a trial.

Afterwards he said it was a case that "should never have been brought" and that "people must be free to state their own opinions without fear of libel action".

"I was right to call out what I clearly saw were anti-vax and antisemitic conspiracy theories, and this judgment reaffirms that right," he added.

Posting on X after the judgment, Bridgen said the three judges at the hearing in May were "clearly thinking about declaring me the winner".

He added: "Yet nine weeks later that same panel produced a unanimous written judgment in which they found against me on every single point, thus handing the victory to Mr Hancock without a trial, and labelling one of my arguments 'egregious', a point not put to my legal team at the oral hearing.

"It is hard to understand why the written judgment does not reflect what took place at the oral hearing."

Bridgen said he would be seeking advice to see if he could take the case to the Supreme Court.

News.title: Amy Winehouse's dad ordered to pay £1m by court
News.content:
Amy Winehouse's father must pay just under Â£1m to two of his daughter's friends after a failed High Court claim over the auctioning of the late singer's items.

Mitch Winehouse also racked up at least Â£950,000 in his own legal costs in the failed attempt against Naomi Parry and Catriona Gourlay.

He claimed the women had profited from selling dozens of his daughter's items at auctions in the US in 2021 and 2023, accusing them of having "deliberately concealed" their sale.

But Ms Justice Clarke threw out the claim earlier this year, finding that he "knew all along" about the intended sale and only afterwards had begun to pursue them for money in an "aggressive and unpleasant way".

In a judgment on Wednesday, she said: "The claimant chose to bring an inherently weak claim, pursue it aggressively and relentlessly to the end, and make serious and unfounded allegations against the defendants which significantly damaged their reputations, career prospects, financial security and health."

News.title: Boy, 7, dies in hospital after beach tragedy
News.content:
A seven-year-old boy has died in hospital after a beach tragedy that also killed his teenage cousin and her mother, his family has said.

Musa Ahmed was on a day trip to West Mersea, Essex, on 22 July, when he and five relatives got into difficulty in the water.

While he was pulled from the water and airlifted to hospital, Shelina Rahman, 41, and 15-year-old Sameeha, died at the scene.

Musa's family said he died "in a state of ease and peace" at the Royal London Hospital on Tuesday evening.

The family had travelled to the island, near Colchester, from Barking in east London that morning.

Three others were also taken to hospital by ambulance after the incident, first reported to Essex Police at 17:35 BST, and were said by the force to be "recovering".

Musa's father, Shahin Ahmed, has said they were swept away by a "very strong" tide and police said they made "significant efforts to help each other".

Posting on Facebook earlier, Ahmed said of his son: "He made every person feel special and never failed to bring happiness."

News.title: Man accused of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor threat faces December trial
News.content:
A man charged with threatening Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor near his home on the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk will stand trial in December.

Alex Jenkinson, 39, is accused of causing the former Duke of York to "fear unlawful violence" during an encounter as he walked his dogs on 6 May.

The trial - which will begin on 21 December - is expected to include evidence from Mountbatten-Windsor via videolink.

Jenkinson is accused of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour and had been due to stand trial on Wednesday. At Westminster Magistrates' Court, chief magistrate Paul Goldspring postponed proceedings over concerns about the defendant's mental health.

News.title: Chief constable resigns before misconduct tribunal
News.content:
The chief constable of Staffordshire Police has resigned, ahead of a gross misconduct hearing regarding his behaviour.

Chris Noble was suspended in August amid inquiries by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), with the watchdog confirming in March that it had opened two more investigations regarding his behaviour.

Noble resigned on Tuesday via a letter to the Police and Crime Commissioner for Staffordshire, Ben Adams.

The misconduct hearing began on Wednesday morning in Noble's absence and has since been adjourned.

He was chosen to lead Staffordshire Police after the retirement of the previous chief constable in 2021.

Prior to this, he was the assistant chief constable of Humberside Police.

In a statement, Staffordshire Commissioner for Police, Fire & Rescue and Crime, Ben Adams said: "I can confirm that yesterday [28 July], I received Chief Constable Chris Noble's resignation, which I have accepted with immediate effect.

"Becky Riggs will remain as Staffordshire Police's acting chief constable.

"The misconduct hearing will continue today as planned, under former officer provisions."

Staffordshire Police said that it would not be appropriate to comment due to ongoing misconduct proceedings.

In a recent statement, the IOPC said: "The chair of the panel has directed that no additional information relating to the detail of the allegations can be released at this time.

"We are continuing to investigate other allegations relating to Mr Noble. Given the sensitivity of those matters, for operational reasons, no further information can be provided at this time."

Major American carriers are expanding restrictions on high-tech travel companions, with Delta Air Lines and United Airlines becoming the latest companies to prohibit humanoid and animal-like robots from aircraft cabins and checked baggage.

The decisions follow a similar move by Southwest Airlines in May, which introduced its ban after a passenger boarded a flight with a robotic companion earlier this year. Airlines have cited general safety and operational concerns as carriers act to set boundaries around the emerging technology.

United instituted its restriction on July 23 as a proactive measure, noting that the policy was not prompted by a specific incident on its flights.

“We believe this change will help further ensure the safety of our customers and crews,” an airline spokesperson told The Independent, adding that lifelike robots often relied on heavy-duty batteries that were already prohibited on flights. The carrier will still allow other automated devices and select toys on board, as long as they adhere to existing baggage limits and battery safety protocols.

Delta implemented a similar policy on June 18, banning any devices built to imitate humans or animals in size, movement, appearance or behavior from both passenger areas and cargo compartments.

open image in gallery Delta Air Lines and United Airlines are the latest companies to prohibit humanoid and animal-like robots from aircraft cabins and checked baggage. The move follows Southwest’s ban on similar devices earlier this year ( AFP/Getty )

“Delta does not permit human- or animal-like robotic devices to be transported in the aircraft cabin or as checked baggage,” the airline said in a statement to The Independent. “We continually review emerging technologies and update our policies to maintain the highest safety standards.”

Delta noted that the prohibition applied specifically to devices powered by lithium batteries exceeding standard Federal Aviation Administration watt-hour limits. The carrier also clarified that these devices did not qualify for medical or accessibility exemptions.

“These items are not classified as assistive devices and do not meet the definition of a trained service animal under applicable regulations,” the airline’s statement said.

Standard toy robots remain permitted on Delta flights, provided they meet size limits for carry-on baggage, fit within FAA-approved storage areas and adhere to existing battery guidelines, according to the airline’s restricted items page.

open image in gallery Delta Air Lines said in a statement that the ban reflected an ongoing review of emerging technology, targeting devices with lithium batteries that exceeded standard FAA limits ( Getty Images )

Though humanoid robotics remain rare outside research laboratories and industrial facilities, tech companies continue to invest heavily in the sector. However, the requirement to transport these systems presents practical challenges for academics and engineers.

Ravinder Dahiya, a professor and roboticist at Northeastern University’s College of Engineering, told CBS News that large lithium-ion batteries posed genuine fire hazards if mishandled or damaged, but noted the complications the bans presented for fieldwork.

“When it comes to safety, I'm not opposed to the bans at all. But as a researcher, you desire to carry out your research freely, without hindrance,” Dahiya said, adding that “sometimes you have to take robots along with you for demonstrations.”

News.title: Burnham explains why £8.4bn nuclear submarine investment will boost UK defence, jobs and apprenticeships
News.content:

Andy Burnham is expected to unveil on Thursday an £8.4bn investment for the UK's next generation of nuclear submarines.

Aimed at preparing Dreadnought-class boats for service by the 2030s, the nuclear-armed vessels are set to replace the current Vanguard-class and will be equipped to launch Trident 2 D5 ballistic missiles.

Powered by a Rolls-Royce nuclear propulsion system, produced in Derby, the submarines will boast an almost unlimited operational range.

HMS Dreadnought is the first of four new submarines.

The funding will primarily support its progress towards readiness, with a portion also allocated to advance the second vessel, HMS Valiant, to its sea trials.

Manufacturers will also be supported to get the third and fourth boats through their construction phases.

Mr Burnham said: “Keeping this country safe is the first responsibility of any government.

“But security is not only about what we build, it is about who builds it, and who benefits from it.

“The submarines produced in Barrow will protect Britain for decades to come, and the 47,000 jobs and apprenticeships will change lives both in this town and in dozens of places like it.

open image in gallery Burnham said ‘keeping this country safe is the first responsibility of any government’ ( Getty )

“British money, spent on British workers, British firms and British skills, in the places that were written off for 40 years.

“To every young person across the country, I want you to know that there is a path for you into a reindustrialised Britain and it starts with the apprenticeships we are funding through this investment today.”

The prime minister’s announcement on Thursday will follow his pledge to tackle joblessness among young people.

On a visit earlier this week to Alstom, a rail manufacturer in Derby, Mr Burnham said the “first thing” he needed to do was stop the rise in young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).

The latest data, published in May, showed the number of young people aged 16-24 neither working nor learning passed 1 million for the first time since 2013, reaching 1.01 million in the three months from January to March.

“It would be wrong to blame the young people when we have an education system that doesn’t set them up properly, where some struggle to find opportunities at 16, where work experience and work placements aren’t there for them,” Mr Burnham said.

“We’ve got to put those building blocks in place, and then, in time, that number will come down.”

The wider UK Defence Nuclear Enterprise is thought to support around 47,000 jobs, including 9,000 in Aldermaston and Burghfield in Berkshire, 8,000 at Devonport naval base in Plymouth, and 13,500 at Barrow in Cumbria.

On the Dreadnought-class submarine programme, £5.9bn of the £8.4bn will go to BAE Systems, with £2.5bn for the wider supply chain.

Mr Burnham faces questions about his defence policies, including how he will pay for a commitment to reach 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence spending by 2035.

Asked at a press conference on Wednesday whether he would meet the commitment, the prime minister pointed to the deadline in the next decade.

“In terms of our Nato commitments, I have been very clear that we will honour those commitments,” he said. “It does mean being prepared to look at challenging issues.”

Mr Burnham’s pick for chancellor, John Healey, resigned as Sir Keir Starmer’s defence secretary last month, warning that the former prime minister was “unable, and the Treasury has been unwilling, to commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats”.

The Defence Investment Plan (Dip) which followed – including a pledge to fund the fitting of four Dreadnought submarines in Barrow – took expected total defence investment over the next four years to £298bn.

Defence spending by the end of the decade will be 2.7 per cent of GDP, according to the document.

It is thought the prime minister will hail Barrow as a case study for how taxpayer investment in major government projects can support opportunities in the long term throughout the UK.

Defence secretary Wes Streeting said: “Our nuclear-armed submarines are essential to keeping the UK secure, acting as the ultimate deterrent to our adversaries in an increasingly dangerous world.

open image in gallery Wes Streeting talks with military personnel during his visit to the UK Military's Permanent Joint Headquarters ( Adrian Dennis - WPA Pool/Getty Images )

“This milestone investment breathes new life into Barrow’s historic traditions and secures our commitment to deliver Dreadnought Class submarines by backing British industry.

“Supporting thousands of skilled local jobs, we are fusing Barrow’s proud heritage with modern technology to build our security for the future, supporting the next generation to keep our country safe as their parents and grandparents did.”

Shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge warned the money “would appear to be a reannouncement of funding previously confirmed in the Dip”, but added: “We nevertheless welcome continued progress on the Dreadnought programme.”

The Conservative frontbencher continued: “It’s concerning that there is still no detail at all on the big promise of the strategic defence review, which was the procurement of ‘up to 12’ attack submarines.

“The Dip was meant to clarify exactly what ‘up to 12’ meant but we are still none the wiser.

“At the same time, Burnham is adding to the uncertainty by failing to commit to the very pathway to 3 per cent which his chancellor demanded when he resigned as defence secretary.

“It’s welcome that we now have a consensus with the government on backing the nuclear deterrent and it’s right we send our adversaries the message that we are all behind the workforce of Barrow and Devonport, which supports and builds our submarines.

“Nevertheless, we hope that the chancellor and prime minister will respond to the threats we face by properly funding a pathway to 3 per cent [by 2030].”

Footage of Jared Leto joking about “high school girls” has resurfaced after four women accused him of sexual misconduct while they were teenagers.

The allegations of sexual assault, statutory rape, grooming and threats of sexual assault are made in a new BBC documentary, Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret.

The women interviewed in the film said they encountered the 54-year-old Oscar-winning actor and musician between 2002 and 2016, when they were each between 16 and 18 years old and he was in his 30s and 40s.

Leto has denied the allegations. In a statement to The Independent, he said: “I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life. These claims are absolutely and categorically false.”

The BBC film also includes a clip of Leto onstage with his band 30 Seconds to Mars at Ex’Pression College in Emeryville, California in 2013.

open image in gallery Jared Leto said in a statement to The Independent that he has 'never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life' ( Daniel Leal/AFP/Getty )

In the resurfaced footage, Leto can be seen inviting a young woman to join him onstage before saying: “Give me a hug, first of all,” and asking her name and where she is from.

After she told Leto that she was from Los Angeles, he impersonated Matthew McConaughey while quoting a line from the 1993 movie Dazed and Confused: “That’s what I like about high school girls. I keep getting older, they stay the same age. Alright, alright, alright.”

Leto first rose to prominence in the 1990s on the television drama My So-Called Life before winning the Academy Award for best supporting actor in 2014 for Dallas Buyers Club. He is also the lead vocalist of Thirty Seconds to Mars, the band he formed with his brother, Shannon, in 1998.

The most serious allegation in the new documentary comes from a woman using the pseudonym Isabel, who alleged Leto sexually assaulted her in a Las Vegas motel bathroom in 2002 when she was 17. “Most of my life I had viewed this event as, I was a stupid girl … and so this bad thing happened,” she told the BBC.

A second woman, identified as Alex, has alleged that Leto threatened her with sexual assault after inviting her to his hotel room following a Thirty Seconds to Mars concert in London in 2013. Alex, who said she was 19 but told Leto she was 17, alleged he replied: “Age is just a number, and anyway, we’re in Europe.”

She said she left after he repeatedly told her she would wake up “with a d*** in her a**”.

open image in gallery Leto attends the premiere of 'Tron: Ares' in 2025 ( Reuters )

Another woman, using the pseudonym Clara, alleged she first had sex with Leto at his California home in 2006 when she was 17 and he was 34. She alleged Leto dismissed a discussion about California's age of consent – which is 18 – and referred to her as “my little girl” while asking her to call him “daddy”.

A fourth woman, identified as Etta, alleged Leto groomed her after meeting her at a Los Angeles modeling agency in 2014, when she was 16. She told the BBC he later made repeated sexually explicit phone calls, asking whether she was a virgin and suggesting they should have sex.

Etta also alleged Leto later attempted to have her sign a non-disclosure agreement. The BBC said it had reviewed the unsigned agreement, along with related emails and text messages.

The investigation also includes accounts from five women who alleged they received sexually explicit phone calls from Leto while they were younger, four of whom said they were teenagers at the time.

Another woman, identified as Taylor, alleged that Leto made a lewd comment about her body and attempted to have a security guard take her backstage after she met him at a music festival when she was 14.

Two former members of Thirty Seconds to Mars’ crew also told the BBC they had been uncomfortable with what they described as Leto’s interactions with teenage girls backstage and at recording locations.

In 2025, an investigation by Air Mail revealed that nine women had accused Leto of sexual impropriety, several alleging they were under the age of consent at the time. The report came weeks after Los Angeles DJ Allie Teilz publicly alleged on social media that Leto assaulted her when she was 17, prompting several other women to come forward with similar claims.

Leto denied any wrongdoing at the time, saying through a representative: “All of the allegations are expressly denied.”

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, contact the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-HOPE (4673).

If you are in the UK, Rape Crisis offers support for those affected by rape and sexual abuse. You can call them on 0808 802 9999 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, and 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland, or visit their website at www.rapecrisis.org.uk.

Reform UK’s deputy leader in Scotland has reported one of the country’s most high-profile lawyers to police over a speech he made at a protest in Glasgow last weekend.

Thomas Kerr revealed in a post on social media site X that he has asked officers to investigate a speech made by Aamer Anwar during a counter-protest to anti-immigration demonstrators on Saturday.

Rejecting Mr Kerr’s claims, Mr Anwar accused the Glasgow MSP of wasting police time and described him as a “wannabe tartan Tommy Robinson”.

Mr Kerr told his social media followers that Mr Anwar’s comments “go beyond robust political debate and, I believe, have the effect of encouraging hostility towards a section of Scots based on their political views, nationality, ethnicity and cultural identity”.

open image in gallery Reform UK Scotland MSP Thomas Kerr said he reported Aamer Anwar to police ( Jane Barlow/PA )

He described the remarks as “abhorrent”, claiming Mr Anwar had described political campaigners as “terrorists” and had spoken about questioning “their culture and religion”.

“His words, I have no doubt, will contribute to increased hostility and community tensions, and I hope Police Scotland investigate the matter fully,” he added.

During his speech, Mr Anwar said “racist thugs” had sought to hold Muslims and non-white people collectively responsible for the actions of “one madman in Belfast”, in reference to the alleged attempted murder in the city in June which sparked riots.

The human rights lawyer compared the incident to the alleged anti-Muslim knife attack in Edinburgh later that month.

He told anti-racism protesters in Glasgow: “I wonder what would have happened if, in response to the knife rampage in Leith, Muslims or members of the non-white community had masked up and organised pogroms against the white community, had set fire to white people’s homes with children running for their lives.

“Would there have been sympathy for their cause? Would the mob have been called campaigners with legitimate concerns? Or would we be calling them exactly what they are: terrorists?

“We would be questioning their culture, we would be questioning their religion, we would be asking which one of their community leaders was responsible for radicalising them – starting at the top with Nigel Farage and Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.”

Responding to Mr Kerr’s report to police, Mr Anwar said he was a “wannabe tartan Tommy Robinson” and he “should know police are busy tracing those masked thugs responsible for inciting and taking part in Saturday’s race hate, attacks on police officers and innocent people of colour.”

open image in gallery Aamer Anwar (C) and protesters display a banner as they take part in an anti-racism "Unity March and Rally", organised by Stand up to Racism, Scotland ( AFP/Getty )

He said while Mr Kerr claims to have called out Saturday’s violence, “several of his Reform members stood next to the thugs, many of whom were masked, whilst racist abuse, threats of violence and Nazi salutes took place”.

He went on: “I doubt Reform has handed over a single name or video of these thugs to the major investigation team at Police Scotland.

“Any decent person would be calling out the pogroms in Belfast and knife attacks in Leith, yet this great defender of free speech, Mr Kerr’s reaction to my words is to waste police time, by labelling it as hate speech.”

He added: “Will he now suspend those Reform politicians that attended the ‘Unite the Klans’ event on Saturday and assist police with their inquiries?”

Glasgow Reform councillor Audrey Dempsey has admitted to speaking at the Unite the Clans rally.

Other speakers at the event spoke of their love of being white and claimed white people in the UK were being replaced.

Police Scotland said around 1,700 people took part in demonstrations in the city on Saturday, with groups engaging in violence, disorder and hate-motivated offending.

Fifteen people have since been arrested and officers have vowed that more will come.

Police said groups engaged in violence, disorder, intimidation and hate-motivated offences, including a large group of around 100 people who made their way into the city centre.

Demonstrators were seen performing what appeared to be Nazi salutes while videos on social media appeared to show a non-white delivery driver being attacked by a group shouting “get them out”.

Chief constable Jo Farrell described the violent scenes as “disgraceful” and said Police Scotland would take further action on those who caused disorder.

First Minister John Swinney branded the protest a “demonstration of far-right hatred”, describing the disorder as “completely and utterly unacceptable”.

A video of the anti-migrant group rushing towards an anti-fascist group was shared and supported by far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.

The protest was the latest in a series of anti-migrant demonstrations in Glasgow amid heightened tensions.

Police Scotland has been approached for comment.

Senate negotiators worked Wednesday to resolve thorny differences with leaders of the Southeastern and Big Ten Conferences over revisions to a bill designed to regulate college sports that sponsors want a vote on before the chamber goes on summer break next week.

“Those conversations are ongoing,” said one of the bill's sponsors, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas.

Cruz and co-sponsor Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., are pushing to bring the Protect College Sports Act to a vote before Aug. 7, the last day the Senate meets before going on break. Senators return for the second half of September, before breaking for all of October -- leaving little time remaining before the November midterms.

A pair of documents outlining concessions the lawmakers have made in the negotiations were headlined by a $20 million-plus “retention pool” that schools could use to keep players from leaving. It would amount to a doubling of the revenue-sharing “salary cap," which is currently set at $21.3 million for this school year.

The conferences are seeking answers on whether the increase in revenue share would impact rules governing third-party payments to players, the likes of which are largely blamed for spiraling roster costs.

There's also the question of whether such an increase would comport with the House settlement — the $2.8 billion lawsuit settlement that dictates rules around revenue sharing. Jeffrey Kessler, the plaintiffs' attorney, has said he would need to see the language before weighing in on whether it impacts the settlement.

Absent from the documents was any mention of rewrites regarding antitrust protection or preemption of state laws. Those have been core requests surrounding legislation from virtually all the conferences and NCAA since Congress began this process.

Earlier this month, the SEC and Big Ten put out a paper outlining 10 “Common Sense Improvements” for the PCSA. The first two— and three of the 10 — entries on their list dealt with those two issues.

Other topics have been addressed in the negotiations, including adding flexibility to requirements over how many Olympic and women's sports programs some schools should have and relaxing language over conference expansion to allow leagues to grow to up to 19 teams.

There has also been language designed to prohibit private equity investors from paying schools to form a super league, though the conferences could seek more refining to that language.

Hospital admissions for ectopic pregnancies in England have seen a significant rise, with new research suggesting that women falling pregnant at older ages may be a contributing factor.

Analysis of data reveals a notable increase in admissions between 2004 and 2012, averaging around 3% annually.

Following a period of stabilisation from 2012 to 2021, figures have again climbed sharply, with an average increase exceeding 4% each year since 2021.

Experts from the University of Liverpool, whose findings were published in the Lancet Regional Health – Europe journal, also highlighted a stark disparity: women residing in England's most deprived areas consistently experienced higher rates of admission compared to those in more affluent regions.

Beyond older maternal age, the study points to other potential influences on this upward trend, including changes in how ectopic pregnancies are managed within hospitals and the impact of infections.

The research further indicates that between 2013 and 2024, the majority of these admissions, accounting for 45–55% annually, occurred among women aged 25 to 34.

Ectopic pregnancies have risen significantly since 2021 ( PA )

Women aged 35 to 39 contributed a further 20–25%, while admissions among women aged 20–24 remained stable at around 15–18% each year.

“Admissions among women aged 40 (and over) increased from around 7% in 2013 to 12% in 2024, consistent with the national shift toward delayed childbearing and potentially contributing to the recent rise in ectopic pregnancy incidence,” the team said.

Experts also looked at hospital admissions for miscarriage, which declined significantly between 2018 and 2021, followed by suggestions of a modest rise after 2021.

The team said several factors may have contributed to a change in hospital admissions for miscarriage, including Covid-19 infections, a change in the care offered during the pandemic, and the “progressive increase in maternal age at conception in the UK, rising prevalence of obesity, and broader environmental and lifestyle changes, all of which are independently associated with miscarriage risk”.

Researchers concluded that throughout 2013 to 2024, women from the most deprived areas consistently had more than twice the hospital admissions for both miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy compared with women from the least deprived areas.

They said this reflects factors such as smoking (19% in most deprived areas versus 6% in least deprived) and obesity (36% versus 22%), and lower access to early maternity care.

An ectopic pregnancy is when a fertilised egg implants itself outside of the womb, usually in one of the fallopian tubes.

The pregnancy usually has to be terminated either through medication or an operation.

Ectopic pregnancy is one of the most common early pregnancy complications with an estimated 11,000 hospital admissions every year in England – around one in every 90 pregnancies.

A recent study indicates that prescribing antihistamines to manage eczema symptoms offers no significant benefit and may "probably increase harms".

Experts have welcomed the findings, saying they address "longstanding uncertainty" surrounding the role of these medications in treating the common skin condition, and are now urging for updated medical guidance.

Eczema, also known as atopic dermatitis, is a prevalent skin condition causing itchiness, affecting an estimated one in five children and one in ten adults in the UK.

Despite existing recommendations, approximately one in five eczema patients in the UK currently use antihistamines.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) already advises against the routine use of antihistamines for managing the condition.

However, they are sometimes offered if flare ups are linked to hives or another allergic reaction, while the short-term use of sedative antihistamines can help those whose itching is severely disturbing sleep.

Experts in Canada reviewed 47 trials including more than 6,200 children and adults with moderate to severe eczema.

They found that, when compared with a placebo, antihistamines led to a “clinically unimportant reduction” in the severity of eczema and itchiness.

Antihistamines may also “not reduce sleep disturbance” and eczema flare ups, the study suggests.

First generation drugs, which often cause drowsiness, may also increase cognitive impairment and could lead to patients discontinuing treatment due to side effects.

Antihistamines are not recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) to routinely manage the condition ( Getty/iStock )

Researchers said their findings, published in the BMJ, address the “longstanding uncertainty surrounding the role of antihistamines” in treating eczema, and show “they likely do not” improve patient outcomes and “while probably increasing harms”.

They added: “Our findings do not support their use in routine atopic dermatitis management.

“We have provided a foundation for an evidence-based change in practice, supporting the development of updated atopic dermatitis guidelines that prioritise efficacy, safety, and patient centred care.”

Could eczema diagnosis and treatment be ‘revolutionised’?

A "groundbreaking" new technology developed at Edinburgh's Heriot-Watt University has secured over £475,000 in funding for clinical research, promising to "revolutionise" the diagnosis and treatment of eczema.

The university states its innovative vibroacoustic sensor could alleviate "years of suffering for millions of patients across the UK."

The device operates by emitting small vibrations onto the skin's surface, meticulously measuring material alterations within each layer.

This process identifies crucial changes in tissue stiffness and fluid content, offering a new pathway for understanding and managing the condition.

Professor Michael Crichton, from the university's school of engineering and physical sciences, emphasised the significance of the development, stating the technology "represents a fundamental shift in how we approach eczema management."

He added: “Rather than relying solely on visual assessments, which haven’t evolved in decades and can be particularly unreliable for patients with darker skin tones, our sensor provides objective measurements of what’s happening beneath the skin’s surface.”

The townspeople of St. Mary's can breathe a sigh of relief. They are finally getting rid of the foul smell of rotten fish that has for years — when the wind blows their way — wafted over their tiny community in Canada 's easternmost province.

And the culprit for the unpleasant odor that has vexed the picturesque town of about 300 people in Newfoundland and Labrador?

About 110 tanks that were left behind — each holding 3,000 gallons of fermented fish sauce — when the Atlantic Seafood Sauce Company was abandoned more than 20 years ago.

The place was left to ruin: windows got broken, the roof blew off, a January storm knocked out a wall. The sauce kept on fermenting as the bacteria did their job — and the townspeople could smell it.

St. Mary's volunteer mayor, Steve Ryan, says it's hard to describe just how bad the smell was.

“The worst rotted fish you ever smelled in your lifetime, times 100,” he told The Associated Press by phone on Wednesday.

As crews kicked off a major cleanup operation at the dilapidated plant this week, Ryan watched with mixed feelings.

“It’s a big relief,” he said, describing the town's lengthy “crusade” to get the provincial government to fund the cleanup. The federal government has not contributed to the cost, he added.

“That kind of makes me a little bit mad,” said Ryan, who had briefly worked at the factory after graduating from high school in 1990. "Every door we came to was just closed in our face. ... They forgot about us."

Over the next few months, workers will drain the vats of left-behind fluid and mix it with peat moss, which will absorb the liquid, he said.

Trucks with giant hoses will then suck up the material and transport it to a pit that has been dug out over three weeks and lined with high-density polyethylene used in landfills. At the end, the pit will be covered with topsoil.

Glenn Sharp, owner of Sharp Management, the company overseeing the task, called it a “unique job.”

“This is a special waste,” he said. “This does not fall under any of the standard classifications.”

Ryan said the project costs 1.7 million Canadian dollars ($1.21 million). The community had to take out a hefty loan of 198,000 Canadian dollars ($140,973) it has to contribute, though the town will get the money back at a later date.

He hopes that when it's all over, the memory of the foul smell will fade.

“We’re such a small town and we were left on our own," he said. “For so many years nobody had our backs.”

But we “kept fighting and fighting,” he added, “because we knew we were right in what we were fighting for.”

News.title: AMR chatbot could prevent drug-resistant infections in African hospitals
News.content:
A phone-based chatbot advising medics how to prescribe antibiotics has helped raise the quality of care in African hospitals and should stop bugs developing dangerous resistance, developers say.

Staff at four hospitals across Zambia and Kenya have been using two digital tools in a pilot project to try to address one of the world’s biggest health threats.

Anti-microbial resistance (AMR) is caused by germs evolving so that medicines such as antibiotics designed to kill them no longer work.

The menace is linked to nearly five million deaths each year and makes it increasingly difficult to treat infections. The annual death toll could nearly double in the next 25 years, according to some forecasts.

The rise in AMR is being significantly driven by the misuse and overuse of antimicrobials in human medicine and in agriculture.

Using antibiotics when they are not necessary, using the wrong ones, or getting the dosage wrong, all add to the chances that bugs will develop resistance.

With a shortage of new drugs in the development pipeline, one push to defeat AMR has been to get medics to stick to existing prescription, dosage and treatment advice.

The Antibiotic Stewardship Programme through Innovation, Research, and Education (ASPIRE) is trying to give them guidance using technology they already have in their pockets.

News.title: Tottenham new boys score in shoot-out win over Sydney FC
News.content:
Tonali was brought on as a half-time substitute, before Robertson took the captain’s armband from Archie Gray after he was introduced in the 65th minute.

The former Liverpool left-back delivered three dangerous crosses which went unconverted, something of a theme for a Spurs team who failed to make the most of long spells of dominance.

James Maddison and Mateus Fernandes were not in the match-day squad, while Pedro Porro, Marcos Senesi, Cristian Romero, Micky van de Ven and Jean Paul van Hecke have yet to join the group after the World Cup.

There was another impressive showing from 17-year-old prospect Luca Williams-Barnett, who is pushing for first-team opportunities this upcoming season.

Penalties followed the final whistle, with Spurs scoring all four of their spot kicks. Goalkeeper Martin Dubravka, signed on a free transfer this summer, saved one and Sydney FC’s Josh Lacey hit the post to give Spurs the spoils 4-2.

News.title: Recovery aids and building muscle: Welsh weightlifter Laura Hughes answers your questions
News.content:
Laura Hughes first discovered weightlifting while training at her local Crossfit gym, making the transition from amateur gym-goer to competitive lifting.

Now a member of the Welsh national weightlifting squad, the 33-year-old holds the Welsh record for both the snatch and the clean and jerk (the two official competitive lifts in weightlifting) and is currently third overall in the women’s Welsh rankings. Hughes won bronze at this year’s Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, following on from her third place at the 2018 Games in Australia.

We caught up with her for our Readers Ask series, where industry specialists answer questions from our Telegraph Recommended Reader Panel.

Who inspired you to get into weightlifting?

Olamilekan, South East

Originally, it was lots of different people, particularly general gym goers who were doing weightlifting at my gym. As I’ve grown as an athlete and become more competitive, I’ve had other inspirations.

Most notably, coming into [the Commonwealth Games], it has to be Gareth [Evans], our coach. Looking back at his performance in 2018 when he won his gold medal is so inspiring. [English lifter] Emily Godley was another competitor in 2018. She won the gold medal in my category and I just remember thinking that she was on fire that day.

What are the best exercises for you to build muscle mass?

Norman, Wales

We spend a lot of time doing our main lifts, so snatches, clean and jerks, but we also do lots of pulls and squats. I spend a lot of time doing accessory work to make sure that my body stays healthy, especially being an older athlete. I’ve put on quite a lot of muscle in this last block just from going heavier and pushing my limits with my main lifts.

What advice would you give to people who want to improve their strength?

David, North West

The most important thing is consistency. As long as you’re doing something, do it regularly, even if it’s twice a week. Don’t be afraid of picking up some dumbbells. If you’ve got somebody that can teach you how to lift weights properly, that’s going to be the best option. Do it safely, do it consistently, and don’t be afraid to try new strength exercises.

News.title: Explosive mpox outbreak causes 3,000 cases in Madagascar
News.content:
More than 3,000 cases of mpox have been recorded in Madagascar after the virus spread from a single port city to some of the country’s busiest coastal hubs.

A total of 3,022 cases and 20 deaths have been recorded as of this week, with cases in Toamasina and Taolagnaro accounting for more than half of all diagnoses.

The outbreak has been linked to Clade 1b mpox, a strain that emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare a global public health emergency at the time.

“The main factor driving the continued spread of the disease is human mobility, seeding new outbreaks in areas where the virus has not circulated before,” Professor Carlos Maluquer de Motes of the University of Surrey told The Telegraph.

“Under-reporting is likely, with the real number of cases exceeding what is being reported.”

News.title: Chelsea in 10-goal thriller as ‘Alonso ball’ brings risk and reward
News.content:
Chelsea’s first match under the management of Xabi Alonso was a 10-goal thriller in Australia, as the Premier League side eventually showed their class in a 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers.

Star striker João Pedro, who was controversially left out of Brazil’s World Cup squad, scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming off the bench with half an hour of the friendly remaining.

Alonso had selected a youthful team for the first hour before bringing nine senior players, including João Pedro, into the side in the second half. According to Transfermarkt, Chelsea’s squad is valued at over £1.3bn while their opponents a more modest £5.86m.

Teenage signing Dastan Satpayev, midfielder Dario Essugo and winger Jamie Gittens also found the net for Chelsea, who were defensively vulnerable for long spells for the game.

Here are five things Telegraph Sport learned from Alonso’s first match.

João Pedro picks up where he left off

João Pedro scored 13 goals in the second half of last season and his impressive performances resulted in the 24-year-old being named Chelsea’s player of the campaign. It was something of a surprise, then, when he was left out of Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil squad this summer.

The good news for Chelsea is that João Pedro’s absence from the World Cup has given him plenty of time to recover ahead of the new campaign, and he looked thrillingly sharp in his second-half performance against Western Sydney Wanderers. The difference in class between João Pedro and Liam Delap, the man he replaced, was clear for all to see.

Two of the Brazilian’s three goals were classy, composed finishes — and he also created a goal for Gittens after surging past three defenders on the left wing. João Pedro looks like he means business.
