World.title: Elle Duncan blames Caitlin Clark, her fans for media smear campaign while ignoring facts
World.content:
On Tuesday, OutKick explained that the conversation around Caitlin Clark cannot shift toward basketball until the players and media members fueling the hysteria acknowledge their role in creating it.

Case in point: former ESPN host Elle Duncan.

Hours after our column was published, Duncan blamed the drama on — wait for it — Caitlin Clark and her fans. Who else? According to Duncan, it's Clark's responsibility to denounce fans who allegedly co-opt her name to serve their own agendas.

SOME WNBA PLAYERS ACT LIKE THEY ARE THE ONLY ONES WHO RECEIVE MEAN SOCIAL MEDIA MESSAGES

"I would love for it to be very clear to the people who think they are her fans but are using her, if she would say, ‘stop that sh--, I don’t want it, I’m tired of it.’ As opposed to what we’ve seen, which is ‘the media makes up these narratives, the media makes up this discourse,'" Duncan said on "The Sports Gossip Show" podcast.

Duncan was referring to Clark telling ESPN over the weekend that the media "controls the narrative" around her and is "sometimes so far out of touch with what is reality."

"The media highlights the stories, and they show it, but at the same time, like, the media did not make up that members of Congress are trying to get literal government intervention into whether you get fouled too hard," Duncan continued. "Like, this stuff has to stop."

Duncan's attempt to defend the media's role in the hostility surrounding Clark is especially telling, coming less than a week after USA Today published an op-ed arguing that Clark's style of play could get Black and queer women lynched like Emmett Till. No, that's not satire. The outlet really published that story.

You almost have to laugh at Duncan's proposed solution. In her view, the way to calm things down is for Clark to denounce the very fans defending her while players drive forearms into her throat and television analysts smear her character.

Moreover, Duncan completely ignores that Clark has repeatedly done exactly what Duncan accuses her of avoiding.

"People should not be using my name to push those agendas. It's disappointing. It's not acceptable," Clark said in 2024. "Treating every single woman in this league with the same amount of respect, I think, it's just a basic human thing that everybody should do."

Perhaps Duncan would prefer that Clark spend less time focusing on her game and more time responding to every manufactured controversy.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

New York Post columnist Kirsten Fleming elaborated on this point Wednesday:

"No matter how many times CC has said the thing everyone wants her to say, it's not enough. They demand more. They want her to respond to every drop of nonsense and give it way more oxygen than it deserves. It gives women a bad name. This isn't Bravo, it's hoops. Let her hoop."

Indeed.

Further, it's not as if Clark has a magic wand to stop random people on the internet from posting. By Duncan's logic, Elle Duncan is responsible for every racist threat directed at Clark on social media.

Later in the episode, Duncan dismisses Clark's supporters as "fake" because she assumes everyone approaches sports fandom the way she does: as an extension of culture and identity politics. Duncan has likely adopted fandom for players like Lamar Jackson, Angel Reese, or Jalen Hurts for reasons that extend well beyond sports.

But that is not how the average fan views sports.

Most fans are simply drawn to compelling, generational athletes. Caitlin Clark is one of them. So were Michael Jordan, Tiger Woods, Steph Curry, Serena Williams and Patrick Mahomes.

Duncan is telling on herself. It's called projection.

OutKick asked Duncan via text message why she discounts the media's role in the firestorm surrounding Caitlin Clark. She did not respond before publication. We will update this story if she does.

As we concluded earlier this week, the conversation around Caitlin Clark cannot return to basketball as long as these bad-faith actors remain at the center.

Racial idolaters like Duncan, Monica McNutt, Angel Reese, Jemele Hill, Nancy Armour and others will never admit fault because of how deeply their resentment of Clark's success runs.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The only way they can reconcile a straight White woman from Iowa transcending their niche sport is by insisting her popularity is merely a product of racism and privilege.

Just listen to the contempt with which Duncan speaks. She claims to care about the WNBA. Based on her commentary, she'd rather see the league revert to obscurity than succeed on the back of Caitlin Clark.

It was Christmas in July night at Sutter Health Park, home of the Sacramento River Cats (and the Athletics), and that's why the team's mascot, Dinger, was barreling around the warning track dressed as St. Nick.

A SQUIRREL INVADES MLB GAME, JUMPS INTO OUTFIELDERS GLOVE AND CAUSES CHAOS IN HILARIOUS SCENE

That was a way heavier hit than I was prepared for.

World.title: Fed holds interest rates for the fifth meeting this year, underscoring inflation fears
World.content:
The Federal Reserve left its key interest rate unchanged Wednesday for the fifth consecutive meeting, despite lingering concerns about inflation that continues to pressure U.S. household finances.

The decision was largely expected by investors, who have seen markets begin to churn amid ongoing concerns about higher oil prices stemming from the war with Iran and AI spending worries.

Nine members of the Federal Open Market Committee voted to keep rates steady at 3.5% to 3.75%. But three policymakers saw the case for raising interest rates and chose to vote against the decision to stand pat. It was the first time since 2016 that there were three dissents in the same direction over a policy change.

The vote split reveals a growing internal divide over whether the central bank is moving too slowly to tamp down on inflation.

In remarks following Wednesday’s announcement, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh reiterated the central bank’s commitment to its inflation goal.

“For some households, businesses and market professionals, five years of high inflation have left a mistaken impression that’s hard to shake that the Fed’s implicit inflation target was somehow above 2%,” he said.

“Let me reiterate: There is no soft inflation target. There is no soft implicit target, not on this committee’s watch. There’s only a target, and it’s 2%.”

Immediately after the decision, the odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed’s next policy meeting in September rose slightly, to 59%, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

The Fed has historically used higher interest rates to curb overall economic activity and rein in inflation. But a debate over the best course continues to swirl. With inflation stubbornly high, many market participants have called for higher rates that would put downward pressure on the pace of price increases.

Yet for many consumers and smaller businesses, current interest rates have already pushed the cost of borrowing money increasingly out of reach. That has cut into sales of items like autos and industrial equipment, which are typically financed.

While parts of the U.S. economy are relatively stable, like the labor market, experts say that stability could be undermined by the potential inflationary impacts of a longer Iran war or the Trump administration’s latest tariff push.

The inflation rate has hovered above the Fed’s 2% target for more than five years, a phenomenon that has aggravated an ongoing affordability crisis. And while some recent inflation indicators have begun showing declines, the pace of rising prices for energy and wholesale items has remained elevated.

“Every month of above-target inflation has compounded the strain on Americans’ budgets,” Dallas Federal Reserve President Lorie Logan said in remarks this month, calling for rates to be “modestly” higher.

Current interest rates have already pushed the cost of borrowing money beyond the reach of many consumers and smaller businesses. Brendan Smialowski / AFP via Getty Images

Among interest rate traders, there is a broad consensus that the Fed will raise rates at least once before the end of the year. According to CME FedWatch, Fed Funds futures contracts point to a 90% probability that rates will be at least a quarter-point higher by January.

There is another question hanging over the central bank’s rate-setting meeting this week: How much of an impact would raising interest rates actually have on prices?

There are several reasons inflation could be less sensitive to higher interest rates than it has in the past.

High energy prices sparked by the war with Iran, for example, and Trump administration tariff policies are helping keep prices elevated for consumers. But experts say higher rates would do little to blunt those kinds of geopolitical forces.

“Hiking [interest rates] doesn’t open up the Strait of Hormuz or end the war,” said Adam Turnquist, chief technical strategist at the asset management group LPL Financial.

The Fed leaders’ opinions about what lies ahead for the U.S. economy will most likely also be more of a black box this week than they have been in recent years.

Warsh, who took the reins of the central bank from Jerome Powell in May, has made it a hallmark of his tenure not to tip the Fed’s thinking about the path of monetary policy — much to the frustration of some market participants.

“Chair Warsh’s communication void has encouraged other policymakers to speak more forcefully,” said Greg Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon, Ernst & Young LLP.

Among those who speak up, the message has been consistent, Daco wrote in a note: Inflation remains too high, and rates must increase.

“After months of upside inflation surprises, patience is wearing thin,” Daco wrote. “If inflation does not soon move back toward 2%, and remains elevated because of persistent supply shocks, stronger AI-related demand, tariffs, or the Middle East conflict, the case for additional policy firming will be clear.”

Other experts are more optimistic that inflation has peaked and that the Fed can afford to keep rates at current levels.

“Housing-related inflation continues to cool, and wage growth—the largest input cost in services — is not inflationary when adjusted for productivity gains,” Angelo Kourkafas, a senior investment strategist at Edward Jones, wrote in a recent client note.

“Moreover, the new tariffs announced are broadly consistent with the previous tariff levels that expired and should not trigger a renewed rise in goods prices,” he added.

President Donald Trump’s latest tariffs — a blanket rate of 10% to 12.5% on dozens of U.S. trade partners — are a continuation of his protectionist trade policies.

But they also introduce fresh uncertainty into many of America’s most vital economic relationships. Several of the targeted trade partners say the U.S. rationale for this round of import duties — an effort to combat forced labor — amounts to a false pretense.

Within days of their announcement, the latest tariffs were challenged in federal trade court, effectively throwing them into legal limbo even as importers prepare to start paying them.

Some experts believe the tariffs are unlikely to survive a legal challenge, adding yet another layer of uncertainty to the economic outlook.

World.title: Trump’s IRS carveout threatens to hold up Todd Blanche attorney general nomination
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Todd Blanche’s path to confirmation as the next attorney general of the United States faced a setback Wednesday as two key Republicans pressed the Justice Department to commit in writing to kill an “anti-weaponization” fund that could give money to President Donald Trump’s allies and restrict the scope of the tax audit immunity given to him and his family members.

The Senate Judiciary Committee had been set to hold a hearing to advance Blanche’s nomination on Thursday morning, and it would have gone to the full Senate if advanced by the committee. But GOP Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, both of whom have clashed with Trump and neither of whom is facing re-election in November, have complicated Blanche’s path to confirmation.

Much of the discussion has been around the so-called Anti-Weaponization Fund that was established under a purported settlement between Trump and the executive branch he controls over a lawsuit the president filed over the disclosure of his tax records. The suit led to a five-year prison sentence for a former IRS contractor.

A federal judge in Virginia indefinitely blocked the fund after a former Jan. 6 prosecutor sued. A federal judge in Florida found that Trump’s IRS lawsuit was brought in “bad faith” for an “improper purpose” and ordered sanctions against several people involved, including Blanche.

But the settlement agreement also had provisions that offered Trump — along with his family members and companies —some protection from IRS audits.

Cornyn, who lost his primary race to Trump-endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, had raised concerns with the purported IRS settlement. On Wednesday, Cornyn told reporters that Blanche’s team had failed to provide written proposals to modify the release that was signed in the tax dispute with Trump and his organization.

“I haven’t seen a single piece of writing that is responsive to what I’ve requested,” Cornyn said.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said he was in active discussions with the Justice Department.

“They’re working on a draft right now,” Tillis said on Wednesday afternoon. “We’ve been in constant daily contact with DOJ, and to their credit, they’re engaging.”

Blanche, who previously served as Trump’s personal defense attorney, had served in the key No. 2 position at the Justice Department until Trump fired Pam Bondi as attorney general in April amid frustrations with her leadership.

After taking over as the acting attorney general, Blanche told NBC News in April that Americans should be “happy” that Trump was so involved in Justice Department matters. Less than two weeks later, the Trump administration brought a case against former FBI Director James Comey, a longtime Trump foe, over an Instagram photo of seashells.

Following the Comey indictment, Trump was said to be happy with Blanche’s job performance and ultimately ended up nominating him for the job permanently. Comey’s legal team argued in a court filing this week that the seashells case came about because Blanche was seeking to “please President Trump” during his “audition” for the role.

During his confirmation hearing this month, Blanche said he was not a “yes man” for Trump.

World.title: St. Paul’s first female Mayor under investigation after police chief’s sexual harassment complaint
World.content:
The St. Paul, Minnesota, police chief has submitted a sexual harassment complaint against the city’s first female mayor, alleging that she behaved inappropriately toward him and other members of his department, the local NBC affiliate reported Wednesday.

The city has now hired an outside law firm to investigate the allegations against Mayor Kaohly Her, who has been in office for just seven months.

Chief Axel Henry, who has led the St. Paul Police Department since 2022, outlined the allegations against Her in an April 1 letter sent by his lawyer to to the St. Paul City Attorney.

“The City is on notice that Mayor Her has engaged in illegal conduct towards City employees,” attorney Christopher Madel wrote in the letter, which was obtained by the NBC affiliate, KARE 11.

Henry sent the letter of complaint against Her after “becoming aware that the Mayor’s conduct has extended beyond isolated incidents and has included sexual harassment of subordinate City employees, including members of the Saint Paul Police Department,” Madel wrote.

“Chief Henry is not only seeking to address the wrongdoing but also create a measure of protection for his team, signaling that such conduct will not be tolerated,” Madel wrote.

Included with the letter is a screenshot of an alleged text message from Her to an unnamed city employee that reads “Happy Weiner (sic) Wednesday! Wish I was having a (hot dog emoji) with you all on 6 today!”

Below the text message is an internet meme showing a swaddled baby with an adult’s head, which has been redacted, The Minnesota Star Tribune reported.

“When she wraps you up in her blanket after you gave her a good weinering,” reads the caption.

Wienering is an internet slang term for sexual intercourse and is frequently misspelled as weinering.

The letter alleges that “Her has used one or more mobile phones to communicate inappropriate, and, indeed, unlawful text messages.”

But it does not spell out any other specific examples of alleged inappropriate communications.

Madel wrote in the letter that future litigation is “reasonably foreseeable” and demanded that the city “immediately take all steps necessary to perform a full filesystem extraction of each of Mayor Her’s mobile phones.”

Matt Wagenius, a spokesperson for the mayor, did not respond to an email from NBC News for comment.

“Chief Henry and the department has no comment at this time,” police spokesperson Nikki Muehlhausen said.

The Star Tribune reported that Resolute Law, based St. Cloud and describes on its website as a “women-owned firm,” has been hired to investigate the allegations against the mayor.

The law firm did not respond to a request for comment on the status of the investigation.

The mayor, 53, was born in Laos and spent part of her childhood in a refugee camp. She was three when she arrived in the U.S. and grew up in Illinois and Wisconsin, according to her campaign biography.

The Star Tribune reported that the mayor had faced an accusation of inappropriate behavior before.

The mayor was hit with a restraining order petition last year by a former friend who claimed she had sent her “inappropriate or sexualized questions” and had gotten her removed from the National Kidney Foundation Board.

The petition was denied by Ramsey County District Court Referee Elizabeth Clysdale who wrote that the text messages filed showed the mayor had not threatened her former friend and that Her’s husband had tried to help resolve the issue.

Clysdale also wrote there was no proof that the mayor had played a role in the woman’s removal from the National Kidney Foundation Board, the newspaper reported.

World.title: Todd Blanche’s rocky road: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, we dig into the uncertain paths forward for Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination and the Iran war.

Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.

— Adam Wollner

Trump’s IRS carveout threatens to hold up Todd Blanche’s AG nomination

Todd Blanche’s bid to be the next attorney general faced a setback today as two key Republicans pressed the Justice Department to commit in writing to kill an “anti-weaponization” fund that could give money to President Donald Trump’s allies and restrict the scope of the tax audit immunity given to him and his family members.

The Senate Judiciary Committee is set to hold a hearing to advance Blanche’s nomination tomorrow morning. But GOP Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who have clashed with Trump and are not facing re-election in November, have emerged as potential roadblocks on Blanche’s path to the full Senate.

Much of the discussion has been around the “anti-weaponization fund” that was established under a purported settlement between Trump and the executive branch he controls over a lawsuit the president filed over the disclosure of his tax records, which led to a five-year prison sentence for a former IRS contractor.

A federal judge in Virginia indefinitely blocked the fund after a former Jan. 6 prosecutor sued. A federal judge in Florida found that Trump’s IRS lawsuit was brought in “bad faith” for an “improper purpose,” and ordered sanctions against several people involved, including Blanche.

But the settlement agreement also had provisions that offered Trump — along with his family members and companies — some protection from IRS audits.

Cornyn, who lost his GOP primary earlier this year to Trump-backed Ken Paxton, told reporters that Blanche’s team had failed to provide written proposals to modify the release that was signed in the tax dispute with Trump and his organization.

“I haven’t seen a single piece of writing that is responsive to what I’ve requested,” Cornyn said.

Tillis, who is retiring at the end of his term, said he was in active discussions with the Justice Department.

“They’re working on a draft right now,” Tillis said this afternoon. “We’ve been in constant daily contact with DOJ, and to their credit, they’re engaging.”

Read more →

After Trump and Netanyahu meet, the Iran war’s future remains hazy

Analysis by Andrea Mitchell

As the United States enters its sixth month of a war with Iran that Israeli and U.S. leaders both said would last only four to six weeks, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met with President Donald Trump Tuesday and other top national security officials for the first time since the conflict started.

In Washington for the funeral of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, a key Netanyahu ally, a senior Israeli official told NBC News and other reporters that they discussed three major options: a good deal to eliminate Iran having a nuclear weapon; no deal, but a sustained blockade and economic pressure; and military action.

Without saying what Israel’s preference is, a senior Israeli official said there was broad agreement — as Trump repeatedly affirms — that Iran cannot be allowed to have a nuclear weapon. But Trump told my colleague Kristen Welker last month that the U.S. has eyes on the nuclear facilities the U.S. and Israel bombed last June, and that nothing can move in or out of those two sites without the U.S. seeing it.

Today, the Israeli official demurred from saying his country disagrees with Trump’s assessments. In particular, he wouldn’t say whether Netanyahu is urging the U.S. to bomb another suspected nuclear site — Pickaxe Mountain. It has been widely reported that U.S. intelligence assesses that site would be impossible to eliminate even with the most devastating U.S. bunker-buster bombs, but it could be effectively closed and made unreachable by Iran.

At the behest of the administration, Israel has not re-engaged in the recurring U.S. strikes against Iran that have taken place since a 60-day ceasefire was officially agreed to in mid-June. At the time, Israel strongly criticized the memorandum of understanding as being far too generous to Iran because it approved the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets. None of that was turned over because of the collapse of diplomacy and reignition of airstrikes by both sides, and more recently, strikes by Iran against U.S. and Arab allied assets in the region.

During his three days in Washington, Netanyahu also met separately with Vice President JD Vance, who was initially skeptical of the Iran war, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and other Pentagon officials. Still at issue: Will economic pressure alone get the Iranian regime to permit open access to the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow international waterway critical to the global economy?

The Israeli official who briefed reporters today acknowledged that sustained economic pressure — if it cut off all supplies to Iran — could be a solution, although it would hurt Iranian civilians. But a second Israeli official said money is still flowing from Iran’s regime through Turkey to Hezbollah, its proxy that Israel is fighting in southern Lebanon.

Both Trump and Netanyahu are facing elections this fall. The big difference is that Netanyahu, despite growing opposition at home, has strong popular support for resuming attacks against Iran.

Trump’s political reality is exactly opposite: The war has depleted the supply of U.S. missiles and interceptors for Patriot air defense systems and is damaging his popularity, even with his own base. It has caused gas and diesel fuel prices to spike and contributed to inflation.

While the Israeli briefer said today that Trump has been an “amazing ally” for Israel in the war, he acknowledged the U.S. president is the senior partner and Netanyahu the junior — making it more imperative for Trump’s political standing to find some diplomatic way out of the current standoff.

World.title: New DOJ rule would allow immigration judges to hold lawyers in contempt
World.content:
The Justice Department is proposing a new rule to empower federal immigration judges to hold attorneys, their clients and witnesses in contempt if they violate court orders, in a move that departs from historical practice and which legal experts warn could be unconstitutional.

The regulatory proposal by the Executive Office for Immigration Review, an office of the DOJ that runs the immigration court system, would allow immigration judges for the very first time to impose fines ranging from $1,000 up to as much as $3,500 if an attorney or other individual continues to defy court orders.

"It is crucial for immigration judges to have every tool available—including the authority to impose civil money penalties—to control the proceedings before them," the Justice Department wrote in its proposal.

The proposal notably exempts federal government employees, such as Department of Homeland Security attorneys, from being subject to any contempt order by an immigration judge — in what critics say represents a lopsided and unfair scenario that would allow potential government misconduct to go unchecked.

In federal district courts, by contrast, Article III judges have the power to hold all attorneys who appear before the court in criminal or civil contempt, if warranted. In its proposal, the Justice Department argues that giving immigration judges the power to sanction government lawyers is not necessary because DHS attorneys can be disciplined by the Office of the Inspector General or the Office of Professional Responsibility.

"By proposing a completely skewed regulation that empowers judges to hold in contempt only the attorneys for immigrants but not ICE attorneys, the Administration has revealed that its goal has nothing to do with the just and balanced rule of law. Instead, this rule is another effort to target immigration attorneys that falls in line with the President's intimidation tactics," said Gregory Chen, senior director of government relations at the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

The new proposal marks the latest in a series of efforts by the Trump administration to more readily crack down on immigration and carry out President Trump's mass deportation policies.

At the Executive Office for Immigration Review, hundreds of longtime federal immigration judges have left since last year, many of whom were fired abruptly without warning or cause. In 2025, EOIR lost 370 attorneys, according to government data analyzed and published by a former FBI analyst.

At the same time it has lost so many judges, the immigration court system is facing a current backlog of more than 3.5 million cases, according to the proposed rule.

Many former immigration judges have spoken publicly about pressures they faced to expedite deportations or detain people without bond. In ads seeking to hire replacement judges, the DOJ has referred to the role as being that of a "deportation judge."

The new proposal that would allow immigration judges to hold noncitizens or their lawyers in contempt "ties into the culture of fear," said Karen Donoso Stevens, a former longtime immigration judge. "First, scare the judges. Then the judges will scare the attorneys."

The proposed rule, published in the Federal Register, states immigration judges would be allowed to sanction lawyers or their clients for a variety of offenses, from repeatedly failing to appear on time or failing to follow orders, up to disorderly conduct or making false statements.

Several legal experts who spoke with CBS News said the proposal is potentially unlawful because immigration courts are part of the executive branch and fall under Article II of the Constitution, which states that the executive branch has no contempt authority. That power belongs exclusively to the judicial and legislative branches.

The proposal is "constitutionally flawed," Chen said.

The public will have 60 days to review the proposal and submit comments.

World.title: Why are workers at leading AI companies calling for a slowdown in AI development?
World.content:
The people who best understand what artificial intelligence is capable of are the very workers calling for its rapid development to be reined in, as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman meets with government officials in Washington, D.C., this week.

Altman's meetings follow the release of a public letter signed by more than 1,000 AI staffers across leading firms calling for the industry to be more tightly regulated.

"To realize AI's potential, industry, government, and society at large may need the option to buy time to address emerging risks, develop security measures, and strengthen oversight," read the letter, whose signatories include Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Meta executives, OpenAI researchers and more.

Slowing AI's development runs counter to firms' business goals as they compete with one another. "And today, the world lacks the technical and governance tools to deliberately pace frontier-wide progress," the letter added.

The letter, and Altman's meetings with national cyber director Sean Craincross, commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and other high-ranking officials, follow a high-profile cybersecurity incident during internal testing of an OpenAI model that went rogue and hacked into another startup, called Hugging Face, compromising customer data.

Altman described the incident on a recent podcast as "a kind of extremely sci-fi cyber incident," which he said set off alarm bells. "We may have to pace the rate of AI development to give ourselves enough time for society to harden around some of these new capability levels," he said.

Altman did not sign the letter calling for the pacing of AI development, but told reporters on Capitol Hill Wednesday that "we agree on a lot of the principles of that."

In 2023, Altman called on the federal government to regulate AI companies so that they wouldn't become dangerously capable without appropriate guardrails in place. And yet, the company continues to improve its own models' capabilities.

"He's really good at saying the right thing in the right moment. But it's important to point out that OpenAI has not actually slowed down the pace," senior TechCrunch reporter Rebecca Bellan told CBS News. "They can be worried about this on a personal level. But at the end of the day, if I'm being cynical...competition is more important."

World.title: What records reveal about Newsom's taxpayer-funded, California-branded free diaper program
World.content:
California waited 66 days to release the records behind Gov. Gavin Newsom's taxpayer-funded diaper program, including a $6.2 million contract awarded to the nonprofit Baby2Baby without a formal competitive bid.

The 356 pages the state released include the executed contract, internal analyses, vendor proposals and email threads between the California Department of Health Care Access and Information (HCAI) and the organizations that responded to the state's request for information.

CBS California Investigates reviewed every page.

Nothing in the released records reveals illegal conduct. The exemption lawmakers added to the budget made it legal for the administration to bypass ordinarily required competitive bidding and state contract review.

Instead, the records raise questions about why the state designed a program its own agency warned could waste taxpayer-funded diapers. They also show the state selected Baby2Baby even though the state's recommendation identified the other finalist as ready to provide the planned direct-to-consumer component.

These are the key findings.

CBS California Investigates sent the state several follow-up questions July 20 and is still waiting for answers.

(Document links in this story open the individual state records on DocumentCloud, redacted to remove personal contact information and confidential pricing information.)
