World.title: LPP Logistics opens 56,000 sqm distribution center near Bucharest
World.content:
LPP Logistics opened a new 56,000 sqm distribution center near Bucharest to support the Polish fashion group's operations in Romania, Bulgaria, and Greece. The facility is expected to strengthen the company's logistics network in South-Eastern Europe and support the continued expansion of the Sinsay brand.

The warehouse has a storage capacity of around 35 million items and is located close to the fulfilment center that LPP Logistics opened near Bucharest in November 2025. The company said the location also offers easier access to the Port of Constanța for sea freight deliveries.

According to LPP Logistics, the new center replaces infrastructure lost in a warehouse fire last year and has been designed to accommodate future expansion.

“We are already able to serve over 450 stores simultaneously, and following the planned expansion, we will double this capacity. This provides a solid foundation for the continued growth of our brands in the region,” noted Sebastian Sołtys, CEO of LPP Logistics.

The facility is currently equipped to prepare deliveries for up to 454 stores simultaneously. A planned expansion in early 2027 is expected to increase that capacity to around 900 stores.

The company said the distribution center will employ more than 300 people by the end of this year, with additional hiring planned as the site expands.

The building incorporates energy- and water-efficiency measures, including LED lighting, greywater recovery, and water and air treatment systems. It has received an A-class energy performance certificate and is undergoing BREEAM certification at the "Outstanding" level.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Romanian air traffic operator ROMATSA gets January 2027 hearing in Pfizer revenue freeze case
World.content:
The Court of First Instance in Brussels announced that it set January 4 as the trial date for the case concerning Pfizer's request to block the tariffs collected by the Romanian Air Traffic Services Administration (ROMATSA) to recover Romania’s debt over COVID-19 vaccines to the drugmaker.

As such, the fate of the funds that ROMATSA has to receive from the European Organization for the Safety of Air Navigation (Eurocontrol) will not be decided before the beginning of next year. Until then, the funds are frozen.

ROMATSA, however, has funds only for a few weeks, so the Romanian government may look to legislative amendments that would allow the continuation of operations, according to News.ro.

"ROMATSA has made a proposal whereby legislation would be changed through a legislative amendment, which could be discussed next week in Parliament. The company's accounts could be funded with the amounts necessary for its operation, at least until the end of August," interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan said at a press conference held at the end of last week.

On June 30, 2026, ROMATSA was notified by Eurocontrol regarding the establishment of a precautionary-executory garnishment measure within enforcement proceedings initiated by Pfizer Romania against the Romanian state. The claimed amount is RON 3.42 billion (principal balance and interest), to which recovery costs of EUR 18.5 million are added.

Both the ROMATSA and the Ministry of Finance have filed appeals for the lifting of the garnishment imposed on the amounts managed through Eurocontrol.

This is the third time that funds intended for ROMATSA have been affected through the collection mechanism managed by Eurocontrol, following the cases generated by the disputes between brothers Viorel and Ioan Micula and the Romanian state in 2015 and 2019.

At the beginning of April, a Belgian court ordered Poland and Romania to take delivery of a COVID-19 vaccine shipment with a combined value of EUR 1.9 billion produced by the American pharmaceutical company Pfizer. According to the court statement, Romania has to pay approximately EUR 600 million of the total sum, about 0.2% of its GDP.

The sum poses a significant burden at a time when the government is attempting to reduce the fiscal deficit. In addition to the principal amount, interest charges continue to accumulate at a rate of approximately EUR 81,000 per day, equivalent to nearly EUR 2.5 million per month.

Romania’s Supreme Council of National Defence (CSAT) warned that a possible suspension of ROMATSA's activity would represent a major vulnerability for national security, affecting the surveillance of Romanian airspace and NATO missions on the eastern flank.

In this context, acting defence minister Radu Miruță said that authorities are also examining the possibility that responsibility for airspace control could, if necessary, be taken over by the structures of the Ministry of Defence.

radu@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Facebook/Romatsa)

World.title: Romania’s Untold opens public investment round on SeedBlink after raising over EUR 500,000 in pre-launch
World.content:
Romanian festival organizer Untold Universe will open a public investment round on the SeedBlink platform on July 30 after raising more than EUR 500,000 during a pre-launch phase. The company said the early funding came from entrepreneurs, investors, partners, and hundreds of festival fans.

Among the investors who participated in the pre-launch round are Romanian entrepreneurs Dragoș Petrescu, Wargha Enayati, and George Copos, as well as entrepreneur Sebastian Dobrincu and producer Codin Maticiuc.

Starting July 30, the investment opportunity will be available to the general public through SeedBlink, allowing retail investors to buy into the entertainment group.

The move marks the first public investment campaign of its kind by a Romanian festival organizer.

Untold Universe said it plans to expand its international footprint over the coming years by building a network of 20 large-scale festivals and entertainment projects across at least 30 countries.

Following the launch of Untold Dubai, the group's next confirmed international expansion is scheduled for Colombia in 2027. The company also said it is in advanced talks regarding projects in Brazil and is exploring opportunities in the United States, Canada, Japan, China, India, South Korea, Egypt, Spain, and Greece.

At home, the company said it will continue developing the Untold festival in Cluj-Napoca, now in its 11th edition, while also expanding Kapital, the music festival launched in Bucharest in 2025.

“We're only at the beginning of a new chapter of development, and we want this community of investors to grow alongside us," said Bogdan Buta, founder and CEO of Untold Universe.

Andrei Dudoiu, CEO of SeedBlink, said the funding round gives investors an opportunity to invest in an established entertainment company seeking international expansion beyond its flagship festivals.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: the organizers)

World.title: Orange Romania reports EUR 690 million turnover for first half of 2026, cybersecurity revenue up by more than 50%
World.content:
In the first six months of 2026, Orange Romania reported a consolidated revenue of EUR 690 million, a slight increase compared with the same period last year.

The company provides mobile services to 9 million customers, fixed broadband internet to more than 1 million customers, and cable and satellite television services to approximately 1 million customers.

By the end of June 2026, its 5G/5G+ network was available in 130 cities, and along Romania's entire Black Sea coast. The company also extended 5G/5G+ coverage to 80% of the Bucharest metro network, with the service now available in 50 of the system's 62 stations and tunnels.

On the fixed network side, Orange upgraded 220,000 households to the latest fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) technology in the first half of 2026 by decommissioning its copper network and replacing its older fiber-to-the-building (FTTB) infrastructure.

Orange Business reported a growth in revenue of more than 20% from IT and telecommunications (IT&C) services and equipment in the first half of 2026.

Cybersecurity remained one of the company's fastest-growing business segments, with revenue rising by more than 50% amid increasing demand for digital protection services from organizations.

Its cybersecurity company SCUT, launched last year, was protecting 2,800 devices for more than 125 customers and had investigated over 8,500 security incidents by the end of June.

Large-scale IT infrastructure projects and equipment deliveries to corporate customers also supported the segment's performance. Revenue from IT&C equipment nearly doubled compared with the first half of 2025, increasing by more than 90%.

At the same time, Fundatia Orange put close to EUR 1 million in digital education, professional training, and social inclusion programs. The foundation partnered with the Administration of the National Culture Fund to co-finance by 20% projects covering inclusion topics through culture.

Through its circular economy program RE, Orange collected 38,000 used mobile phones and returned more than 5,000 refurbished devices to the market, up 35% from the same period of last year.

To complement the existing program, Orange introduced a new buyback partner across its retail network, with stores now equipped with Dipli's solution. The partnership is designed to streamline the in-store buyback process nationwide, making it easier for customers to trade in their old devices for purchasing power.

"The telecommunications industry is entering a new stage of maturity, in which connectivity is becoming the foundation of a much broader digital ecosystem. Competitive advantage will no longer be determined solely by network performance, but by the ability to integrate digital services, cybersecurity, and innovation into a value-added customer experience. That is why, even in a volatile economic environment, Orange's investments are always part of a long-term strategy. We are building the infrastructure our customers will need for many years to come," Julien Ducarroz, CEO of Orange Romania, said.

(Photo: Lcva/ Dreamstime)

simona@romania-insider.com

World.title: Two Greek Firefighters Die Battling Wildfire on Crete
World.content:
Two firefighters have died while battling a forest fire in the Krya Vrisi area of ​​Rethymno, on the island of Crete, the Greek Fire Service announced on Wednesday. State television reported that one was a seasonal firefighter and the other was a five-year veteran. They were reportedly trapped in their vehicle in the flames.

The Fire Service expressed its condolences to the families and loved ones of the deceased in a statement issued on Wednesday: “They fell heroically in the line of duty to protect the lives and property of citizens and the natural environment.”

The fire in Rethymno started in a forest area due to strong winds. Currently, 110 firefighters are operating on the front in six groups on the ground, with 27 vehicles, four helicopters as well as water tankers.

Strong winds are blowing in the area. Emergency messages have been sent to nearby residents to evacuate their homes. The villages of Krya Vrysi, Saktouria and Melampes have already been evacuated.

The Rethymno Arson Investigation Unit is investigating the causes of the fire.

Wildfires have also broken out in Messinia and Laconia in the Peloponnese and on the island of Mytilene, in the North Aegean.

A fire broke out on Tuesday on the island of Paros, in the Cyclades, which was brought under control – but a battle is still being fought to prevent a resurgence.

World.title: Counting the Dead: Kosovo Compiles List of 13,190 War Victims
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Twenty-seven years after hostilities ended, Kosovo will publish on Wednesday the first official list of victims of the 1998-99 war – dead and missing.

Based on physical files stretching hundreds of metres and more than 22 terabytes in digital form, the list compiled by the state Institute of Crimes Committed During the War in Kosovo, ICCW, runs to 13,190 names, but remains ‘preliminary’.

“For each victim, at least eight different sources of information were used before being included in this preliminary list, and I believe each case underwent thorough verification,” said Atdhe Hetemi, director of the institute.

“This is a preliminary institutional list and remains open to additions and revisions based on new documents and evidence.”

World.title: Why Serbia’s Most Successful Football Club and Party Appear Unchallengeable
World.content:
Ludogorets Razgrad surrendered their title to Levski Sofia last season in the Bulgarian league, ending their streak of 14 consecutive league titles. The ripple effect of that reached Belgrade – the nine-time consecutive champions of the Serbian SuperLiga, Red Star Belgrade, now possess the longest winning streak in European football, dating back to the 2013-14 season.

The domestic winning streak enjoyed by Red Star (or Crvena Zvezda, as they’re known at home) is surpassed only by that of the Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, whose election victories began in 2012. The SNS has “scored” six successful election wins since then. Meanwhile, Red Star will be looking to continue their victories in the new Serbian SuperLiga season, which just got underway this month.

Football and politics are often the two biggest topics in many European nations and Serbia is no different. What is starkly different to other European nations, however, is how connected and similar Serbia’s football and politics are.

Usually, when looking at sporting success, such as Red Star’s title victories, fans would refer to this as a dynasty – the type of dynasty that deserves praise for every aspect of the club, from the top to the bottom.

World.title: After the Flock: A Greek Island Mourns its Sheep, Ponders its Future
World.content:
Less than 80 kilometres from Mytilene, the capital and main port of Lesvos, the road to Chrousos – a small coastal village in the municipality of Mesotopos – crosses the western side of Lesvos through low hills and sloping, silvery olive groves before reaching the coast.

Come midday, the heat settles over the fields and the reeds barely move, while dust still hangs above the roadside long after the dirt track disappears beneath asphalt.

Stavritsa, Stavros’s wife, was setting tables when I arrived at her family restaurant.

From the terrace, the Aegean stretched out beyond a line of pine trees, although hardly anyone seems to notice the view anymore. Just weeks earlier, the couple had watched as their flock of around 500 sheep and goats was destroyed as part of the effort to contain the outbreak.

As lunch was being prepared, Stavros strolled slowly through the yard, stopping every few steps to point to a stone wall or a flowerbed. “I built this,” he said, as if reminding himself.

The restaurant has evolved over the time, shaped by what he calls his ‘sevdas’, a quiet, lifelong devotion, and ‘meraki’, meaning ‘to leave something of your soul in what you do’.

After long days spent on building sites, Stavros would return in the evenings to lay another row of stones or tend the plants before dark. A pomegranate tree stood near the entrance, its branches reaching towards the fields beyond while geraniums and rosemary spilled over the garden’s low walls.

Lunch arrived, starting with courgette flowers filled with rice and herbs, followed by wild greens and marathos dressed in lemon, as well as ladotyri cheese and bread that had barely had time to cool.

Preserved in olive oil for months, the cheese brings together the two products that have shaped Lesvos for centuries, a marriage of sheep milk and olives. Few families could get by on one source of income alone; instead, they moved between their herds and their orchards and did seasonal work as required.

In 2025 alone, Lesvos produced around 52,000 tonnes of sheep and goat milk. The island accounts for 5-6 per cent of Greece’s PDO feta production. When thousands of animals were slaughtered, those income streams disappeared overnight, with consequences for dairies, cheesemakers, feed suppliers and transporters.

Almost everything on the table in front of me had come from the surrounding fields: so it was only a matter of time before someone noticed that much of what we were eating could easily have been absent. The conversation drifted organically from lunch to livestock.

More than a flock

World.title: Montenegro Approves Paid Leave for Menstrual Pain Sufferers
World.content:
Rights groups have expressed satisfaction after Montenegro’s parliament amended the Health Insurance Law for women diagnosed with secondary dysmenorrhea – painful menstrual cramps – to grant two days of “menstrual leave” per month.

The measure, adopted by MPs on Monday, applies to women suffering such symptoms as a result of serious underlying conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, endometrial polyps, ovarian inflammation and polycystic ovary syndrome.

The initiative was submitted in March ahead of International Women’s Day by independent MP Jevrosima Pejovic. The bill previously received support from the parliamentary Health, Labour and Social Welfare Committee and the Legislative Committee.

The Women’s Rights Centre, an NGO, welcomed the adoption of paid menstrual leave, describing it as an important step toward recognising women’s health needs in the workplace. It also praised the persistence of MP Pejovic, who advocated for the measure.

“This is a valuable example of how the presence of women in politics helps give political significance to women’s experiences, which have long been pushed into the private sphere and treated as ‘secondary’ issues,” the NGO said on Tuesday.

The Centre recalled that it had proposed including this right into law two years ago, but the relevant ministry rejected the initiative at the time. “What matters now is that it does not remain merely a right on paper but becomes a concrete opportunity that provides women with safer, healthier and more dignified working conditions,” it said.

According to the explanatory note accompanying the legislation, the amendments are intended to properly regulate diagnosed pathological conditions, eliminate prejudice against women in the workplace and help balance their health needs with professional obligations.

The law defines the condition as symptoms caused by previously diagnosed gynecological disorders and lists symptoms including pain in intercourse, painful urination, infertility and unusually heavy menstrual bleeding. Diagnosis must be confirmed by a medical specialist.

Women seeking the new benefit will be required to renew their medical certificate by December 31 each year and submit it to their employer by January 30 of the following year.

The amendments also regulate compensation during leave. Under Montenegro’s Health Insurance Law, compensation for temporary incapacity for work is generally set at no less than 70 per cent of the salary base, while employers may provide a higher amount through collective agreements.

The law provides 100 per cent compensation for certain categories of illness and medical conditions, including occupational diseases and injuries, pregnancy-related complications, malignant diseases, haemophilia, cystic fibrosis, epilepsy, muscular dystrophy, cerebral palsy, paraplegia and quadriplegia, systemic autoimmune diseases, chronic renal failure requiring dialysis, HIV, psychoses and some other serious conditions.

The amendments do not say how the law will be implemented, including how employers and state institutions will verify eligibility and prevent possible abuses of the new entitlement.

BIRN was unable to reach MP Pejovic for comment on implementation of the law and safeguards against potential misuse.

The amendments are expected to enter into force after their publication in Montenegro’s Official Gazette.

World.title: Mayor Acquitted of Obstructing Justice in Kosovo War Crimes Trial
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



The defendants celebrate the acquittal at Pristina Basic Court, July 28, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Pristina Basic Court cleared local wartime commander Sami Lushtaku and seven others on Tuesday of obstruction of justice, witness intimidation and participation in a criminal group.

Sami Lushtaku, a commander in the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, for the region of Drenica, was accused of having from 2013 until 2015 forced two defendants to change their testimonies in the so-called Drenica case, in which Lushtaku and other KLA commanders from the Drenica region were accused of committing war crimes.

Lushtaku was not present when the judge announced the verdict, which was applauded by the public in the courtroom.

“The court could not find any convincing evidence which would prove the guilt of the defendants,” Judge Leon Perlaska said, reading the verdict. “The court assessed the testimony of the witness codenamed ‘Witness C’ where he denied that he was forced to change his statement,” Perlaska added.

Lushtaku, now mayor of the Kosovo town of Skenderaj/Srbica, was sentenced in 2015 to 12 years in prison by the Basic Court in Mitrovica for a murder committed in 1998, although the victim’s name was unknown and no body was found.

He was cleared on appeal in 2016 but his conviction for “command responsibility for allegedly violating the [bodily] integrity and health of an undefined number of civilian Albanians held at the Likovc detention centre” was upheld.

His sentence was reduced from 12 to seven years in prison by the Appeals Court. He was cleared by the Supreme Court in July 2017.

World.title: Kosovo Retrial Confirms Serbian Police Ex-Inspector’s Ten-Year Sentence
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Sacir Lutvija in court om July 28, 2026. Photo: BIRN.



Sacir Lutvija, a 65-year-old ethnic Gorani former member of the Serbian police force, was sentenced to ten years in prison in a retrial at the Pristina Basic Court, for war crimes committed during the 1998-99 war in Kosovo.

Serbian police and military forces staged a campaign of arrests of ethnic Albanian civilians and 11 of them were taken to Prizren police station in southern Kosovo, where Lutvija was among the inspectors who questioned them, according to the indictment.

Prosecutors said those arrested were beaten during the interrogation and subjected to electric shocks on their hands and genitals. One civilian died and ten others sustained serious injuries.

Lutvija, who has both Kosovo and Serbian citizenship, was arrested in October 2023 and has been in detention since then. The time in custody will be counted towards his sentence.

The Kosovo Special Prosecution charged Lutvija with unlawfully arresting and beating civilians, inhumane treatment and murder in his capacity as an inspector and police officer in Prizren. Lutvija pleaded not guilty in September last year.

Judge Kujtim Krasniqi on Tuesday ordered Lutvija to pay a court fee of 400 euros as well as 100 euros to the crime victims’ fund.

The verdict can be appealed.

Lutvija was initially sentenced to 10 years in prison by the Pristina Basic Court in November 2025.

But the Court of Appeals sent the case to a retrial in June this year having concluded that the Pristina Basic Court had not “concretely clarified the actions attributed to the accused in relation to each of the injured parties”.

The Court of Appeal also said the Basic Court failed to explained the accused’s participation in committing the crimes and “did not clarify the evidence upon which the conclusions presented in the verdict were based”.

The Gorani are a small Slavic ethnic group who mostly follow Islam and inhabit a highland triangle between Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia.

World.title: Left High and Dry: Drought Exposes Central Europe’s Water Crisis
World.content:
Water management and retention

Described as the proverbial “roof of Europe”, Czechia sees all its rivers, streams and waterways flow out of the country – a systemic and geological drainage which makes the country particularly dependent on precipitation from above.

“This is a significant disadvantage, because most of the water we manage has to be retained: in the landscape, soil, hydrogeological structures or water reservoirs,” says Adam Vizina, head of the hydrology department at the Water Management Research Institute.

Water management and retention are, therefore, key for this landlocked country, yet the authorities appear short on solutions.

“Water will always flow away, but we can reduce our vulnerability,” argues Vizina, listing measures such as slowing runoff, interconnecting water supply systems, managing water reservoirs better, or protecting the quality and quantity of groundwater.

The state reportedly spent 75 billion crowns (about 3 billion euros) in the past three years on drought adaptation, yet experts – including a report by the Supreme Audit Office published last March – have criticised the slow pace and limited scope of the measures.

The Slovak Academy of Sciences recently released its “Vision for Slovakia 2040”, an extensive 90-page framework document commissioned by the government of Robert Fico laying out the key policy challenges for the next 15 years.

Among those, the forward-looking blueprint “identifies more frequent droughts as a key consequence of climate change and argues that strengthening water management, increasing landscape water retention and improving the resilience of agriculture and ecosystems should be central priorities for Slovakia’s long-term development.”

Whether the authorities will act on the recommendations is another matter, with experts long highlighting key shortcomings in Slovakia’s water management practices, from fragmented governance between different institutions and ministries, a lack of concrete follow-through, and scattered water data hindering real-time monitoring.

Czechia and Slovakia’s subpar water-management has deep roots dating back to decades of intensive farming that followed its collectivisation in the 1950s and 1960s under Communism – with all that entailed in terms of land consolidation, water erosion and reduced soil fertility, among other environmental impacts.

On the upside, the Czech Republic continues to receive roughly the same amount of rain on average every year as it used to, according to some estimates. But the way, time and place it does are changing, as must the measures meant to retain and manage it more effectively, experts say: less rainfall in the spring but more in the fall, more intense precipitation during storms, but less frequent episodes of long-term and widespread rain.

According to Milan Vitek from the local branch of Greenpeace, Czechia might soon be faced with the choice of keeping its scarce water either in the rivers or in its fields, but won’t be able to do both. “Adaptation is something that we are decades behind when we could’ve been much further ahead,” he previously told BIRN.

Water management or retention are also recently being cited as a silver bullet to solve Hungary’s problems. Although Hungary has a renewable water reservoir of 11,833 cubic metres per person, one of the largest in Central Europe (only Slovenia and Serbia have more in the region), 95 per cent of that originates from outside and simply flows through the country.

The building of dams or hydroelectric power plants has been a politically sensitive issue since the controversial plan to build the Bos-Nagymaros dam on the Danube helped trigger popular revolt against the Communist government in 1990. Since then, proposals for new dams and hydropower projects have remained politically off-limits in Hungary.

But times are changing. Laszlo Gajdos, the new Hungarian government’s environment minister, said at the height of the extreme heat at the beginning of July that “water is one of our most valuable resources for the future”.

Gajdos said the government must do everything it can to improve water retention, even with dam construction where necessary. “We should not let water flow through Hungary; it needs to be retained somehow. Personally, I don’t like this method, but it seems inevitable building some dams,” he told RTL.hu.

The government of Peter Magyar is working on a new climate and environmental law, expected by late autumn, which is set to address water management issues.

Gajdos, who became Hungary’s first environment minister in 16 years, stressed that water retention is a regional issue requiring cooperation with neighbouring countries.

Andras Szollosi-Nagy, who used to advise international organisations including the UN on water diplomacy and is the founder member of the World Water Council, could not agree more.

“Water retention is always somehow part of national sovereignty,” Szollosi-Nagy says. “The country upstream believes all the water is theirs, but if they retain it, neighbouring countries are affected. We need integrated water management in the region.”

He says there is no silver bullet to solve all the problems: dams, reservoirs, new technologies, satellite-based monitoring and controlled flooding could all play a role.

“Hungary’s water management system has been systematically dismantled in recent decades,” he says. “Now we need to rebuild it from scratch.”

World.title: Dinamo Secure European Autumn for Ninth Consecutive Year
World.content:
Dinamo Zagreb have booked their place in the third qualifying round of the Champions League following a dramatic victory over Thun, with their next opponents now confirmed. The result also guarantees the Zagreb club a ninth successive European autumn, with at least a place in the Conference League already secured.

Dinamo to face Kauno Žalgiris

Dinamo will face Lithuanian champions Kauno Žalgiris in the third qualifying round after Željko Sopić’s side edged out Faroe Islands champions KÍ Klaksvík across two legs. The first leg ended goalless, before Žalgiris claimed a 1-0 victory in the return fixture thanks to a goal in the 85th minute from former Hajduk player Leon Kreković. The first leg against Dinamo takes place on August 4th at Maksimir, with the return fixture scheduled for August 11th in Lithuania.

The comeback against Thun

Dinamo’s passage to the third round came via one of the more dramatic evenings in recent European memory. Thun raced into a 2-0 lead inside 22 minutes through Brighton Labeau and Marco Burki, and Dinamo looked helpless in the early stages. Everything changed in the 67th minute when Burki was shown a red card following a VAR intervention, and the Zagreb side took full advantage. Dion Drena Beljo leveled matters in the 74th minute before Lukas Kačavenda made it 2-2 in the 78th. The tie was forced into extra time, where Moris Valinčić produced a moment of brilliance in the 112th minute to seal a memorable 3-2 victory.

Should Dinamo overcome Žalgiris, they advance to the Champions League play-off round and secure at minimum a place in the Europa League group stage. Elimination at this stage would send them into the Europa League play-off instead. Either way, Dinamo’s European autumn is already guaranteed; even in the event of further exits, a place in the Conference League group stage awaits.

World.title: Croatian Inspectors Step Up Crackdown on Illegal Holiday Rentals
World.content:
July the 29th, 2026 – Croatian inspectors have begun stepping up their crackdown on illegal holiday rentals up and down the coastline in particular, with plenty of fines already issued.

As Poslovni reports, Croatia’s State Inspectorate has intensified its inspections of holiday accommodation advertised on platforms such as Booking.com and Airbnb, targeting property owners who rent to tourists without meeting the country’s latest, strict legal requirements. The inspections form part of a broader effort to combat the shadow economy in the tourism sector and ensure fair competition among registered accommodation providers.

thousands of euros seized, thousands fined…

According to the State Inspectorate, inspectors have already uncovered numerous cases of illegal short-term rentals during this year’s tourist season. As a result, authorities have confiscated 343,000 euros in income believed to have been earned through unlawful renting, while fines imposed have exceeded 81,000 euros.

The inspections focus on identifying individuals advertising tourist accommodation without the required registration or operating in breach of Croatian tourism regulations. Authorities are checking online listings as well as conducting on-site inspections to verify whether accommodation providers comply with the law.

inspections will continue throughout summer

When inspectors discover illegal activity, they can issue fines, prohibit further renting and confiscate the financial gains obtained through unlawful operations. Officials say these measures are intended to discourage unregistered rentals and protect hosts who operate legally and meet all regulatory obligations. The State Inspectorate said inspections will continue throughout the peak summer tourist season, with online booking platforms remaining one of the primary tools used to identify suspected illegal accommodation.

Officials stress that the goal is not only to punish offenders but also to ensure equal market conditions, protect consumers and improve the overall quality and transparency of Croatia’s tourism sector. As demand for private accommodation continues to grow, authorities say stronger enforcement is necessary to prevent unfair competition and safeguard public revenue.

World.title: Airbnb Loses Its Advantage Over Booking.com for Croatian Hosts
World.content:
July the 29th, 2026 – Airbnb no longer has any advantages or particular benefits over Booking.com for Croatian hosts after the company announced significant changes recently.

As Ana Roksandic reports for Poslovni, Croatian private accommodation hosts are facing a significant changes after Airbnb announced a new commission model that many say removes one of its biggest advantages over Booking.com. Under that company’s new system, Airbnb will no longer charge guests a separate service fee. Instead, hosts will pay a 15.5% commission, replacing the previous model in which hosts paid around 3% while guests covered most of the platform’s fee.

According to Vedran Tomić, president of the Save Small Family Renters Association (SMOi), the change has been met with negative reactions from Croatian hosts. He said Airbnb’s biggest advantage had been its lower direct cost for hosts, but that will now disappear. He also pointed out that Croatian hosts must pay VAT on the commission, meaning they will now pay VAT on the full 15.5% fee instead of just the previous 3% commission.

one last summer of airbnb advantage for croatian hosts…

The new commission structure will apply as of the 13th of October. Airbnb says the change responds to feedback from hosts who found the previous pricing model confusing because guests saw an additional service fee added to the advertised accommodation price. Under the new model, guests will simply see the final price, while the commission is deducted from the host’s payout.

The changes come as Croatia’s short-term rental market is already evolving. Data from analytics platform AirDNA shows that the number of active listings has fallen in the country’s largest cities. In Split, active listings dropped from around 10,300 in June 2025 to 8,906 in June 2026, a decline of 13.5%. Zagreb recorded an even steeper fall of 25%, with analysts linking the decline to more property owners switching to long-term rentals. The market is increasingly favouring larger and more professional operators, while less profitable listings are leaving the sector.

Tomić believes the commission change is unlikely to reduce demand from travellers, but it could weaken Airbnb’s position in Croatia because it no longer offers hosts a financial advantage over Booking.com. He estimates that Booking.com controls around 70% of the Croatian market, while Airbnb accounts for roughly 20%, with the remaining 10% shared by other booking platforms.

accommodation competitiveness isn’t even the biggest issue for croatian tourism

Damir Krešić, director of Croatia’s Institute for Tourism, said higher commissions are not good news for the sector, but argued that accommodation is not the biggest competitiveness issue facing Croatian tourism. In his view, greater concerns are the rising costs of food, drinks and transport services, where Croatia has become less competitive.

Krešić also encouraged private hosts not to rely on a single booking platform. He said global platforms have given small Croatian hosts access to guests worldwide, but becoming too dependent on one intermediary weakens their bargaining position. Instead, he recommends that hosts advertise across two or three platforms to diversify their bookings and reduce risk.

World.title: Luka Modrić Visits Unfinished Villa Construction Site in Istria
World.content:
July the 29th, 2026 – Croatian footballing legend Luka Modrić has paid a visit to an unfinished villa construction site in Istria before heading off on a yacht. Could he be thinking of buying it?

As Poslovni reports, a jet black limousine with tinted rear windows stopped at a construction site in Istria a few days ago, shortly before midday. Luka Modrić, 40, captain of the Croatian national football team, got out at the parking area in front of an unfinished villa that still requires final stonework for a Mediterranean appearance.

He was accompanied by experts who went around the site with him explaining different things and pointing out important construction details. The group then entered the private property and remained inside for about half an hour. According to one of the site’s neighbours who contacted the media about the group, Luka Modrić appeared interested in the property as a possible investment, though that is not confirmed.

The same day he was later seen boarding a yacht that he rents each summer for roughly a week or ten days of family holiday along the Adriatic coastline. Media reports state that, after earlier investments in central Dalmatia and the far south of Croatia, members of the Modrić family have shown interest in property in Istria. Vanja Modrić is said to have expressed interest on several occasions in locations around Rovinj, but no purchases have so far been officially completed.

the football legend has acquired multiple properties in both croatia and spain

Over the course of his career Modrić has acquired several residential properties in Croatia and Spain.

In the elite Zadar suburb of Kožino, near where he grew up, the family owns a villa with an outdoor pool, children’s playground, garden, sea view, wine cellar, ten-car garage, gym, an eighteen-seat cinema, children’s playroom and massage room. It is used as a family base during the summer break in the football season. In October 2024 a storm damaged the access road; the damage was later repaired. The property had earlier attracted attention over reports of beach concreting in front of the estate; Modrić stated that the area in question is public land, not a private beach.

In Zagreb, the family owns a 286-square-metre villa on Pantovčak, purchased back in 2017 from former footballer Zvonimir Boban. Land-registry records show Modrić transferred ownership to his wife Vanja shortly afterwards. Before that purchase the family had lived in apartments in Ravnice and Babonićeva Street. Modrić also owns a 220-square-metre penthouse with a 29-square-metre loggia in a newly built building on Tkalčićeva Street in the city centre; media estimates placed its value at around 1.4 million euros.

Over in the Spanish capital of Madrid, where Luka Modrić spent many years playing for Real Madrid, the family owns a villa in the La Moraleja district, acquired in 2019 on a 10,000-square-metre plot. Spanish media describe it as having nine bedrooms and nine bathrooms, with the main living areas, kitchen and sitting room on the ground floor and guest rooms upstairs, plus an outdoor pool, garden and recreation space. According to media reports, part of the portfolio is formally registered in Vanja Modrić’s name.

World.title: Croatia Opens Its First Biological Swimming Pool in Čazma
World.content:
July the 29th, 2026 – Croatia has opened its very first biological swimming pool in the continental town of Čazma, representing a significant step forward in terms of sustainable tourism.

Croatia has officially opened its first biological swimming pool, marking a milestone in sustainable tourism and environmentally friendly recreation. Index reports that the new facility is located in the town of Čazma, around 60 kilometres east of Zagreb, the new facility is part of the much wider Čazma Natura project, which has the primary goal of transforming the town into a leading green tourism destination.

Unlike conventional swimming pools, the biological pool uses natural filtration instead of chlorine or other chemicals. Water is purified through biological processes involving aquatic plants and microorganisms, creating a safe swimming environment while preserving the natural ecosystem. It is the first public facility of its kind in Croatia.

The swimming area spans approximately 1,665 square metres and is divided into separate sections for swimmers and non-swimmers. Alongside the pool, visitors will find sunbathing areas, changing rooms, showers, a catering facility, children’s amenities and recreational spaces designed for families and visitors of all ages.

The pool forms part of the Bio Park Čazma complex, which also includes educational facilities, walking trails and nature-focused attractions. The project promotes sustainable tourism while highlighting the area’s biodiversity and encouraging visitors to explore the surrounding landscape.

Officials say the biological pool represents a new direction for Croatian tourism, combining recreation with environmental protection. Similar facilities have become increasingly popular across areas of Europe because they reduce chemical use, consume less energy and blend more naturally into their surroundings. With the opening of the country’s first biological swimming pool, Čazma is hoping to attract visitors looking for a different kind of summer experience, one centred on nature, sustainability and chemical-free swimming.

World.title: Croatian Firefighters Continue Battling Bordeaux Wildfire
World.content:
July the 28th, 2026 – Croatian firefighters are continuing to battle the intense Bordeaux wildfire ravaging southwestern France, and which keeps being rekindled by problematic winds.

Croatian Air Force firefighting pilots are continuing their mission in southwestern France, where they are helping battle the massive wildfire near Bordeaux. Index reports that this intense operation has now entered its fifth day, with crews facing increasingly difficult conditions as strengthening winds threaten to reignite areas that had previously been brought under control.

The members of the 855th Firefighting Squadron are operating in the Saumos area, just west of Bordeaux. According to Major Ivan Dukić, conditions improved after overnight rain, but rising temperatures and stronger afternoon winds have caused the fire to become active once again.

“The situation is much better than it initially was thanks to some rainfall. However, temperatures are increasing, and as the day progresses the wind is strengthening. The fire has been waking up again, so we’ll see what the days bring,” Dukić said from France.

Since arriving in France, the Croatian crews have carried out 118 flights, logged 20 hours of flying time, and dropped 576 tonnes of water on the catastrophic French wildfires. They are working alongside French and other international crews as part of the rescEU civil protection mechanism.

Despite the demanding mission abroad, Croatia’s aerial firefighting forces remain heavily engaged at home during the peak wildfire season. Between the 15th of June and the 27th of July, the 855th Firefighting Squadron took part in extinguishing 39 wildfires along Croatia’s coastline and on the islands.

Commander Colonel Željko Bukvić said Croatia’s ability to respond both domestically and internationally is the result of careful planning, good organisation and the experience of its firefighting crews. He stressed that the squadron remains ready to assist both Croatia and its European partners whenever needed. The enormous wildfire near Bordeaux remains one of France’s most serious emergencies, with strong, problematic winds, high temperatures and dry vegetation continuing to fuel the blaze repeatedly despite efforts. Croatian pilots remain on the front line as authorities work to prevent the fire from spreading further.

World.title: July 1377: Dubrovnik Introduces Organised Isolation of Arrivals to Combat Plague
World.content:
July the 28th, 2026 – Turning the clock back to July 1377, we saw how the ever-diplomatic Dubrovnik organised the isolation of new arrivals in order to combat the plague.

In July of the aforementioned year, the former Great Council of the Republic of Dubrovnik adopted a decision requiring people arriving in the city (and then autonomous state of Ragusa) from plague-affected areas to undergo a period of isolation before entering the city or its surroundings.

trentina – strict isolation for a period of one month

Dubrovnik was one of the most important medieval trading centres on the Adriatic. Its wealth depended on shipping, merchants and goods arriving from across the Mediterranean and the European hinterland. Those same connections also carried infectious diseases. After the Black Death swept through Europe in the mid-14th century and caused catastrophic issues, the authorities faced a clear problem. A complete ban on foreign arrivals and goods would have protected the population but would also have severely damaged an economy based on trade. Instead they introduced a compromise.

Arrivals from infected regions were not allowed to enter Dubrovnik immediately. Index writes that they had to spend a fixed period separated from the local population so that any symptoms of disease could appear. The initial isolation period lasted 30 days and was known as the “trentina”.

dubrovnik tried to stop the disease at the city gates

Isolation was carried out at Cavtat and on nearby islets such as Mrkan; later Bobara and Supetar were also used. The underlying principle was that a person who showed no signs of illness after a sufficiently long interval posed a substantially lower risk of introducing infection. Medieval physicians had absolutely no knowledge of the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which was identified much later at the very end of the 19th century. They did, however, observe from experience that the disease spread through contact and the movement of people, and that symptoms could appear only after a delay. Dubrovnik therefore tried to stop the disease at the gates rather than respond only after an outbreak inside the city.

Rules were strict. People from affected areas had to complete the prescribed isolation, and contact between Dubrovnik residents and those in isolation was limited, creating a sanitary buffer.

dubrovnik’s decision eventually became a global practice in epidemiology

The period was later extended from 30 to 40 days. The modern word “quarantine” derives from the Italian quaranta (forty). The precise reason for choosing 40 days is not certain; explanations range from medical observation to the symbolic importance of the number in Christian tradition.

In subsequent centuries Dubrovnik developed a more elaborate system, including lazarettos where travellers, merchants and goods could complete the required period of observation before entry. The arrangement allowed trade to continue under controlled conditions rather than forcing a choice between an open city exposed to disease and a completely closed one without commerce.

The 1377 decision is regarded as one of the earliest organised applications of a practice that later became a standard method of epidemic control worldwide.

World.title: Split is Launching One of Croatia’s Largest Environmental Projects
World.content:
July the 28th, 2026 – Split is set to launch one of Croatia’s largest environmental projects as part of a massive 100 million euro investment.

Poslovni reports that construction works on this enormous project will last 28 months from the contractor being introduced to the site until the start of the plant’s trial operation. The total duration of the contract itself is 43 months, including the trial operation period and obtaining the operating permit.

One of the most important infrastructure projects in Croatia’s water management sector is now beginning in Split. On Tuesday, the 28th July 2026, the start of construction works on the Stupe Wastewater Treatment Plant (UPOV Stupe) will be officially marked. The project is a key part of the “Improvement of Water and Utility Infrastructure of the Split–Solin Agglomeration” initiative.

With the expansion of the Stupe wastewater treatment plant, Split will receive a modern wastewater treatment system that, once completed, will become the second-largest wastewater treatment facility in all of Croatia and the central point of a unified sewage system serving the Split–Solin agglomeration.

The value of the contract for the design and expansion of the facility amounts to 99,056,751.25 euros including VAT. The works will be carried out by a consortium consisting of WTE Wassertechnik GmbH (lead partner) and HERING d.d.

The future facility will have a capacity of 275,000 population equivalents, with secondary biological wastewater treatment. The construction of the Stupe wastewater treatment plant will provide modern treatment of municipal wastewater for Split and the surrounding area, helping to further protect the environment, preserve the quality of the Brač Channel, and improve the quality of life for residents.

As part of the second phase of the project, eligible costs amount to 243,149,745.48 euros. Of this, €165,365,077.30 euros will be financed through non-refundable European Union funds from the Cohesion Fund, while the remaining amount will be secured through Croatian national sources.

World.title: US-Saudi strikes test Iraq’s fragile security balance
World.content:
Baghdad – US-Saudi strikes on Iraq killed at least 20 militants, including several Iranians, on Wednesday, according to the Hashed al-Shaabi, an armed Iraqi alliance that includes pro-Iran groups.

The United States and Saudi Arabia said they had struck Iran-backed armed militants in Iraq in response to attacks on US forces and Saudi oil facilities.

Washington and Tehran are Iraq’s main allies, but their enmity has long turned the country into a proxy battleground and left successive governments struggling to maintain a delicate balance between the foes.

The Hashed al-Shaabi, also known as the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), said that at least 20 fighters “were martyred and another 32 wounded according to a preliminary toll”.

Two Hashed officials told AFP that five Iranian advisors were among those killed in a strike in the central province of Diyala.

AFP correspondents saw coffins wrapped in Iranian flags during a funeral organised by the Hashed al-Shaabi in Baghdad for those killed.

The Hashed alliance was created in 2014 to fight jihadists before it was formally integrated into the Iraqi armed forces.

It now includes brigades belonging to Iran-backed groups reputed for acting unilaterally.

US President Donald Trump said the strikes were coordinated with the Iraqi government, according to Fox News.

They follow growing US pressure on Baghdad to disarm pro-Iran armed groups, which have frequently targeted US facilities in the country and have long called for the withdrawal of US troops.

Iraq’s new Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who came to power this year with Washington’s blessing, vowed to ensure those groups would hand over their weapons, but has faced pushback from some powerful factions.

Earlier this month, Zaidi visited both the United States and Iran.

– ‘Inevitable response’ –

The strikes came after Riyadh said its forces had intercepted drones targeting oil facilities, blaming the Iran-backed groups in Iraq.

The most active pro-Iran armed groups are united under an alliance known as the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, which has acted in support of Tehran during the Middle East war, claiming hundreds of attacks against US bases in Iraq and across the region.

The Islamic Resistance in Iraq said “our response to the American enemy is inevitable, and may target its tools in Saudi Arabia”.

But the group added that it would only retaliate after the Arbaeen day of pilgrimage, which falls on Tuesday.

The Arbaeen marks one of the most significant events in the Shia Muslim calendar, during which pilgrims, many from Iran, flock to Iraq to visit the holy shrines.

The pro-Iran groups denied attacking Saudi Arabia and they haven’t claimed any attacks since the US-Iran war resumed earlier this month.

– Violation –

Iraq denounced the US-Saudi strikes and said it rejects “all acts of aggression, regardless of the party responsible or the justifications presented.”

The Ministerial Council for National Security said it would “confront any violation of Iraq’s sovereignty, and prevent any source from using Iraqi territory to threaten neighbouring states”.

It reaffirmed its commitment to ensure the state’s monopoly over weapons.

Zaidi’s government has given those groups that Washington designates as terrorist organisations until September 30 to disarm.

Oil-rich Iraq has been trying to move past decades of war and unrest, but it remains vulnerable to regional and internal flare-ups.

World.title: Iraq condemns US-Saudi strikes, vows tighter control over armed groups
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq condemned U.S.-Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday that targeted Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) sites, calling the attacks a violation of its sovereignty, and announced new measures to tighten state control over security and prevent Iraqi territory from being used to threaten neighboring countries.

Following the attacks, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over an emergency meeting of the Ministerial Council for National Security, which the government said killed and injured many Iraqis.

As regional tensions rose, Al-Zaidi cancelled a planned visit to Saudi Arabia on Thursday.

In a statement published after the meeting, the council said that the strikes happened when Baghdad was already in talks with US and Saudi authorities over suspicions that Iran-aligned armed organizations operating from Iraq committed drone assaults on Saudi land.

“The government was actively engaging with the relevant parties to verify and address the concerns raised by both the Saudi and US sides,” the statement stated, adding that the military action hampered such efforts.

The council authorized a comprehensive security strategy aimed at strengthening state authority across Iraq, combating breaches of Iraqi sovereignty, and prohibiting any party from exploiting Iraqi territory to threaten neighboring nations.

The steps reflect Baghdad’s efforts to guarantee that no armed organization may launch assaults from Iraqi soil that could pull the nation into larger regional wars, while also confirming the government’s goal of bringing all security actions under state control.

The council also directed the Foreign Ministry to take legal and diplomatic measures under international law and the United Nations Charter to record the attacks and protect Iraq’s legal rights.

The government condemned the attacks but emphasized that responding to security threats and enforcing the law is solely the responsibility of Iraq’s constitutional institutions.

“The government rejects all acts of aggression, regardless of the party responsible or the justifications presented,” the statement read.

The council underlined Baghdad’s commitment to addressing regional conflicts via diplomacy while maintaining efforts to keep all armaments under state control.

It also restated Iraq’s commitment to carrying out the security agreement guiding the departure of the US-led international coalition by the end of September 2026.

The emergency conference occurred hours after US President Donald Trump claimed that the midnight attacks were coordinated with the Iraqi government, something Baghdad has not officially verified.

Iraqi authorities have openly opposed the operation, emphasizing the political sensitivity of the attacks.

The events highlight Al-Zaidi’s increasingly precarious situation, as he seeks to boost Iraq’s connections with the US and Gulf Arab governments while retaining relations with Iran.

His decision to cancel the Saudi visit underlines the gravity of the problem, as Baghdad seeks to temper regional tensions while preventing Iraqi land from becoming a battlefield for opposing forces.

The government’s current security strategy also suggests a renewed desire to prevent armed groups from operating outside official control, as Baghdad wants to reassure neighboring nations that Iraq will not be used as a springboard for assaults that endanger regional peace.

World.title: Uptime Institute partners with T964 to expand Iraq’s digital infrastructure
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Uptime Institute, based in the United States, and Iraqi digital infrastructure company Tech964 Holding Limited (T964) have formed a strategic partnership to help develop Iraq’s digital infrastructure, marking the latest technology agreement to result from Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s investment-focused visit to Washington.

The agreement, signed earlier this month at the U.S.-Iraq Business Summit hosted by the US Chamber of Commerce, names T964 as Uptime Institute’s business partner in Iraq to promote international data center standards, professional training, and the development of resilient digital infrastructure.

The agreement is part of Baghdad’s larger effort to diversify its economy beyond oil by increasing digital infrastructure, attracting technological investment, and bolstering industries including cloud computing, artificial intelligence, financial technology, and cybersecurity.

T964, one of Iraq’s major private digital infrastructure businesses, has announced that it would collaborate with the Uptime Institute to implement internationally recognized standards for the country’s expanding network of data centers, as well as increase technical competence and operational best practices.

The partnership is anticipated to help establish carrier-neutral data centers, telecommunications infrastructure, cloud services, and AI-ready digital platforms, all of which the government believes are important to modernizing public services and stimulating private-sector investment.

The pact follows a series of technological ties announced during Al-Zaidi’s tour to the United States, during which Iraq inked more than 50 agreements totaling more than $60 billion in the energy, banking, infrastructure, industrial, and technology sectors.

Improving digital infrastructure has become a key component of Iraq’s long-term economic plan, as the country strives to lessen reliance on oil earnings and establish a knowledge-based economy capable of attracting foreign technology businesses while also encouraging homegrown innovation.

The alliance also underscores increased US private-sector interest in Iraq’s digital economy, especially as demand for secure data centers, cloud computing capacity, and AI infrastructure in the Middle East grows.

Iraq has increasingly prioritized digital infrastructure for foreign investment alongside energy and transportation, with officials claiming that internationally certified data centers and modern telecommunications networks will be critical to supporting e-government services, digital banking, e-commerce, and artificial intelligence, as well as strengthening Iraq’s role as an emerging regional technology hub.

World.title: OpenAI says rogue AI agent attack hit other companies
World.content:
San Francisco – ChatGPT maker OpenAI has revealed that an autonomous artificial intelligence agent which hacked a popular platform for computer programmers also attempted to breach four other companies during the incident.

In an update late Tuesday to a blog post detailing its probe into the incident, OpenAI said its AI agent affected these “publicly-available services,” though it did not name the companies.

The revelation broadens a cyber incident that OpenAI described as unprecedented and which began when two of its models hacked Hugging Face, a site developers use to store and share AI models and code.

OpenAI admitted last week that during testing, the models powering the agent broke out of their confined environment and connected to the internet to find ways to infiltrate Hugging Face.

AI agents — systems that act autonomously to complete tasks rather than just responding to step-by-step prompts in a chatbot — are hailed across the industry as the next chapter in AI.

But they raise the specter among the public of rogue computers acting on their own.

In its update of the events leading to the hack, OpenAI said it found a handful of instances where the AI models came across login details that other companies had left exposed online, and used them to get into accounts on outside services.

In the Hugging Face episode, the models broke into four accounts across four different services, OpenAI said. One served as a “staging path” — a kind of pit stop to route the agent’s activity and cover its tracks — and another as a place to store data.

The remaining two were only accessed in a “read-only manner” and were not used to help break into Hugging Face, OpenAI said.

The company said it was contacting the owners of the affected accounts and had “not seen evidence of broader impact to these providers or other accounts on their services.”

– Better sandbox –

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview published Tuesday that the company had “paused” its own testing after the incident while it improved the security around its “sandboxing” — the process of isolating safety testing in a controlled environment.

The incident also triggered a petition signed by over 1,000 employees at cutting-edge AI companies, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, calling on the US government to help slow the release of the most advanced AI models.

This in turn has sparked accusations from other Silicon Valley players close to the White House that the companies are inviting tighter government regulation on AI in order to protect their business models and block the emergence of rivals.

The incident has also drawn rumblings from some observers that OpenAI is taking advantage of it to market the power of its state-of-the-art models.

The same accusation was leveled at Anthropic when it held back the public release of its powerful Mythos model over cybersecurity concerns.

Anthropic released a stripped-down version of Mythos, called Fable 5, but the US government quickly forced it to take it down, citing national security risks.

It gave the green light in late June after some modifications were made.

World.title: Syria’s Kurds still waiting to go home despite govt deal
World.content:
Hasakeh – At a desolate Syrian camp, home to thousands of displaced Kurds, Ahmad Oussi appealed for help to return to his hometown, seven years after a Turkish offensive drove him out.

Residents of the Talaeh camp complain former Turkish-backed fighters are squatting in their properties in the Ras al-Ain area, around 70 kilometres (40 miles) away.

“The factions are living in our homes,” Oussi, 26, complained. “We get calls from them telling us, ‘You can’t go back to your homes … they’re our homes now’.”

Oussi is among tens of thousands of Kurds who were displaced when Turkey and allied Syrian fighters seized an Arab-majority strip of border territory, including Ras al-Ain, from Kurdish control in 2019 during the civil war.

Some of the fighters subsequently settled in the area with their families, with some reportedly still living in Ras al-Ain, a formerly ethnically-mixed region in Syria’s northeast.

Oussi said the former fighters “have nowhere to go, that’s why they haven’t left our homes”.

“I hope the Kurdish administration and the Syrian government, foremost the defence ministry, will get us out of this camp and return us to our town as soon as possible,” he said.

– ‘No safety’ –

Some 5.5 million people remain internally displaced in Syria following the more than 13-year civil war, according to the United Nations.

Near tents at the camp outside the city of Hasakeh, some people have built small mud-brick homes as refuge from the scorching summer heat and bitter winter cold.

A woman hunched over to sweep the dirt as people sold fuel in soft-drink bottles by the roadside.

“We’re always told we’ll go back this week or next but it hasn’t happened yet,” said mother-of-seven Kubar Qader, 43, picking through second-hand clothes stall.

“There’s no safety because they’re still living in our homes. We’re afraid of returning… we want to go back and live in our home without fear or threat,” she said.

Turkey launched successive military offensives against Kurdish-led forces in northern Syria before the new Islamist authorities, who are close to Ankara, ousted longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024.

Human rights groups say residents’ homes and belongings were seized or looted after the 2019 offensive to capture Ras al-Ain.

The return of displaced Kurds was part of a deal reached in January between the under-pressure Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) and Damascus on integrating Kurdish institutions into the state.

Since then, displaced people have returned to the Kurdish-majority Afrin region in northwest Syria, the scene of a 2018 Turkish-led offensive, but Ras al-Ain residents are still waiting.

– ‘Die there’ –

Abdel-Karim Omar, the Kurdish authorities’ representative in Damascus, said the return of the displaced to Ras al-Ain was one of the deal’s “main outstanding issues requiring implementation”.

Jawan Isso, from a committee representing displaced people from the area, said preliminary steps had been taken on returns, including visits and de-mining operations.

But “significant obstacles” remain, he added, citing the security situation and saying the town “is still under Turkish influence”.

According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights monitor, Turkish troops are mainly present in three positions in the Ras al-Ain area.

A Hasakeh province official played down the problem, telling AFP that “dozens of families have returned” to their homes in Ras al-Ain.

“Some factional members were living in properties and homes but they left immediately after the owners” approached the local authorities, he said, requesting anonymity.

Some displaced Kurds, he added, are linked to the SDF and fear “acts of revenge and accountability unless they return through the state officially”.

Camp resident Fatna Abdel-Qader, 65, still dreams of Ras al-Ain.

“This tent is nothing like the home I left seven years ago,” she said, wiping away tears. “I long for the land of Ras al-Ain, and it is my wish to die there.”

World.title: Trump: US-Saudi strikes in Iraq coordinated with Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that US-Saudi airstrikes against Iran-backed militias in Iraq were carried out in coordination with the Iraqi government, a statement that, if confirmed, would represent a significant shift in Baghdad’s approach to powerful armed groups aligned with Tehran.

In an interview with Fox News, Trump referred to Iran-backed militias in Iraq as “a cancer on the world” and stated that he is considering “additional warnings” against Iranian proxy groups following the strikes.

The strikes were coordinated with the Iraqi government, referring to a joint US-Saudi operation.

The Iraqi administration did not immediately respond to Trump’s accusations.

The raids targeted outposts of Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), an umbrella organization that encompasses multiple Iran-backed militias and is officially incorporated into Iraq’s military forces.

The PMF said that at least 20 of its members were murdered and 32 were injured in assaults across seven Iraqi regions.

The action followed a series of drone strikes on Saudi Arabia’s eastern oil installations, which Riyadh said were carried out by Iran-backed militias operating from Iraqi territory.

The attacks were one of the most important military actions within Iraq in years, surprising many Iraqis and sparking fears that the nation was becoming a battleground for a broader regional conflict.

Hours after the strikes, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi canceled a scheduled travel to Saudi Arabia and held an emergency conference with top security officials, condemning the assaults as a breach of Iraqi sovereignty and urging caution.

Trump’s claim that Baghdad coordinated the operation seems to contradict his first public pronouncements.

If proven, however, it would imply that Iraqi officials covertly authorized action against forces that they increasingly see as acting beyond governmental authority.

Although the PMF is technically part of Iraq’s security apparatus, many of its most prominent sections have strong links to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and have repeatedly carried out military operations autonomously of the Iraqi government.

Baghdad’s regional allies have accused these organizations of dragging the country into conflicts that are detrimental to its national interests.

Analysts believe that any clandestine Iraqi collaboration with the attacks would signal rising irritation inside Baghdad with armed organizations suspected of working on behalf of Iran rather than the Iraqi state.

This change would also reflect Al-Zaidi’s larger attempts to reestablish government authority over security policy while boosting relations with the US and Gulf Arab governments.

The strikes occurred just one day after Al-Zaidi returned from a high-profile visit to Turkey, where Iraq signed agreements on energy, trade, and the Development Road transportation corridor, and weeks after visits to Washington and Tehran aimed at balancing relations with rival regional powers while attracting foreign investment.

The recent escalation highlights Baghdad’s increasingly precarious position as it strives to maintain relations with Tehran while strengthening security and economic ties with Washington and its Gulf allies.

Whether Trump’s assertion represents a major shift in Iraqi policy is likely to be one of the most keenly followed issues in the wake of the strikes.

World.title: Iraqi leaders condemn attacks on Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Prominent Iraqi figures, notably Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, have openly criticized Iran-backed militias for seeking to pull Iraq into a larger regional conflict by launching unlawful drone attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia.

In a statement on X, al-Sadr strongly criticized the militias for their dangerous actions, which jeopardize the security of the Iraqi people.

Al-Sadr’s remarks came after the United States and Saudi Arabia launched coordinated airstrikes on Iran-backed groups in several Iraqi provinces on Wednesday.

Influential Iraqi political and religious figures are escalating the pressure to disarm militant groups across the country.

The US-Saudi airstrikes were an immediate response to many drone assaults carried out by militias in the past few days against US interests in the region as well as oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.

Baghdad has initiated investigations into cross-border drone assaults in an effort to strengthen national sovereignty and prevent illegitimate military actions.

Iraqi officials confirmed that the country will not be used to launch attacks against countries in the region.

World.title: US Embassy issues new security alert, urges Americans not to travel to Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The U.S. Embassy in Baghdad on Wednesday issued a security alert advising American citizens to avoid travel to Iraq, following a series of attacks that it said were carried out by Iran-aligned militias targeting locations inside Iraq and across the region.

In the alert, the embassy urged U.S. nationals currently in Iraq to remain vigilant, closely monitor local media, and follow instructions issued by Iraqi authorities.

The embassy also warned that air travel could be affected without prior notice, including possible flight delays, cancellations, or temporary airspace closures.

As a result, American citizens planning to travel were advised to check directly with their airlines before heading to airports, as flight schedules may change at any time.

The mission reiterated that Iraq remains under the U.S. State Department’s Level 4: Do Not Travel advisory, citing terrorism, kidnapping, armed conflict, civil unrest, and the U.S. government’s limited ability to provide emergency services to its citizens in the country.

In addition to avoiding unnecessary travel, the embassy encouraged U.S. citizens already in Iraq to maintain communication with family members, ensure travel documents remain valid, and keep mobile phones fully charged.

The advisory also urged Americans to avoid protests and demonstrations, maintain a low profile, stay aware of their surroundings, and enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security updates.

Furthermore, the embassy advised citizens to follow official U.S. State Department security alerts and remain prepared for rapidly changing conditions.

The advisory comes amid heightened security tensions across Iraq and the wider region.

Earlier this week, Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said the region had recently come under drone attacks launched from the direction of Nineveh, stressing the need for an effective air defense system to protect the Kurdistan Region.

Days earlier, coalition forces intercepted eight explosive-laden drones targeting Erbil. The Kurdistan Region’s Counter-Terrorism Service said all of the drones were successfully destroyed before reaching their targets, with no casualties reported.

The U.S. Embassy continues to operate in Iraq, although the mandatory departure order for non-essential U.S. government personnel remains in effect.

World.title: With 90 out of 128 companies & 64% of investments, Karnataka top beneficiary of Centre's Electronics Development Fund
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Karnataka has emerged as the biggest beneficiary of the central govt's Electronics Development Fund (EDF), accounting for 90 of the 128 companies backed under the scheme and nearly two-thirds of the total investment made by its associated venture funds.

The eight "daughter funds" supported by EDF have invested Rs 1,335.7 crore in the 128 startups and companies as of June 30, electronics and information technology ministry told Lok Sabha Wednesday. Of these, 77 firms were working in electronics system design and manufacturing, and 51 in information technology.

Bengaluru alone accounted for 89 companies - 56 in electronics manufacturing and 33 in IT - while one company was based in Belagavi.

Together, Karnataka-based firms received Rs 854.5 crore, or about 64% of the total investment.

Telangana was a distant second, with seven Hyderabad-based firms receiving nearly Rs 130 crore. As many as eight companies in Mumbai and Pune received Rs 142.4 crore, while six Delhi firms were allotted Rs 99.2 crore. Five Chennai companies received Rs 62.2 crore.

The remaining investments went to companies in Haryana, Kerala, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.





No company from Dadra and Nagar Haveli, and Daman and Diu figured among the beneficiaries, according to the state-wise data submitted in Parliament.

EDF was established as a "fund of funds", with govt investing Rs 257.7 crore in eight professionally managed, Sebi-registered venture funds. These funds subsequently deployed more than five times that amount in technology companies. The supported firms have collectively raised around Rs 22,553.8 crore and created or acquired 373 intellectual-property assets, the ministry said.

World.title: Here's why many MBBS graduates can't take foreign licensing exams
World.content:
Thousands of students who have completed MBBS are unable to appear for any foreign licensing examination as the colleges they have graduated from have not initiated the process for an "ECFMG sponsor note" in the World Directory of Medical Schools.

This is a formal note on a medical college's listing in the world directory indicating that it meets standards set by Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG).

The directory aims to list all medical schools which have been recognised by the local govt or ministry concerned, globally. However, colleges listed here might not have sponsor notes that make their students eligible for ECFMG certification, a credential evaluation agency.

Colleges can apply electronically for credential verification only after their first batch of graduates, or roughly five years after the first batch is admitted.

Usually, colleges start the process when their first batch starts the 12-month compulsory rotating medical internship. However, many students have discovered after MBBS graduation that their colleges have not got ECFMG sponsor notes. Most students who join colleges don't check whether their college has ECFMG sponsor notes till after graduation when they want to sit for USMLE (United States Medical Licensing Examination), UK's PLAB (Professional and Linguistic Assessments Board) or other licensing exams.





Many graduates of Kalpana Chawla Medical College in Karnal, Haryana, discovered that their college did not have ECFMG sponsor notes though it admitted its first batch in 2017. Some at AIIMS have not got ECFMG sponsor notes.

In response to an RTI query , National Medical Commission (NMC) stated that "as and when any information or documents to update ECFMG sponsor note in respect of Indian medical colleges is asked by ECFMG, the same is provided to ECFMG immediately after due process and approval of competent authority".
