World.title: Russian lawmaker makes another bid to enter South Ossetian politics
World.content:
North Ossetia parliament member Dzambolat Tedeyev, who represents the A Just Russia – Patriots – For Truth party and is a former head coach of Russia’s national freestyle wrestling team, is officially returning to South Ossetian politics. What role he intends to play, however, remains unclear. His previous attempts to establish himself in the region’s political scene have all ended in failure.

A native of South Ossetia, Tedeyev once even sought to become the region’s president.

At the recent third congress of the Patriots of Alania party, which was already under Tedeyev’s influence, he was elected its chairman. The high-profile move in Tskhinvali coincided with the party’s nomination of Murat Valiyev — a serving officer in the State Protection Service and former KGB officer — as its presidential candidate.

Tedeyev said the party’s main goal would be to ensure that the views of South Ossetian citizens are heard by the republic’s leadership.

“Our position has never changed, but now we have our own platform from which we can defend the interests of our citizens and our country. Today, we see people leaving because they cannot find work. Despite an investment programme aimed at creating new businesses, unemployment remains a serious problem.

There are many issues to address. But today we have hope because, thanks to you, we now have a party where we can make our voices heard. We must unite and build the future of our republic together,” he told delegates at the party congress.

Commenting on the nomination of little-known State Protection Service officer Murat Valiyev as the party’s presidential candidate, Tedeyev appeared to acknowledge that Valiyev was being put forward as a “technical candidate.” He urged acting president and election frontrunner Marat Kambolov to “rely on” Valiyev and his allies.

Tedeyev also recalled his own failed presidential bid in 2011, when the Central Election Commission refused to register him as a candidate.

“There was a time when I wanted to run, but I wasn’t allowed to. Today, I see that Marat has greater potential, stronger connections, and is capable of achieving more. Why shouldn’t he rely on me? That’s why I decided that even if we nominate Murat Valiyev today, Marat should rely on him, on us, on all of us.

And let’s all put our ambitions aside a little. We all know what we’re capable of.”

Tedeyev’s remarks have prompted mixed reactions in South Ossetia. Local analysts say it remains unclear whether he genuinely intends to challenge for power or is instead demonstrating loyalty by putting forward his ally as a “technical candidate” in the hope of negotiating with Kambolov after the election.

The events of 2011, when Dzambolat Tedeyev unsuccessfully challenged the outgoing president, Eduard Kokoity, for power, remain fresh in South Ossetia’s collective memory.

After the Central Election Commission refused to register his presidential candidacy, Tedeyev threw his support behind former education minister Alla Dzhioyeva. Although the former official had been accused of corruption and placed under house arrest, her alliance with Tedeyev helped unite the protest vote and secure victory in the election.

The pair, however, were never allowed to take power. The Supreme Court annulled the election results, triggering days of street protests. The opposition, led by Dzhioyeva and Tedeyev, unsuccessfully sought to defend what they said was their electoral victory.

The standoff ended in a compromise that ultimately fell short of Tedeyev’s ambitions. Kokoity announced his resignation, even though his second and final term was already nearing its end, while the opposition agreed to end the protests. A repeat presidential election was scheduled for March 2012, but Dzhioyeva did not take part.

Since then, Tedeyev has periodically sought to influence political developments in South Ossetia, but without much success. Ahead of the 2024 parliamentary elections, for example, he formed an alliance with the parliamentary People’s Party, whose members were once supporters of former president Eduard Kokoity.

According to local analysts, in exchange for Tedeyev’s financial backing, the party agreed to include his allies on its electoral list. However, the alliance ultimately failed to secure a majority of seats in parliament.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Dzambolat Tedeyev takes over South Ossetia party

World.title: ‘Moscow will only push Armenia out of Russian-led blocs’: Reaction to Russia’s foreign intelligence claim
World.content:
SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

“Brussels understands that Armenia will face a severe economic crisis if Yerevan leaves the Eurasian Economic Union,” Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service said on the previous day.

The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) is a Russia-led economic bloc. Its members are Russia, Armenia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.

“Brussels should not expect the EAEU countries to keep Yerevan’s political crew afloat or bankroll its marathon swim toward the European Union,” the SVR said.

In Armenia, observers noted that the statement followed a phone call between Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin on July 27. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said one of the main topics was a referendum in Armenia on European Union membership or continued participation in the EAEU.

“We stressed the need for Armenia to hold a referendum as soon as possible so Armenians can decide which direction they want to take,” Peskov said.

The Kremlin’s readout of the call did not mention Pashinyan’s response. However, the Armenian prime minister’s office said he told Putin:

“Holding such a referendum would only become possible after Armenia submits an official application to join the European Union and the issue takes on practical significance.”

The Armenian authorities have given Russia the same response on several previous occasions.

Local analysts viewed the Kremlin’s remarks and the SVR statement as another attempt to pressure Armenia.

In their view, the crisis in bilateral relations continues, and “there is still no solution in sight”. They also questioned why Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, rather than the EAEU itself, had spoken on the bloc’s behalf.

The Armenian prime minister’s office said that, during the call, “Pashinyan stressed that restrictions on exports of Armenian-made goods to the Russian market violate the legal framework governing Armenia-Russia relations and Eurasian Economic Union regulations. He asked Russia to take steps to resolve the issue.” Pashinyan appears to have called Putin primarily over Russia’s ban on imports of numerous Armenian food products and other goods. Russia introduced the restrictions at the end of May.

Statement by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service

The SVR titled its statement, “The EU Lures Armenia but Cannot Help It.” The statement argues that Armenia would face a severe economic crisis if it left the EAEU.

“Armenia will lose the income it currently receives from Eurasian integration. The remaining EAEU members will not bankroll the Armenian authorities as they row toward the European Union. EU institutions acknowledge that the bloc’s worsening economic problems, driven by anti-Russian sanctions and what they describe as Brussels’ obsession with supporting the war in Ukraine, will leave the EU unable to offset Armenia’s multi-billion-dollar losses. Several European countries have already told EU leaders they are unwilling to open their markets to Armenian goods at the expense of domestic producers.”

Russia’s foreign intelligence service also claims the EU will continue to assure Yerevan of its unwavering support.

“The EU plans to explain the lack of tangible assistance by arguing that accession depends entirely on Yerevan and on its own ‘progress’ toward European integration.”

According to the SVR, the EU has already presented Pashinyan’s government with the following demands:

reduce the presence of Russian businesses in strategic sectors;

sever humanitarian ties with Russia;

suppress domestic opponents who resist those policies.

The statement adds that the EU will encourage Armenia by “holding out the prospect of visa liberalisation for Armenian citizens and promising that, at some distant point in the future, Armenia will become a ‘prosperous crossroads of peace.’

How Armenians View European Integration: Poll Results

Against the backdrop of Russia’s call for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether to remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership, local broadcaster Factor TV conducted an online poll. Participants answered the following question: “If a referendum on choosing between the EAEU and the EU were held this Sunday, which would you vote for?”

According to the broadcaster, more than 3,300 people have already taken part in the poll. The results are as follows:

74% said they would vote for EU membership;

said they would vote for EU membership; 21% said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU;

said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU; 5% said they were undecided.

Reactions

Political analyst Samvel Melkisetian said:

“Statements like these from Moscow are nothing new. They fit a long-established Russian pattern. The aim is to show both domestic and international audiences that Russia remains actively involved in regional developments. They also seek to expose what they portray as the EU’s and the West’s ‘hidden mechanisms’ of harmful influence across the post-Soviet region.”

He also noted that Moscow’s rhetoric often portrays Armenia not as a sovereign state making its own decisions, but as an object of external influence.

Political analyst Hovsep Khurshudyan said:

“What does Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service have to do with the EAEU that allows it to speak on behalf of the bloc’s member states? Has the SVR become the press office for the EAEU or its members?”

Khurshudyan also questioned Russia’s intelligence service:

“How can Brussels be accused of driving Armenia’s economy into crisis when it is Brussels that is compensating for the losses caused by the sanctions Russia has imposed?”

He was referring to EU support programmes launched after Russia restricted imports of Armenian goods.

Khurshudyan argues that, in the end, Russia’s actions will only accelerate:

Armenia’s withdrawal from Russian-led integration structures, including the EAEU and the Collective Security Treaty Organization;

the withdrawal of Russian border guards from Armenia’s borders with Iran and Turkey;

the termination of the concession agreement under which a Russian company operates Armenia’s railways.

Khurshudyan believes Armenia still has room to take further steps, while Russia has already exhausted most of its leverage.

SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

World.title: Imam of Georgia’s Akhaltsikhe mosque and family members brutally beaten
World.content:
Georgia‘s Interior Ministry has launched an investigation into an attack on the family of a Meskhetian Muslim in the city of Akhaltsikhe. According to the victims, more than 10 people assaulted the imam of the local mosque, Shevket Dvalidze, and members of his family during the incident on 18 July.

The attack was first reported by the news outlet Batumelebi. According to the publication, the assault began after the imam’s son and an underage relative visiting from Turkey were heard speaking Turkish to each other.

Meskhetian Muslims, also known as Meskhetian Turks or Ahiska Turks, are a Turkic ethnic group originating from the historical region of Meskheti in southwestern Georgia.

Shevket Dvalidze, imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque

According to the imam’s family, the group initially confronted them verbally, hurling insults over their use of the Turkish language, before the argument escalated into a physical assault.

The victims said the attackers followed them to their home and brutally beat them in the courtyard. Shevket Dvalidze, the imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque, sustained the most serious injuries and was later taken to hospital.

Batumelebi reported that Dvalidze was also urged to withdraw his police complaint.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry said it had opened an investigation under Article 126 of the Criminal Code, which covers physical violence.

The Georgian-based Social Justice Center responded to the incident by calling on the authorities to conduct a prompt and effective investigation and to properly assess whether the attack was motivated by discrimination.

According to the organisation, the victims said that between 10 and 12 people took part in the assault, and that most of them had been identified. However, only two suspects were arrested and were later released on bail by a court.

The Social Justice Center said the circumstances suggested the case could constitute not only an act of violence but also a hate crime, as the attack may have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation said investigators should examine whether the assault was motivated by the victims’ ethnic, religious or linguistic identity and ensure those circumstances are properly reflected in the legal classification of the case.

According to the Social Justice Center, correctly classifying the attack as a hate crime is important not only because of its legal consequences, but also because it acknowledges the true nature of the offence and helps prevent similar incidents.

The organisation called on the Interior Ministry and the Prosecutor’s Office to identify all those involved in the attack, rather than limiting the investigation to the two detained suspects. It also urged investigators to examine allegations that pressure had been put on the imam to withdraw his police complaint.

The Social Justice Center also called on the government and the Office of the State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality to publicly condemn the violence against the Meskhetian Muslim family, which it said appeared to have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation further urged the authorities to strengthen policies promoting equality, rebuilding trust and supporting cultural diversity in Akhaltsikhe’s Meskhetian Muslim communities, while reviewing barriers related to the repatriation and citizenship of Meskhetian Muslims.

Imam beaten in Georgia after speaking Turkish

World.title: Nauru cuts diplomatic ties with occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The Pacific island nation of Nauru has cut diplomatic ties with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, Georgia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

According to the ministry, Nauru’s cabinet decided on 21 July 2026 to terminate diplomatic relations “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of South Ossetia, also known as the State of Alania,” and “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of Abkhazia.”

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation based on shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions to be independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to back the Moscow-backed move.

Nauru is a small island nation in the Pacific Ocean, in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 square kilometres, the country is smaller than several districts of Tbilisi, while its population is estimated at around 12,000 to 13,000 people.

Nauru ends ties with Abkhazia and South Ossetia

World.title: Five fined and four jailed in Tbilisi activists’ case
World.content:
A court in Georgia has concluded hearings in the cases of 10 activists detained outside Tbilisi City Hall on 26 July. Four were sentenced to administrative detention, while five were fined. Proceedings against one remaining activist have been postponed until 31 July.

What happened

The incident began when activist Tornike Toshkhua staged a solo protest outside Tbilisi City Hall holding a banner reading: “Bidzina d*ck? Yes – No.” The slogan referred to Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Police detained Toshkhua at the scene.

Tornike Toshkhua

In response, a group of activists gathered outside Tbilisi City Hall carrying banners with the same slogan to express solidarity with Toshkhua. Within minutes, police began detaining them as well. In total, nine more people were arrested alongside Toshkhua.

They have been charged with using abusive language in a public place and disobeying lawful police orders.

Fines and detentions

The activists began appearing in court from the afternoon of 28 July, before the 48-hour detention period had expired.

The first ruling was delivered in the case of Vaso Beridze. The judge fined him 5,000 lari ($1,850), rejecting the Interior Ministry’s request to place him under administrative detention.

In the case of Ia Melitauri, the Interior Ministry sought the maximum administrative detention, but the judge sentenced her to five days in custody instead. Police accused Melitauri of using abusive language in a public place and disobeying lawful police orders. The judge found no evidence that she had disobeyed police and convicted her only of petty hooliganism.

Melitauri had previously been found guilty twice of administrative offences involving disobeying police and insulting a police officer. A third offence under the same provision carries criminal liability.

According to people present at the hearing, Melitauri told the court she had been mistreated by police following her arrest and showed the judge injuries she said she had sustained during her detention.

The hearing in the case of the third detainee, Tornike Tikaradze, was postponed until 31 July. Tikaradze did not attend the hearing in protest.

Another judge heard the cases of seven other activists and, after several hours of witness testimony and reviewing video evidence, delivered the following verdicts:

Tornike Toshkhua was fined 3,000 lari ($1,110);

Mariam Mekantsishvili was fined 6,000 lari ($2,220);

Nato Bolkvadze was sentenced to five days of administrative detention;

Shako Bagdoshvili was sentenced to 10 days of administrative detention;

Lasha Dgebuadze was sentenced to 10 days of administrative detention;

Marine Nanava was fined 5,000 lari ($1,850);

Sandro Sekhniashvili was fined 5,000 lari ($1,850).

Scuffle outside the courthouse

Several reports of scuffles between members of the public and court bailiffs emerged throughout the day as the hearings were under way.

Videos circulating on social media showed bailiffs forcibly removing people from the courthouse.

During the final hearing, activist Ruska Mchedlidze and lawyer Marika Arevadze said court bailiffs used force against them.

Ruska Mchedlidze

“Zonder bailiff Davit Matiashvili and other zonder bailiffs physically assaulted me in the courtyard of this unjust court. Yes, I spat at them, and yes, I spat at them again after the assault, once I was outside the gates.

These bruises will heal, but everyone will remember his disgrace forever. His, and that of the other zonder bailiffs carrying out unlawful orders. There were around 20 police officers standing there, watching as these aggressive men assaulted me, and not one of them intervened,” Mchedlidze wrote on social media.

Activist Lado Jakhua also shared footage showing several court bailiffs dragging Ruska Mchedlidze out of the courthouse courtyard.

Tbilisi activists sentenced over protest

World.title: Opposition grows in Abkhazia over monument to citizens killed in Ukraine war
World.content:
A group of Abkhaz politicians and public figures has spoken out against plans to erect a monument in Sukhum to citizens of Abkhazia who were killed while fighting in the war in Ukraine.

They appealed to the republic’s president, Badra Gunba, and the city authorities to cancel or postpone the decision, which was approved by the Sukhum City Assembly at the initiative of the city administration.

The appeal was signed by former parliament speaker Valery Kvarchia, People’s Artist Batal Jopua, historian Guram Gumba, former education minister Adgur Kakoba, Akhyatsa civic organisation head Akhra Bzhania, and former leader of the Aruaa veterans’ movement Ilya Guniya.

The signatories argue that any memorial erected in the Abkhaz capital should commemorate historical events only after they have stood the test of time.

“Fighting is still under way, people are dying, yet the local authorities in Abkhazia have taken the unprecedented decision to erect a monument to a war that has not yet ended.

“No one knows how, when or on what terms these two closely related peoples will first reach understanding and then reconciliation. But that will inevitably happen. Only then, years later, will we be able to return to the question of creating a memorial to this historical event,” the appeal says.

The authors also point out that Sukhum still has no monuments to Abkhazia’s first president, Vladislav Ardzinba, or to volunteers from the North Caucasus republics who fought alongside Abkhazia during the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war.

“If we intend to begin preserving our historical memory, we should start with them. Otherwise, not only the people of Abkhazia but also our friends in the North Caucasus and the parents of the fallen volunteers will not understand us,” the appeal says.

The signatories also argue that the issue has an important foreign policy dimension. Despite its strategic partnership with Russia, they say, Abkhazia is not at war with Ukraine.

“Our state has never carried out any mobilisation or organisational measures in connection with what Russia calls its ‘special military operation’. The relevant authorities have no information about either the total number of our citizens in the conflict zone or the terms under which they entered military service,” the appeal says.

They argue that officially recognising the participation of Abkhaz citizens in the fighting would provide diplomatic grounds for Ukraine and its regional allies, including Turkey, to regard Abkhazia as a party to the conflict. As a result, they say, “our citizens’ participation in the war would cease to be a matter of personal choice and instead become our collective choice.”

Although the appeal has been signed by only six people, its authors say they believe their views are widely shared across Abkhaz society.

“We are in contact with people from all walks of life and can say with confidence that thousands of residents of Sukhum and citizens of Abkhazia share our views and the arguments set out above.”

The signatories call on the president and the city authorities to act with prudence and wisdom.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Monument to Abkhazians who fought in Ukraine

World.title: Turkey takes practical steps to restore rail link with Armenia
World.content:
Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

Turkey has begun restoring the entire railway infrastructure along the Akyaka–Gyumri route, the section connecting it with Armenia. Preliminary estimates suggest the work will take two to three months to complete. Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas told this to a group of Armenian journalists visiting Turkey.

According to Toptas, the construction work now under way in Turkey signals preparations for reopening the Armenian-Turkish border. He said reopening the border would give Turkey another route to the Caucasus. It would also allow Armenia to establish transport links with Middle Eastern countries through Turkey.

Kadir Bozan, chairman of the Kars Chamber of Commerce and Industry, also told the Armenian journalists that freight traffic on the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway has increased by 400% in recent months. He did not specify whether Armenia uses the route for exports or imports.

However, on 24 May, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said that “the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway is now open for exports from Armenia and imports into Armenia.” He described the development as extremely important for the country’s economy.

Armenian journalists’ impressions from their visit to Turkey

According to official information, a group of Armenian journalists travelled to Turkey as part of a journalist exchange programme. The purpose of the visit was to observe progress on the work to reopen the railway on the Turkish side.

The journalists also wanted to see how Turkey’s railway infrastructure operates more broadly. In particular, they travelled by train from Kars to Akyaka. The 57-kilometre journey took just 50 minutes.

After returning, they wrote that Akyaka station lies only 18–20 kilometres from the Armenian city of Gyumri. That means the journey would take just 30–40 minutes. However, the closed border currently makes it impossible to travel from Akyaka to Gyumri.

Tender announced for Akyaka–Gyumri highway

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas said Turkey plans to restore not only the railway but also the highway.

“The tender for the construction of the road from Akyaka to Gyumri has already been announced. We now expect work on that project to begin as well,” he said.

According to Toptas, these developments indicate that both governments are moving towards establishing good-neighbourly and friendly relations.

The mayor said reopening the Armenian-Turkish border and expanding bilateral economic cooperation would benefit both countries. He believes the two sides have opportunities to cooperate in both agriculture and industry.

The Armenian journalists also spoke with residents of Turkish settlements near the Armenian border. Most said they hope the border will reopen as soon as possible. They also believe it will create new economic opportunities for local communities on both sides of the border.

“We do not expect any obstacles to reopening the border”

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas expressed optimism about the prospects for normalising relations between Armenia and Turkey. In his view, once Armenia and Azerbaijan normalise their relations, reopening the Armenian-Turkish border should not present any difficulties.

He said that, on the instructions of the Turkish president and under the coordination of the transport ministry, officials have begun preparatory work at the border crossing points ahead of the border’s reopening. Railway infrastructure also requires restoration. However, he said the closed border remains the main obstacle to resuming rail services.

At the beginning of 2026, Armenian media reported that the Armenian-Turkish border would open on 1 February to third-country nationals and holders of diplomatic passports. Armenia’s and Turkey’s special envoys for normalisation, Ruben Rubinyan and Serdar Kilic, reached that agreement in July 2022. The Margara border crossing on the Armenian side has stood ready to receive travellers since December 2023. Despite those agreements, however, Turkey has kept the border closed.

Even so, the two countries periodically announce positive steps. For example, from 1 January 2026, Armenia and Turkey simplified visa procedures for holders of diplomatic, special and service passports. They can now obtain a free electronic visa (e-visa) for short-term trips of up to 20 days.

Background

Since 2008, Armenia’s railway network has operated under a concession held by the South Caucasus Railway company, a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The concession agreement runs for 30 years, with an option to extend it by another 10 years if both sides agree.

Armenian experts say freight traffic on the country’s railways has halved since 2008. Some routes have ceased operating, while the mandatory investment commitments have never materialised.

Despite this, Yerevan asked Moscow to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

Rebuilding these lines would reconnect Armenia with the borders of Azerbaijan and Turkey. This is strategically important for Yerevan, which seeks to fully unblock regional transport links.

Russia has neither acted on Armenia’s request nor indicated a willingness to do so. At the same time, Moscow has said it does not intend to give up its railway concession.

Meanwhile, the Armenian government is considering revoking Russia’s concession and taking control of the railway network itself. It has also left open the possibility of transferring the concession to a third party.

At the beginning of July, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan announced that Armenia had begun preparatory work to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

“We will carry out this work ourselves. As for the remaining sections, we will continue working-level discussions, including with our Russian partners,” he said.

Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘Dictator wants to be liked by everyone. Those who don’t like him must be neutralised’
World.content:
Transparency International Georgia researcher Zviad Koridze believes that Georgia’s current system of governance is built on fostering civil confrontation and deepening divisions within society. In his view, authoritarian regimes rely on social polarisation and the portrayal of people with different opinions as enemies in order to maintain power.

Koridze said that Georgian society still retains the capacity to resist, and that, ultimately, it is civic engagement that will serve as the main force pushing back against these processes.

On 26 July, MMA (mixed martial arts) fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, together with several supporters, announced the creation of a civic movement that will “respond immediately” to issues involving ancestors, religion, history and other subjects that the group considers offensive. According to Kartvelishvili, the movement will be “highly active, well-organised and constructive”, and any “patriotic Georgian” will be able to join. Members of the group also said they were prepared to take responsibility for their actions, including serving prison sentences if necessary.

Zviad Koridze: “the system of governance that has taken hold in Georgia — Bidzina Ivanishvili’s dictatorship — regards civil confrontation as its natural state, just like any other dictatorship. Without it, those in power cannot consolidate their rule. They cannot persuade citizens that their continued grip on power and authoritarian governance serve the public interest. To do that, they need civil confrontation.

“All dictatorships are structured and develop in exactly this way. They need to identify groups and segments of society whose views differ from those of the autocrat. Then another social group must emerge to confront and suppress them. That is the language of civil confrontation.”

“When parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili says that we do not need to join the European Union because we should have the right to make our own decisions, that is clearly not his independent position but Bidzina Ivanishvili’s. Papuashvili’s role is to voice that position and to support the creation of precisely these kinds of vigilante groups. He is expected to welcome their emergence. He sees this as a form of sovereign governance, and that is exactly why he does not want Georgia to join the European Union.

“How can a writer be liked by everyone? Is there a single writer who is universally admired? How can anyone even make such a claim? Or say that a public figure must be liked by everyone? Only a dictator wants that. He wants everyone to like him. And anyone who does not must be neutralised, driven out, persecuted and beaten. That is why he creates groups like these.

“These restrictions are designed to instil a climate of irrational fear, discouraging people from thinking independently, protesting and speaking out. The current situation is exactly the one Bidzina Ivanishvili wants most, and he is using every mechanism at his disposal to maintain it. The only force capable of dismantling these mechanisms is society itself — a society with a firm stance. I do not believe society is silent. I am convinced that our society will resist.”

Civil confrontation in Georgia

World.title: Tasmanian producer pulls products after Four Corners report
World.content:
Stuart Young has been hand-producing small batches of jarred goods on his farm in southern Tasmania for more than a decade.

His business, Range Tasmania, says ingredients not grown on the farm are "sourced from further afield", meaning mainland Australia.

But this week Mr Young learned one of those ingredients may have come from much further afield than he could have imagined.

A Four Corners investigation has found that more than 80 per cent of forensically tested samples of Leggo's tomato paste had chemical profiles consistent with tomatoes grown in China.

Stuart Young says his products labelled as having ingredients from "further afield" meant the Australian mainland, not China. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

That is despite the company advertising the use of Australian-grown produce.

The revelation prompted Mr Young to pull three of his own products containing Leggo's tomato paste off the shelf.

"[We are ] taking the products out of sale temporarily until we learn more will certainly affect our bottom line and possibly our reputation," Mr Young said.

"But our customers deserve transparency in the truth."

Stuart Young says his search for answers has been eroding his faith in the system. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Fears of flow-on effects

Range Tasmania told its customers the decision was made "as a precaution" while the business sought further advice from authorities and independent varification.

When 'Australian grown' is grown in China One of Australia's biggest tomato brands and two major supermarkets are selling products that exclusive forensic testing shows have misleading labelling.

Mr Young says trying to get clear information has been "frustrating" and has made him lose faith in the system.

"I want some assurance or some guidance from food regulators as to what we should do," he said.

" I don't know if there's other small producers or large producers out there that use Australian tomato products in their produce only to learn that they're in the same boat. "

Stuart Young says his customers deserve transparency. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Leggo's owner Simplot declined an interview with the ABC but, in a statement, said it rejected the test results.

"Simplot maintains comprehensive traceability, supplier verification and audit processes across its supply chain," a spokesperson said.

"We work closely with our suppliers through quality assurance, sourcing verification and compliance programs to ensure our products meet our quality, sourcing and regulatory requirements."

The company said it had supply chain documentation tracing the failed products back to Australian farms where the tomatoes were grown. But it said it had not done forensic testing.

Leggo's tomato paste products failed country-of-origin testing conducted by a lab for Four Corners. (Four Corners: Jack Fisher)

Modern slavery concerns

As part of the Four Corners investigation, forensic laboratory Source Certain tested more than 900 samples of 221 tomato products from 39 brands.

Its analysis showed that about half the products that contained tomatoes from China were traced to Xinjiang, where forced Uyghur labour is known to be used.

Of the failed Leggo's products, two thirds were linked to Xinjiang.

Although the testing cannot determine whether forced labour was involved, Nationals Leader Matt Canavan described the results as "greatly concerning".

Last week the Trump administration imposed a 12.5 per cent tariff on Australian goods, citing Australia's failure to effectively ban forced-labour imports.

Food fraud investigation A Four Corners investigation has uncovered products whose labels did not match independent scientific testing, raising serious questions about the integrity of Australia's food supply.

Mr Canavan said although the tariffs were "unjustified", that should not stop the federal government from acting on modern slavery.

"It is very important that the government doesn't just say that we have world-leading legislation against slavery — we actually follow it up and enforce it," Mr Canavan said.

"These sorts of allegations need to be taken seriously, they need to be followed up, and we just can't have any truck with products or supply chains that involve slave labour.

"They should not be welcome in our country."

Testing conducted for Four Corners indicated that Coles Italian tomato paste contained tomatoes grown in China. (Four Corners: Jack Fisher)

Mr Canavan said the government needed to examine the allegations and crack down on companies using misleading labelling.

"If anybody has been lying, they need to be held to account," he said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese defended the government's record on food safety, but would not say whether he supported a ban on products from Xinjiang.

"We have strong laws when it comes to food security and we'll continue to examine all of those issues," he said.

Australia's broken food labelling system Industry insiders reveal how Australians are being deceived by marketing and labelling that makes ultra-processed foods appear healthier than they really are.

A spokesperson for the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said it was "considering the issues and allegations raised in the Four Corners report".

"Businesses have obligations under the Australian Consumer Law to not make false or misleading representations," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"Whether there is a breach of the Australian consumer law will depend on the specific facts and circumstances of each matter, including understanding details of the available testing methods."

The spokesperson said the ACCC had previously issued penalties against businesses which make misleading claims, including in regard to country-of-origin food labelling.

World.title: Rushdie's attacker convicted of terrorism in US court
World.content:
A man has been convicted of federal terrorism charges in the 2022 stabbing of author Salman Rushdie.

A US federal court jury found Hadi Matar guilty of all charges against him on Wednesday, New York time, including engaging in an act of transnational terrorism.

Matar, 28, is already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence on an attempted murder conviction related to the August 2022 attack. The federal conviction carries a potential life sentence.

Rushdie, who has faced decades-old death threats, was about to speak on writers' safety when he was slashed 15 times in front of a stunned audience.

The attack left him gravely wounded, and he lost sight in his right eye.

Matar declines to testify

Prosecutors asserted that Matar was motivated by the late Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khamenei's 1989 call for Rushdie's death because of his book The Satanic Verses.

Defence lawyer Nathaniel Barone countered that the government had no proof of what was going through Matar's mind.

Matar himself declined to testify, but Rushdie did, telling jurors, "I can't say what his ambitions or his aim was, but the wounds were dispersed across my body."

Rushdie testified telling jurors "the wounds were dispersed across my body". (Reuters: Fabrizio Bensch)

The Satanic Verses, a novel about the lives and dreams of two actors who survive a plane explosion, was published in 1988.

It drew critical acclaim in the United Kingdom but engendered protests around the Muslim world over what some believers saw as blasphemous suggestions about Islam's Prophet Mohammed, particularly in a dream sequence.

Rushdie, who was born into a Muslim family, has said the dream sequence was just that. But he went into hiding for years, gradually emerging after Iran's government distanced itself in 1998 from Khamenei's fatwa, or religious edict.

"For two decades or more, I led a public life without a hint of trouble", Rushdie testified at the trial in Buffalo, New York.

Loading...

Yet the fatwa was never rescinded; indeed, Khamenei's successor, the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, indicated in 2017 that it remained in effect.

An Iranian foundation has offered a more than $3 million bounty for killing Rushdie.

Matar's messages showed him zeroing in on Rushdie

Matar repeatedly broached the fatwa with contacts in messaging apps in 2021 and 2022, according to exhibits shown in court.

The messages showed Matar felt Rushdie had attacked Islam and, by surviving, emboldened others to insult the faith.

Matar alluded to a 2006 comment along those lines by the late Hezbollah militant group leader Hassan Nasrallah, the messages showed.

A timeline of Iran's fatwa against author Salman Rushdie Indian-born novelist Salman Rushdie was ordered killed by Iran in 1989 because of his writing. Here is a timeline of all that followed.

Born in the US, Matar also holds citizenship in Lebanon, where Hezbollah is based.

Prosecutors said that photos in Matar's New Jersey bedroom and on his computer indicated his support for Hezbollah, which the US has designated a terrorist organisation.

Matar aimed to fulfil the fatwa and "wanted everyone to know he was doing this for Hezbollah", assistant US attorney Timothy Lynch said in an opening statement.

The messages showed Matar initially talked about wanting to "expose" Rushdie, then about taking his life.

In a private note to himself, he wrote, "We need to kill him ASAP", according to Mr Lynch.

The prosecutor said Matar framed the planned killing as part of what he considered a jihad, or holy war.

By spring 2022, the electronic chats showed Matar wrote that he had discerned where Rushdie lived and was tracking his public appearances, eventually pointing out his scheduled August 2022 talk at the Chautauqua Institution, a western New York arts and intellectual centre.

As Rushdie was being introduced, his attacker climbed on stage behind him, then stabbed him 15 times as the audience gasped.

Spectators and another speaker, Henry Reese, scrambled to aid Rushdie.

Law enforcement officers, assigned to the event, arrested the attacker — soon identified as Matar — after civilians restrained him.

Rushdie published a 2024 memoir about the attack, and then returned to fiction with last year's The Eleventh Hour.

The author, who Britain’s late Queen Elizabeth II knighted, received a Dayton Literary Peace Prize lifetime achievement award in November.

AP

World.title: Two-decade-old Toyota Corolla stuns Gibb River Road onlookers
World.content:
"Where there's a will, there's a way" has been the mantra of Jonny Charles as he ventured onto one of Western Australia's most famous four-wheel-drive tracks in a 2002 Toyota Corolla.

Hailing from the Gippsland region in Victoria, the 24-year-old has been on the road since February, most recently traversing the Gibb River Road in WA's Kimberley.

His trip around Australia has become a social media sensation, attracting support from thousands online.

Mr Charles stopped in El Questro in the East Kimberley and crossed the Pentecost River in his Corolla. (Supplied: Jonny Charles)

Mr Charles said he wanted to get out and explore, and the Corolla just so happened to be the car he owned.

The vehicle cost him $2,000 and originally served him well as a delivery driver through university.

Taking on the Gibb

The Gibb, his most recent challenge, stretches 660 kilometres from Derby in the west to Kununurra and Wyndham in the east, around 2,300km north of Perth.

The route attracts thousands of adventurous visitors each year.

"The Gibb is a beautiful road," he said.

" I'd heard so many good things about it and thought, 'why not give it a crack?' "

The road includes river crossings, corrugations and rocky terrain, but Mr Charles said he was never too concerned.

"I just love the challenge," Mr Charles said.

"I love it when stuff goes wrong and breaks."

Makeshift river crossing

His engineering degree and experience at a mechanic's workshop was put to use for the Pentecost River Crossing, located between El Questro Wilderness Park and Home Valley Station.

Framed by the towering red sandstone cliffs of the Cockburn Range, the crossing is about 60 metres long.

The 2002 Toyota Corolla has been suitably adapted to tackle the Gibb. (Supplied: Jonny Charles)

To keep his engine dry Mr Charles fashioned a homemade snorkel from a $2 pool noodle and duct tape.

"Worked a treat," he said.

His successful crossing was met with cheers from onlookers.

Loading...

"There was a good number of people, with the camp there," Mr Charles said.

"They hadn't seen that before, I don't think."

The Corolla is not the first aging two-wheel-drive to tackle the Pentecost.

A charity event held in 2025 saw cars worth just $1,500 make it across.

The challenge was held by S***Box Rallies, an organisation encouraging teams to take on some of Australia's most formidable roads to raise money for cancer support and prevention.

'Cafe Corolla'

Tucked away in the boot of Mr Charles' car is a commercial grade coffee machine, grinder, beans and cartons of milk.

The 'Cafe Corolla' charges a flat rate of $5 per coffee, and is helping fund Mr Charles' travels.

The Gibb River Road is a 660km-long unsealed road, the perfect place for coffee. (Supplied: Jonny Charles)

He said it had also been a great way to meet people out on the road.

"I've solo-travelled in the past and kind of struggled to make too many friends," Mr Charles said.

" But the coffee brings people out in the morning. You have a quick chat and I love that. "

He plans to continue his lap of Australia down the WA coast after conquering the Gibb.

"If you see me, come say g'day," he said.

"I'll try and make you a coffee if I can."

World.title: Weightlifter Cikamatana claims Glasgow gold after Paris pain
World.content:
Australian weightlifter Eileen Cikamatana struggled through days when she wanted to give up and "be a baby in my mum's arms".

But the 26-year-old has found consolation after her Paris Olympics heartbreak, bouncing back in Glasgow to win her third Commonwealth Games gold medal.

Cikamatana was a class above in the women's 86kg event, nailing a 108kg snatch and a 140kg clean and jerk for a Games record total of 248kg.

England's silver medallist Madias Ngake lifted a total of 239kg, while Canadian teenager Rose Beaudoin (230kg total) took bronze.

Eileen Cikamatana in action during the weightlifting in Glasgow. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

In tears after narrowly missing out on a bronze medal when she finished fourth on Olympic debut at Paris 2024, Cikamatana was in tears again in Glasgow, just of a different kind.

"Mission accomplished. I came for one thing, and I got that one thing," Cikamatana beamed.

"I had days that I just wanted to go back home and be a baby in my mum's arms.

"I had days that I wanted to exit the door, but I'm glad I pulled that left leg back in.

"The original plan was to finish off after the Paris Olympics, but we (with coach Paul Coffa) didn't get what we wanted."

Madias Ngake (left), Eileen Cikamatana, and Rose Beaoudin celebrate their medals. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Cikamatana is the third female weightlifter in history to achieve the Commonwealth Games feat of three titles in a row, joining India's Mirabai Chanu (women's 48kg) and Canadian weightlifter Maude Charron (63kg) after they also won gold in Glasgow.

The 26-year-old has dominated her weightlifting categories since winning gold for Fiji in the 90kg event at the 2018 Gold Coast Games.

Cikamatana then switched allegiance to Australia the following year due to a local dispute with Fiji's weightlifting governing body, and to keep working with Coffa and his wife Lily.

Eileen Cikamatana (centre) representing Fiji at the 2015 Commonwealth Youth Games. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour)

Taking out the 87kg title at the 2022 Birmingham edition, Cikamatana is also the first woman to win Commonwealth Games gold for two countries in an individual sport.

Cikamatana is adamant about making the podium at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, but has pressing matters to attend to first.

"I'm going to go have some cake, because I've been wanting to have them ever since I got here," Cikamatana said.

"Cheesecake, obviously. I'm a cheesecake girl."

Ngake's incredible journey to silver

Ngake took silver in a remarkable career comeback.

The Cameroon-born English weightlifter was belatedly awarded a bronze medal from the 2012 Olympics after multiple rivals returned positive drug tests.

But the medal was sent to Cameroon, and she has never seen it.

Madias Ngake absconded from the Cameroon Olympics team in 2012. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Ngake, fearing persecution in her birth country because of her sexuality, absconded from the Cameroon team during the London Games.

Living homeless in London before working as a cleaner for 10 years, Ngake rekindled her desire to compete after a chance meeting with her former Cameroonian coach during the 2022 Commonwealth Games.

The 34-year-old, sporting sparkling red hair that matched her England uniform, threatened to pull off an upset after setting a Games snatch record of 111kg, but fell short of setting a clean-and-jerk benchmark of 135kg.

Cikamtana's win is Australia's third weightlifting medal in Glasgow, with youngster Ollie Saxton emulating his father and four-time Games medallist Andrew Saxton by winning bronze in the men's 94kg event earlier on day six of the Games.

Saxton had logged a total of 336kg, pulling off a 156kg snatch and a 180kg clean-and-jerk lift.

Saxton finished on the podium 40 years after his father won 100kg sub-heavyweight bronze for England at his debut Games in Edinburgh.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: FIFA hits Argentina with World Cup charges for scuffle, 'Malvinas' banner
World.content:
FIFA has lodged disciplinary charges against two Argentina players for striking Spain opponents moments after the World Cup final and have charged Argentina's soccer federation for players showing a political banner about the Falkland Islands after beating England in the semifinals.

A list of disciplinary cases FIFA has opened against Argentina also include "discriminatory chants and gestures" by fans, alleged assault by an assistant coach after the final and "throwing of objects by spectators in relation to several matches" at the World Cup.

Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes faces three charges of assault over the post-game clashes after Spain's 1-0 win on July 19, defender Nahuel Molina faces two charges and coach Roberto Ayala one.

Molina and Thiago Almada also are charged with unsporting behaviour. The same charge has been levelled against Spain player Gavi.

Argentina's players carried a banner with the slogan "Las Malvinas son Argentinas", meaning "The Malvinas are Argentine", after beating England 2-1 in the semifinals.

UK urges action over Falklands banner The British government urges FIFA to investigate after Argentine players held up a banner declaring the Falkland Islands were Argentinian.

Argentina refers to the Falkland Islands as Islas Malvinas. The islands were invaded in 1982 under orders from Argentina's then-military dictatorship, triggering a 10-week war won by Britain.

British government officials urged FIFA to investigate the display of the banner, and the soccer body said on Wednesday the formal charge was "using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature."

FIFA said all the people charged had "now been provided with the opportunity to present their position, following which a decision will be issued by the FIFA Disciplinary Committee in due course".

AP

World.title: 'If you've got a lane, you've got a chance': The Aussie Dolphins' way
World.content:
There's a ritual for Australians before every night of swimming at the Commonwealth Games: we run a rule down the schedule and count how many gold medals are locked in and how many others might be possible.

We did it on Tuesday, when the Dolphins' all-time gold medal record was in peril, ultimately equalled in the mixed 4x100m medley relay. And again on Wednesday, we knew the record would be broken, but by who?

The women's 50m freestyle was the first lock of the night, followed quickly by the men's 50m butterfly.

Trust this team to get greedy and nab three golds for the price of two races, with Kyle Chalmers and Ben Armbruster winning matching golds, trailed by Cameron McEvoy, just after Meg Harris led Alex Perkins and Shayna Jack in the first podium sweep of the night.

Two for the price of one as Kyle Chalmers and Ben Armbruster touched at the same time in the 50m butterfly. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

But neither were the first gold of the evening and the record-breaking 29th of the meet.

That honour went to young Kai Taylor, who won his first international individual gold medal with a wire-to-wire victory in the men's 200m freestyle.

Despite Taylor entering these Games as an elite 200m practitioner, he fell into the "possibly if not likely" category during that pre-night perusal.

More fool us, as his last 200m swim three days prior was one of the moments of the campaign for Australia.

Live: Commonwealth Games day six We are past the halfway mark in Glasgow, which means the end of the swimming program as athletics kicks into high gear. Follow live.

After being a lead-off heat swimmer in the 4x200m freestyle relay at the Paris Olympics two years ago, the 22-year-old was chosen to anchor the final swim in Glasgow.

He entered the water about a body length and 0.24 seconds behind England's Max Litchfield and not only caught and put a gap on him within a lap, but powered ahead to a victory by 3.51 seconds.

But on Wednesday he swam a 1:47.23, two seconds slower than his personal best at June's trials, to qualify in seventh place.

He was placed in lane one for the final, and it seemed he simply wasn't feeling it on the day.

Taylor wasn't alive when Kieren Perkins famously won 1,500m gold from lane eight at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics. But many of us were.

Taylor's mum, Hayley Lewis, certainly was as a member of many of the same teams as Perkins.

All that to say, we should have known better. And Kai did.

Kai Taylor is an international individual medallist for the first time. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"If you've got a lane, you've got a chance," he said.

"I managed to get myself into the final tonight after a bit of a slow swim this morning, but you've always got a chance when you're in the race, and I just went out there with no fear."

Unlike his stunning relay swim, he led the entire way, first staying clear of Jack McMillan and then the rest of the field that swallowed up the Northern Irishman but couldn't catch the Commonwealth Games debutant on his desperate charge for history.

Taylor's victory was followed by the aforementioned podium sweeps and victories in five of the final six races of the night.

That started with a swimmer at the other end of the spectrum as Lakeisha Patterson, one of only two swimmers returning to Glasgow after competing in 2014, flew home in the 100m freestyle S9 for her third Commonwealth crown.

Still somehow 27, it feels like "Lucky" has been around and will be around forever.

Australia has come to expect gold rushes from the Dolphins for decades, so much so that the epic victories and unrivalled dominance are frequently met by little more than a thumbs-up, while minor medals elsewhere at the Games are welcomed as historic events.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

But Chalmers urged Australians not to take this moment for granted.

"We are in a golden era of swimming and it's not normal for swimmers to stand up and win gold medals and break world records, break Commonwealth Games records night in and night out," he said.

"But we draw so much inspiration from each other … we've got some generational talents on the team right now and I think we as a country really need to enjoy that while we can because it's not going to last forever."

Chalmers would know, having made his debut as a 17-year-old at the 2016 Olympics and winning one of Australia's three gold medals in the pool in Rio.

Ten years on, he is a seasoned veteran of the team with one eye on retirement.

Nothing is permanent in this game, so as the swimming ends and attention turns away from Tollcross, take a moment to recognise the brilliance we just witnessed.

Thirty-seven gold medals, 16 silver and 23 bronze. New names unearthed, old crowns getting a spit-shine and another reminder of this team's perpetual performances of the least appreciated but most anticipated feats of brilliance.

World.title: Prisoner detained for 'several months' after release date, ombudsman finds
World.content:
An inmate was erroneously kept in a South Australian prison for "several months" after his sentence ended, and the Department for Correctional Services says it "respectfully disagrees" it should pay compensation to him.

The "failure" was investigated by Ombudsman SA, which found the male prisoner was detained beyond their sentence release date due to "insufficient" processes — something the department said it has since made changes to.

In a statement on the investigation, the ombudsman reported that the department took "immediate action" to release the inmate once it identified the error.

But the ombudsman found the department took five years to advise the prisoner what had happened "and only did so following engagement from the ombudsman's office".

"It did not appear the department had any intention of advising the prisoner of its error until the ombudsman requested it do so," the ombudsman report said.

" The ombudsman considered the delay in advising the prisoner to be serious and unacceptable. "

The investigation found the department's letter to the inmate "did not offer an apology or inform the prisoner of their legal rights against the state".

"The seriousness of the department's error was exacerbated by the fact that the department knew it had held the prisoner in error and failed to provide timely advice of this fact, offer an apology or make him aware of the compensation options available to him," the ombudsman report said.

"The ombudsman commented that this had the potential to impact the prisoner's ability to seek redress for the department's action."

Recommendations to the department

The investigation found the department was "in breach" of the Correctional Services Act and acted "inconsistently" with international and national human rights standards for not releasing the prisoner on time.

It also determined by failing to immediately notify the prisoner of the error, the department also "acted inconsistently" with human rights standards and "the reasonable expectations of the community in regard to the state's treatment of prisoners".

"South Australian government agencies are required to take accountability for errors when they have an impact on people," the ombudsman report said.

The Department for Correctional Services says it "respectfully disagrees" it should pay compensation to the prisoner. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

The ombudsman made three recommendations, including reviewing the practices and systems across correctional facilities and asking the department to consider an "ex gratia payment" to the prisoner.

In a statement, the Department for Correctional Services said it acknowledged the ombudsman's statement.

"Since this incident occurred six years ago, the department and G4S have implemented new processes to manage prisoner release dates," a spokeswoman said.

"The government respectfully disagrees with the ombudsman's request to pay compensation."

World.title: Family 'failed' by WA's mental health system moves interstate
World.content:
A West Australian mother says she was forced to move interstate to get adequate mental health care for her daughter after she was failed by the state's health system.

Simone Meyer spent 60 hours across emergency departments in two Perth hospitals with her daughter Indi in November last year.

The 16-year-old needed care for complex mental health issues, including autism, OCD and depression.

The Margaret River mother said the family could not access adequate support services locally, so were forced to make the 270 kilometre trip to Perth.

"The local support services that we were referred to, we didn't think, get or feel like we received good enough care," she said.

"It just felt like [they] got you in, risk managed you, once you were sort of classed as non-risk, off you went again."

Struggles in Perth

Indi waited outside the emergency departments at Fiona Stanley and Joondalup hospitals for hours in the cold, as she could not cope with the loud noises in ED.

Simone with her 16-year-old daughter Indi. (Supplied)

When she was eventually admitted to Joondalup, a bed did not become available.

The family left, returned home and began thinking about interstate options.

"We knew we definitely couldn't stay in the South West," Ms Meyer said.

" We'd already experienced the emergency departments in Perth, so there was no way we were going to do that again. "

The family moved to Albury-Wodonga in December and have not looked back.

Simone and her husband have moved their family to Wodonga, on the NSW-Victorian border. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

"There is so much more support over here, there's just there's so many to choose from," she said.

"Luckily we haven't needed the hospital because the support services outside have been so good."

New mental health beds, crisis team

The family's story reflects the pressure on WA's mental health system, particularly in communities outside Perth.

The state government apologised last month after a 17-year-old Busselton girl was forced to wait five days in Busselton Hospital's emergency department for an acute mental health bed.

On Wednesday, Health Minister Meredith Hammat announced a number of fast-tracked improvements to the region's mental health services, including a new "observation area" with six 72-hour mental health beds at Bunbury Regional Hospital.

Bunbury Hospital is undergoing a multi-million-dollar redevelopment. (ABC News: Jon Daly )

Ms Hammat said the beds provided more appropriate options for people needing urgent mental health care.

"It allows people who might otherwise have to wait in an emergency department to come through into this purpose built area and be seen by multi-disciplinary teams," she said.

Meredith Hammat, with Collie-Preston MP Jodie Hanns and Bunbury MP Don Punch. (ABC News: Jon Daly)

The move partially addresses an earlier reduction in mental health beds at the hospital from 23 to 11 in August last year, despite an ongoing $470 million redevelopment of the wider hospital.

A new youth acute response team will also now be available in regional areas five days a week during office hours.

The team will provide mental health treatment outside hospital settings, including at home and in the community.

"What we ultimately want to achieve is a situation where people don't need to be admitted to these formal care environments," Ms Hammat said.

One of the beds in the new mental health observatory unit. (ABC News: Jon Daly )

Mixed response from community

For Busselton-based mental health support service Lamp, the increased acute care is welcome.

But chief executive Jesse Malseed said other services also needed to be bolstered.

"With more beds in the region, there are potentially more people being referred to community organisations that aren't receiving an increase in funding or capacity," he said.

Shadow Health Minister Libby Mettam said the Cook government's efforts to improve mental health services for children and young people had been unacceptably slow, despite a 2021 promise to overhaul the system.

Libby Mettam says the state government has failed to overhaul the child and adolescent mental health service. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"It is welcome that this service will go to families and individuals in their homes, because emergency departments are simply not suitable for youth that are experiencing mental health distress," Ms Mettam, Bussselton's local MP, said.

" Outside of Bunbury we know that the city of Busselton and other regional towns have been completely neglected when it comes to supporting youth mental health. "

"We are increasingly seeing emergency departments across the region bear the brunt of the mental health crisis."

Ms Meyer said the acute response team could have been a great help to her daughter.

"It is definitely something we would have used," she said.

World.title: ‘Never sexually assaulted anyone’: Jared Leto denies criminal allegations by four women
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCrime ‘Never sexually assaulted anyone’: Jared Leto denies criminal allegations by four women Emily Kaine and Kayla Olaya Updated July 30, 2026 — 8:48am ,first published 7:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oscar-winning actor Jared Leto has been accused of criminal sexual conduct by four women who alleged the offences occurred when they were teenagers. Leto has denied sexual misconduct allegations made by a total of ten women who detailed their encounters with the actor and Thirty Seconds to Mars frontman to the BBC in a new documentary titled Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret. Jared Leto pictured in 2025. Getty Images for Disney “I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life. These claims are absolutely and categorically false,” Leto said in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter. In the documentary, one woman alleged she was sexually assaulted inside a motel bathroom at the age of 17, while another said Leto threatened her with sexual assault when she was 19.



A third woman said she had under-age sex with the star in California when she was 17, and said he had “shrugged off” a conversation about the age of consent being 18 in the US state. The fourth woman claimed she was groomed by the star, and alleged he abused his celebrity status by repeatedly making sexually explicit phone calls to her when she was 16. She also said he suggested they should have sex on at least one occasion. Four more women also alleged they received odd and often very sexual phone calls from the star when they were younger. During these phone calls, the women alleged Leto asked them questions such as: “Are you a virgin? Do you have any kinks?” All the women allege their encounters with the actor took place between 2002 and 2016, when he was in his 30s and 40s. He is now 54.



One of his alleged victims told the BBC: “This was 25 years ago … He has gotten away with it.” Leto has been a prominent Hollywood figure since the 1990s. He won the 2014 Academy Award for best supporting actor for Dallas Buyers Club, and has appeared in hit films such as Fight Club, Blade Runner 2049, and Suicide Squad. Leto in Los Angeles in 2022. AP In June last year, Leto was accused by nine women of inappropriate behaviour – including claims his conduct was “predatory, terrifying and unacceptable” – in an Air Mail exposé. At the time, Leto “expressly denied” the accusations, including an allegation from one woman who said the actor approached her in 2006 when she was 16, and he was 35.



Another woman alleged that when she was 18, Leto “suddenly pulled his penis out and started masturbating”. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Anyone affected by sexual, domestic or family violence can also access 24/7, free and confidential trauma-specialist counselling through Full Stop Australia (1800 385 578).
