World.title: Pretty Woman the movie is beloved. Does it work as a musical?
World.content:
Key points MUSICALS: Pretty Woman: The Musical lands in Melbourne

THEATRE: Theatre Works presents Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity

OPERA: A touring version of Don Giovanni by Opera Australia arrives in Nunawading

MUSICALS: Grey Gardens reimagines the iconic documentary as a musical

MUSIC: Jayson Gillham and Iyad Sughayer perform together in Keys to Life

MUSICAL THEATRE

Pretty Woman: The Musical ★★★

Regent Theatre, until September 13 Pretty Woman was always going to be hot property as far as movie-to-musical adaptations are concerned. Its gender and class politics might be icky – perhaps inevitable when you rework Cinderella into a yuppie fantasy that hinges on the so-called “hooker with a heart of gold” trope – but the 1990 film with Julia Roberts and Richard Gere remains one of the most bankable Hollywood romcoms of all time. In Pretty Woman: The Musical, almost all the looks and scenes from the film are resurrected. Eddie Jim The cha-ching is only fitting. Although the story does make weak gestures towards pretending otherwise, money is the real love language of Pretty Woman. Its cultural influence relies at least as much on celebrating conspicuous consumption – the Rodeo Drive shopping scenes, the fabulous frocks and fast cars, and the opulent banquets with too many forks – as it does on the romantic chemistry of the leads. For fans of the movie, this musical adaptation has its finger pressed firmly on the nostalgia button in a way that should put bums on seats. Almost all the iconic looks and scenes are resurrected, and short of bringing Roy Orbison back to life, you couldn’t ask for better music.



Songs from Canadian songwriting duo Bryan Adams and Jim Vallance range from a base of ’80s-style soft rock ballads, with strong melodies and a romantic charge. While the score isn’t always doing enough dramatic work, it does unleash vocal pyrotechnics, and occasionally a rock concert vibe that compensates for some of the looser stage business. Samantha Jade as Vivian Ward. Eddie Jim Chemistry is integral to making the fairytale fly, and Samantha Jade and Ben Hall are both charismatic and well-matched vocally. They create intimacy, and even a few tasteful erotic scenes that don’t look silly, even if they’re a bit hamstrung in replicating the dynamic from the film. Jade gives a pocket-rocket performance of the Julia Roberts role; Hall cops most of the show’s cringe moments, suddenly bursting into song in the Richard Gere part – an uneven performance, though, to be fair, Jade’s extroverted naif is easier to reconcile with the artifice of musical theatre than an introverted male lead.



The supporting cast includes a larger-than-life comic contribution from Michelle Brasier as Vivian’s wisecracking bestie Kit, and a versatile one from Tim Omaji as a homeless man and a classy hotel manager. Douglas Hansell has the unenviable task of playing a nasty corporate lawyer – a character responsible for a troubling late plot point involving attempted sexual assault. Editor's pick Visual art If you’ve ever felt lonely, this show is for you It’s a reminder that gender politics have changed since Pretty Woman first appeared, though that isn’t, in the end, the show’s chief stumbling block. That comes from various aspects of the craft not being in service to one another, from the sense of a show that doesn’t wield musical and dramatic art to create something greater than the sum of its parts. Pretty Woman has entertaining sequences, some memorable music, and fans of the movie should enjoy the nostalgia hit. Yet it does feel overstretched as a full-length musical – and could have been trimmed into a play with songs or performed as a staged concert without losing much.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead



THEATRE

Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity ★★★

Theatre Works, until August 1 Art and war collide in Heather McDonald’s Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. It’s a volatile three-hander with absurdist echoes (and the only play I know of, apart from Eugène Ionesco’s Rhinoceros, that calls for a rhino onstage), set within a bombed-out museum in a world that’s been at war for 100 years. Laila Thaker and Jane Montgomery-Griffiths in a scene from Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity Sarah Clarke The ruined cultural institution has been transformed into an ad hoc prison, where art restorer Layla (Jane Montgomery-Griffiths) is held by a soldier, Mitra (Kate Cole), and attended to by an unobtrusive nurse, Nadia (Laila Thaker). In a grim irony, the nurse isn’t there to ensure caregiving, but to render torture invisible. In fact, she may not be a nurse at all, though that thread will be revealed only after the desperate clash between soldier and prisoner reaches flashpoint.



Laila Thaker is a breath of fresh air Sarah Clarke Mitra, you see, has been tasked by her superiors with extracting Layla’s aid to restore famous paintings. Layla refuses point-blank to assist: her help would only be used as propaganda for the enemy. When frustration spirals into rage, and a sudden act of violence, the three women find themselves in a vicious struggle in which the value of art, and even human survival, is called into question. Director Nadia Tass made her name in Australian cinema with films such as Malcolm and The Big Steal. She’s also an accomplished theatre director, and here corrals a strong cast in a work that veers between traumatised conflict, absurd humour, flashes of shared humanity, and more philosophical terrain. Montgomery-Griffiths and Cole are a little typecast. The former has a history of playing strong, academic women up against it (notably her tour de force as a dying literature professor in Wit); the latter pulled off no less impressive a feat in the monodrama Grounded, where she delved into the psyche of a female fighter pilot.



Neither actor is allowed as much room to move here. Still, the high intensity battle between these characters allows trauma to fly like shrapnel, and Ishan Vivekanantham’s staging creates a ruined, monumental quality, even if it also sometimes militates against intimacy. And Thaker is a breath of fresh air, introducing unexpected ferocity as the Muslim nurse. What I like most about this thought-provoking play is its relative lack of sentimentality, and its refusal to assume a virtue without arguing for it. McDonald does universalise the cliched hypothetical: “What would you save from your burning house?” to address the common heritage of humanity, but art isn’t portrayed as intrinsically and necessarily a good thing, a priori. The politics and human mess behind hierarchies of aesthetic value are exposed. Different approaches to what might constitute a “masterpiece” are explored, including the Japanese aesthetic of wabi-sabi, or finding beauty in imperfection and impermanence, as it is practised in the art of kintsukuroi (repairing pottery with gold to make the brokenness part of its appeal). The play’s title references UNESCO’s world heritage project, and perhaps unsurprisingly, it reminded me of the outrage at Juukan Gorge, but also of Afghanistan’s Bamiyan Buddhas. Destroyed by the Taliban in 2001, restoration has since commenced and stalled, but even in its shattered state, the site of the lost Buddhas remains a popular tourist attraction, and it has inspired other artworks across the world in remembrance, most recently Tuan Andrew Nguyen’s sculpture The Light that Shines Through the Universe – a large-scale homage to the Buddhas currently installed along the High Line in New York City.



In its own way, this play has a similar ambition and effect.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead OPERA

Don Giovanni ★★★

Opera Australia, The Round, Nunawading, July 23 A night at the opera isn’t high on the priority list for most, these days. Cost, time, travel into the city – few people are in a position to afford themselves an expensive, time-consuming treat right now. Stephen Marsh as Leporello and Jennifer Bonner as Donna Elvira Claudio Raschella One possible path to success is to actually bring the thing to the people. In Opera Australia’s case, the path leads through regional South Australia, Victoria, New South Wales and Tasmania. It’s bringing the operatic mountain to Mohammed.



This year marks the 30th anniversary of Opera Australia’s national tour, and it’s a format that might just be more relevant and required than ever. It is a difficult production to program; choose an opera with broad appeal, with no large chorus or set pieces and that won’t sound tinny with a small orchestra. This year, it’s a 1950s-inspired Don Giovanni, which fits the aforementioned criteria well. This tour has always been seen as a stepping stone for young singers, and as such, the standard is perhaps not quite what you’d hear at Hamer Hall. Occasional uncomfortable-sounding high notes, some underdone characterisations, some sections slightly out of time with conductor Simon Bruckard, who leads a 10-piece chamber orchestra admirably. But these misgivings are perhaps only present to someone who has seen Mozart’s masterwork over and over, someone this tour is not really for. Benjamin Del Borrello as Masetto and Jane Magão as Zerlina Claudio Raschella Standout performances came from Benjamin Del Borrello as Masetto and opposite him, Jane Magão as Zerlina. Del Borrello’s baritone boomed, with clarity and depth; Magão’s sweet soprano was perfectly cast, she could do this role on much bigger stages. Stephen Marsh (Leporello) and Jessica Blunt (Donna Anna) are also thoroughly commendable.



The tour, which worth noting, is double cast, opened in South Australia last week and the Nunawading show was packed to the rafters with an appreciative local audience. As the circuit continues, hopefully for OA it’s a sign that if you bring it, they will come.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies THEATRE

Grey Gardens ★★★★★

Clovelly Fox, fortyfivedownstairs, until August 2 The fine line between exploitation and empowerment has always been muddied in the case of “Big Edie” and “Little Edie” Beale, a mother and daughter whose fall from the heights of America’s elite was made infamous by the 1975 cult classic documentary Grey Gardens. The first half of Grey Gardens takes place over a single day in 1941. Ben Fon Once scions of the upper class, the Beale women fell into disrepute, poverty and squalor in a crumbling 28-room mansion in East Hampton. That they were aunt and cousin respectively of Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis only accentuated the mystique of their unthinkable predicament.



Debates over whether the celebrated documentary is exploitative and makes victims of the pair have raged since its release, and the 2006 Tony Award-winning Broadway musical Grey Gardens, currently being staged at fortyfivedownstairs, plays in this grey area. Were the Beales a transgressive pair of iconoclasts punished by the repressive social mores of the time, or was their fall the result of mental illness and trauma? Was their relationship one of deep and profound love, or a toxic co-dependency that killed their every chance of happiness? The musical is cleaved in two. Set in 1941, the first half is an almost entirely fictionalised precursor to the two women’s isolation, taking place over the course of a single fateful day. The second half transports us 32 years into the future into the more familiar territory traversed by the documentary. The ghostly figures of the past haunt the second half of the musical. Ben Fon Under Tyran Parke’s expert direction, the tale unfolds with a bubbling undercurrent of dread. Prone to bursting into song and scorned by her father (an imposing David Hobson) and husband alike, Big Edie (the mercurial Helen Dallimore) is preparing for her daughter Little Edie’s (a coquettish, bewitching Meg Williams) engagement to a sneer of a Kennedy (Luke Ward). Grey Gardens is at the height of its splendour – a sprawling manor serviced by servants and clamoured over by socialites – but the day won’t unfold as any of them plan.



Big Edie was a singer, which makes the musical treatment of Grey Gardens all the more poignant. Composer Scott Frankel and lyricist Michael Korie’s songs are both the embodiment of her societal disobedience and a vehicle – brought to the fore by Dallimore’s stunning voice – through which her thwarted dreams, vicarious transference and barely concealed envy are materialised. The Beales are never romanticised; they’re products of their time, accurately represented by the racist ditties that Big Edie guilelessly recites. Related Article Arts ‘She could have been a Kennedy’: A cult documentary has been reimagined as a musical When we rejoin mother and daughter decades later, the set has been transformed; grandeur into clutter, and spectres of the pair’s past loom over the present as ghostly apparitions of characters from the first half. Dallimore plays the increasingly unhinged Little Edie in an effective simulation of how the past is constantly imprinting itself upon the present and Deidre Rubenstein is Big Edie, ever sonorous but made increasingly desperate by the indignities of ageing. It’s in the apoplectic exchanges between Dallimore and Rubenstein that Grey Gardens conjures the spectacular cruelty innate to many mother-daughter relationships, and the diminishment Little Edie inflicts on herself to avoid being belittled any further by her emotionally manipulative, increasingly cantankerous mother.



Grey Gardens strips away the artifice of the crumbling detritus that governed so much of these two women’s lives in favour of something starker, bleaker and darker. There are no easy answers in this elegiac reimagining, but what we’re left with as the haunting melody of The Girl Who Has Everything is reprised one final time is the sheer tragedy of unfulfilled potential, unrealised futures and unrepentant love.

Reviewed by Sonia Nair MUSIC

Keys to Life ★★★★

Jayson Gillham and Iyad Sughayer, Melbourne Recital Centre, July 19 In his first Australian performance after losing his unfair dismissal case against the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, pianist Jayson Gillham made no comments about the recent events. Sunday night’s collaboration with friend and fellow pianist Iyad Sughayer demonstrated not only superb artistry but the non-verbal potency of music. Iyad Sughayer and Jayson Gillham preform together in Keys to Life at Melbourne Recital Centre, July 19. Fred Kroh Unmistakeably radiating the joy of making music together, Gillham and Palestinian-Jordanian Sughayer (making his Australian debut), displayed a finely honed artistic synergy.



Such synergy imbued the impressionistic works on the program with a nuanced sense of colour and an admirable flexibility of line. Debussy’s Petite Suite conjured up an idyllic innocence, while Ravel’s Introduction and Allegro revelled in a more abstract voluptuousness. Mozart’s Sonata for Two Pianos in D major, K. 448 provided a perfect contrast; the elegance of the music matched by the crystalline elegance of the performance. The duo’s impressive versatility effectively captured the various guises of Khachaturian’s rhythmic modernism in his Three Pieces for Two Pianos. Receiving its premiere, Isolated by Palestinian-Lebanese composer Houtaf Khoury was conceived, he writes, “in a very difficult time…isolated from the peace world and positive vibes”. Also noting “there is always a way to get out from the tunnel”, Khoury’s optimism clearly percolates through this highly personal score with its oblique reminiscences of the bell-like and subaquatic world of Debussy’s Submerged Cathedral. Gillham and Sughayer unashamedly delighted in the old-fashioned Russian pianism of Anton Arensky’s Suite for Two Pianos No. 1, giving a bravura account, confirming the composer’s intention of putting Chopin’s style on steroids. A rhythmically and melodically infectious account of Chabrier’s Espana provided an ebullient finale before an encore filled with delicate nostalgia: The Fairy Garden from Ravel’s Mother Goose Suite. Before an enthusiastic and near-capacity audience, Gillham and Sughayer eloquently demonstrated how powerfully music can reach beyond words. The challenge for all artists is to trust in that power.

Reviewed by Tony Way



JAZZ

Oehlers / Grabowsky / Svoboda / Beck ★★★★

The JazzLab, July 19 Bassist Helen Svoboda was the ‘newcomer’ in the group Celeste de Clario The powerhouse quintet that was booked to perform at JazzLab on Sunday shrank to a quartet at late notice, when one player (trumpeter Paul Williamson) pulled out of the gig due to illness. Fortunately, the other four players are all masters at thinking on their feet, open to – and inspired by – unpredictability and moment-to-moment adaptation. Indeed, Perth-based saxophonist Jamie Oehlers chose the players for this concert specifically for their sense of adventure. His compositions are designed to be interpreted rather than slavishly reproduced from charts. So while the absence of one instrument led to some swift reworkings of arrangements just before the gig, there was no sense of anything missing from the music.



Oehlers has a decades-long association with pianist Paul Grabowsky and drummer Dave Beck, lending their interactions the ebb and flow of an open-ended conversation where trust is key and each participant’s contribution is equally valued. Bassist Helen Svoboda was the “newcomer” in this setting, having never worked with Oehlers before. Yet she was able to slip into these musical conversations with unflappable ease, even while navigating angular melodies, shifting time signatures and unexpected rhythmic fillips. On Nostalgia, her arco bass glided beneath Oehlers’ swirling arpeggios and Grabowsky’s tempestuous ripples, spliced with bursts of fidgety, free-form commentary: percussive popping, abstract chords, spidery harmonics and scraped cymbals. Saturday in Central Park was set to a brisk, boppish strut, interspersed with lighter interludes and an occasional splash of Latin cross-rhythms, before melting into a delicate coda of hushed, almost hymnal beauty. And on Anthem (the night’s final number), Beck coaxed the band into a laid-back swagger with an increasingly heady backbeat, all four players – and the audience – revelling in the languid groove to bring the show to a soulful, deeply satisfying conclusion.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas



THEATRE

Rabbit & Watson ★★

Darebin Arts Speakeasy, Northcote Town Hall, until July 26 Chinese folk religion and homophobia in the AFL make uneasy bedfellows in this cross-cultural queer romcom. Emerging playwright Shane Woon takes Tu’er Shen – the Rabbit God from Chinese legend, known as a gay matchmaker and patron deity of homosexual love – and thrusts him into a world of closeted young footy players. Rabbit & Watson is at its best in epical and comedic modes. Darren Gill Originally a soldier from Fujian who fell in love with a handsome Ming official, Tu’er Shen was, according to legend, caught perving on his beloved and subsequently executed for it. He was transformed into Rabbit (Sean Yuen Halley), the celestial protector of same-sex lovers – although each time his own beloved is reincarnated, Rabbit falls head over heels again and neglects his duties, with chaotic results. This time, the wheel of reincarnation has landed on a talented dreamboat of an AFL player named Watson (Anton Pan-Cassin). Watson has come out to his “stereotypical Asian mum” (played with an exaggerated sense of fun by Dr Cindy Pan), who’s ambitious for him and tremendously spiky about his growing affection for Rabbit.



As love blossoms and Watson’s career belatedly takes flight, Rabbit begs the aid of other celestials – the Monkey God (Jesse Vasiliadis) famed from Chinese classic Journey to the West, and Guanyin, Goddess of Mercy. But Watson isn’t the only one struggling against homophobia in the AFL, and Rabbit’s distraction falls hard on others (Charlie Morris, Gabriel Partington) involved in the game. Rabbit & Watson’s sense of camp serves it well. Darren Gill Will this centuries-old romance finally get a happy ending? Rabbit & Watson is at its best in epical and comedic modes and opens with elaborate pageantry. A spectacular lion dance sees two Chinese lions with laser-green eyes roaring to life, leaping and cavorting around the stage, accompanied by riotous percussion.



The show’s sense of camp also serves it well – notably in Pan’s mischievous performance, and amusing touches brought to the courtship between the romantic leads. I suppose I would have liked to see more heated rivalry (or chemistry, or something) between them. It’s a same-sex love as chaste as the moon, and the Boy Love cultural influence should perhaps have made it a little raunchier. All that yearning deserves a payoff. Related Article Arts Australian theatre is caught in a cancellation crisis – this obscure 1970s Ned Kelly musical offers hope Yet it’s the AFL stuff that produces the most dispiriting theatre. Both racism and homophobia remain serious issues in professional sport. That isn’t an excuse to oversimplify, or to beat audiences over the head with them, and the acting is so wooden, the characterisation so thin, and the dialogue so pedestrian in many of these scenes, that the show risks trivialising, or imprecisely diagnosing, the problems it seeks to highlight. It’s all rather dull and coarsely observed compared to the mythical love story, interferes with the colourful sense of picaresque, and distends the show to around two hours without interval.



The good news is that there’s enough promising material here for a charming queer epic. But I fear only a substantial rewrite could cut out the dead dialogue, refocus the dynamics on the romcom fantasy, and clarify and distil exposition (including through nonverbal aspects of theatrical storytelling) to avoid substantial longueurs.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead DANCE

The Nutcracker Act II and other works ★★★

Bunjil Place, until July 18 Who would have thought the Australian Ballet would emerge as a key supporter of Melbourne’s independent dance scene? Well, it has – just look at its touring program, which in recent years has provided a valuable platform for the creation of new contemporary dance works. Hannah Sergi in The Nutcracker Act II by Paul Knobloch. Kate Longley Last year, the company took on a new work by Lucy Guerin: the wonderful Ground Control. And this year we get not one but two premieres – by Sandra Parker and Stephanie Lake – and both are very strong.



But the program is not all contemporary. It begins with company members Hugo Dumapit and Larissa Kiyoto-Ward in the glittering, exacerbated classicism of the Tchaikovsky Pas de Deux. Kiyoto-Ward is crisp and sure-footed, while Dumapit has an impressive leap. Then we fall into the austere, highly prescriptive world of Parker’s We Dance. This is a work for four dancers built from short but suggestive phrases, chiselled poses and densely organised sequences all performed with extreme largo. With its repetitions and exhausting variations, the work recalls Samuel Beckett’s late choreographies, while the hostile soundscape intensifies the sense of interminable crisis. Some may wonder if the title is ironic, but for me, this is bleakness of the most thrilling kind. Chrysalis by Stephanie Lake. Kate Longley Stephanie Lake’s Chrysalis deploys a large Australian Ballet School ensemble in a very different mode. Kinetic, comic and pop, it sends dancers in striking red costumes scurrying insect-like across the stage. The duets and trios are a little rough but the larger massed effects are great.



After the interval, we enter the Kingdom of Sweets for the second act of Paul Knobloch’s version of The Nutcracker. Sara Andrlon and Jeremy Hargreaves bring a mature assurance to the Sugar Plum Fairy and her Prince, with Hannah Sergi as the Floral Fairy and Yaru Xu as Clara. Related Article Visual art ‘I’ve seen a lot of Monet’s water lilies. Do I really need to see any more?’ There is a bit of whiplash in the transition from the dim monasticism of We Dance to The Nutcracker’s candyfloss skies and giddy smiles, though the creepy fun of Chrysalis, squeezed between them, provides a kind of bridge. The tour continues through Albury, Ballarat, Horsham and beyond.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: ‘Eye-watering’: Prince Harry, celebrities face $35m legal bill after Daily Mail court loss
World.content:
WorldEuropePrince Harry ‘Eye-watering’: Prince Harry, celebrities face $35m legal bill after Daily Mail court loss Michael Holden July 30, 2026 — 8:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Prince Harry and other high-profile claimants face paying tens of millions of dollars toward the legal costs of Associated Newspapers after they lost their privacy lawsuits against the Daily Mail publisher, London’s High Court has heard. A judge at London’s High Court this month comprehensively ruled against King Charles’ younger son, along with singer Elton John, Liz Hurley and four other British figures, and rejected allegations that the Mail titles had engaged in widespread unlawful activities, such as phone hacking. Prince Harry outside London’s High Court in January, during his legal fight against the Daily Mail’s publisher. AP Associated said it was an overwhelming victory for its newspaper and journalists, and “for a free press generally”, while the prince, 41, described the ruling as a “complete and obvious whitewash”. At a hearing on Wednesday (London time) to determine how much of the Mail’s legal costs the claimants should pay, Associated’s lawyer, Antony White, KC, argued they should do so on an “indemnity basis”, under which the losing party must cover the other side’s charges without the need to show they were proportionate.



Related Article Analysis

Royal family Here’s how it all went wrong in Harry’s ‘creepy’ hacking case. No wonder he’s furious The court heard that Associated had incurred a legal bill of £34.5 million ($66.4 million), while Harry and other claimants only have an insurance policy that covers about £16 million – leaving a potential shortfall of more than £18 million ($35 million). In a scathing attack on the claimants’ case, which he said had been designed to create “a banquet of litigation” against Associated, White argued they had made wide-ranging and “egregious” allegations without supporting evidence, which had added to their costs. He also said Harry’s statement following the ruling was an abuse of his position and celebrity status. “It was entirely inappropriate and unreasonable,” White said.



Associated said it was seeking an interim payment of £10 million. Related Article Royal family ‘Obvious whitewash’: Prince Harry lashes judge after losing Daily Mail privacy case Nicholas Bacon, KC, the lawyer for the claimants, said in their submissions that Associated’s £34.5 million legal bill was “eye-watering” and far exceeded its agreed budget, and there was clearly a shortfall from the level of security they had in place. He said it had been reported that Associated wanted “to go for the jugular” and teach the claimants a lesson by obtaining indemnity costs. The claimants have offered an interim payment of £8 million by August 28.



In his ruling rejecting the case, Judge Matthew Nicklin said the claimants had needed to prove that information published about them had been obtained unlawfully, but had failed to do so, and that suspicion alone was not enough. In written submissions, the claimants’ lawyers also said any application for permission to appeal the judge’s ruling had been deferred until after Nicklin gave judgment on the costs. The hearing continues on Thursday. Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Alleged underworld assassin boasted about killing gang boss, jury told
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Alleged underworld assassin boasted about killing gang boss, jury told Riley Walter July 30, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An alleged killer bragged about his involvement in the assassination of Sydney crime figure Bilal Hamze at the height of an underworld feud, a Supreme Court jury has been told. Hamze was gunned down in Sydney’s CBD after dining with a sex worker on June 17, 2021, amid a spate of retaliatory shootings between the Hamzy organised crime network and the rival Alameddine organised crime network. Organised crime figure Bilal Hamze was shot dead in Sydney’s CBD. Artwork: Monique Westerman Samuel John Rokomaqisa is standing trial in the NSW Supreme Court, accused of murdering Hamze, 34, and conspiring to murder Hamze’s younger brother, Ibrahem Hamze, over several months in 2021. Rokomaqisa has pleaded not guilty to the charges. In her opening address on Monday, Crown prosecutor Kate Ratcliffe told the jury the Alameddine and Hamzy organised crime networks had a “history of hostility” in the lead up to Hamze’s murder, including several shootings between the groups.



“These two crimes were committed in the context of a feud between two warring gangs in Sydney,” Ratcliffe said. Ratcliffe said that prosecutors would rely on several admissions Rokomaqisa allegedly made to associates after Bilal Hamze’s killing. Mourners carry the coffin of Bilal Hamze after a service at Lakemba Mosque. Kate Geraghty Hamze, who the jury heard was a “high-ranking” member of the Hamzy organised crime network – which uses an alternative spelling – had relocated to the CBD from Western Sydney with his wife and child to avoid attempts on his life by rival crime groups. Ratcliffe said Rokomaqisa had shown an associate a news item about Hamze’s murder, telling them he and his cousin “did the job” and that he had been “the driver”.



On another occasion, Ratcliffe said, Rokomaqisa was captured on an intercepted telephone call telling an associate that he was owed $200,000 for “the thing”, which prosecutors allege was Hamze’s murder. Samuel John Rokomaqisa allegedly said he was owed $200,000 for “the thing”. Ratcliffe told the jury that Rokomaqisa had committed “criminal acts” to gain the trust of the Alameddine network and demonstrate his loyalty in exchange for “significant payments”. Hamze was killed as retaliation for the shooting of an Alameddine crime associate 10 days earlier, Ratcliffe said. The failed plot to murder Ibrahem Hamze, she said, was also planned by the Alameddine crime network as retaliation for the shooting. During a covertly recorded meeting the day after the June 7 shooting of the Alameddine associate, several members allegedly discussed retaliation against the Hamzy family.



“Tell Raf Ibby needs to go,” one member allegedly said. The plot to kill Ibrahem Hamze was foiled on August 14, 2021, when a NSW Police patrol car noticed a Mercedes-Benz parked in a no stopping zone, the jury heard. When police attempted to pull the vehicle over, it fled. Rokomaqisa’s DNA was found on items inside the car after it was abandoned shortly after the police pursuit, Ratcliffe said. Ibrahem Hamze (in grey hoodie) at the funeral of his brother Bilal, was allegedly the target of a murder plot. Dean Sewell Rokomaqisa is accused of assaulting an elderly man and stealing his Toyota Camry after abandoning the Mercedes-Benz in North Sydney. He has pleaded not guilty to that charge. When interviewed by police after being arrested in late 2021, Rokomaqisa allegedly said he had never been in either vehicle. Rokomaqisa denied having any knowledge of Hamze’s murder or having any contact with members of the Alameddine family when he was charged with the 34-year-old’s murder in late 2022. However, Rokomaqisa had made admissions about his connections to the gang during telephone intercepts and conversations captured on recording devices, and was a member of the KVT – a subgroup of Fijian men used to assist the Alameddine network in “criminal activity”, Ratcliffe said.



Defence barrister Nicole Carroll said in her opening address on Monday that Rokomaqisa denied any involvement in the crimes he has been charged over. “The accused, ladies and gentlemen of the jury, did not murder Bilal Hamze,” Carroll said. Carroll said Rokomaqisa was not aware of a plot to murder Ibrahem Hamze, or anyone else. ‘How did the shooters know exactly where Bilal Hamze was going to be at 10.20pm?’ Defence barrister Nicole Carroll She said the defence case would raise questions about whether other people, including the sex worker who dined with Hamze moments before his murder, had any involvement in his killing or whether she had been used by others to “get to Bilal Hamze”.



“The key to the murder surrounds them,” Carroll said. “How did the shooters know exactly where Bilal Hamze was going to be at 10.20pm on the 17th of June 2021?” Rokomaqisa’s defence will also examine the Hamzy network’s conflicts with the Comanchero motorcycle gang and the Haouchar crime network at the time. “The Hamzys were trying to kill senior members of both groups,” Carroll told the jury. The Alameddine network, too, was in dispute with several crime groups at the time of Hamze’s killing, Carroll said.



“Which criminal group is responsible for the murder of Bilal Hamze is in dispute,” Carroll said. The trial before Acting Justice Robert Allan Hulme continues. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Dictator’s grandson blasts ‘unfair’ result after disqualification in first fight
World.content:
SportCommonwealth Games Dictator’s grandson blasts ‘unfair’ result after disqualification in first fight Hannah Kennelly July 30, 2026 — 8:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: It took less than 10 minutes for one of the most highly anticipated boxing matches on the Commonwealth Games schedule to descend into chaos. On Thursday morning (AEST), a large crowd flocked to the SEC Centre to watch Uganda’s Aziz Abdul take on Englishman Damar Thomas in a super heavyweight bout. Aziz Abdul was disqualified for headbutting in the third round. Getty Images Abdul is the grandson of the late Ugandan dictator Idi Amin, who once proclaimed himself “the king of Scotland” and had a fixation with the country. Amin, a former heavyweight boxer, ruled Uganda for eight years. Human rights groups say as many as 500,000 people were killed and the country’s Asian population expelled during that time, and he also presided over the country’s economic collapse. He was forced out in 1979 and was never tried for his crimes in an international court. He died in Saudi Arabia in 2003.



Abdul had courted media attention earlier this week by saying, “My grandfather’s achievements inspired me,” and saying he wanted to become the “baddest man in the Commonwealth, the baddest man in Glasgow and the new king of Scotland”. Related Article Commonwealth Games Idi Amin’s boxer grandson vows to win gold and be ‘the new king of Scotland’ However, Abdul’s ambition to take Commonwealth gold was short-lived. He was disqualified in his match against Thomas during the third round for headbutting his opponent. His disqualification and the referee’s decision prompted a lashing of boos and jeers from his supporters in the crowd. Abdul was furious when speaking to media after the aborted fight, beginning the media conference by pointing at a journalist in the scrum. “You I don’t like,” he said pointing at the reporter, shaking his head. He then spoke to a member of the Ugandan team, going back and forth before taking questions from journalists.



“That decision is not correct,” he said when asked for his reaction to the disqualification “That decision was on one side.” “All I can say about this ... I’m not happy about the decision.” Abdul was unhappy after his disqualification. Getty Images Abdul then referred to his opponent by the n-word, adding, “I will get him next time … anywhere in the future I’ll get him … if not now, anytime in the future, after five years or two years or 10 years ... I will show him that Aziz Ringo is a real warrior.” When asked to expand on why the disqualification for headbutting was unfair, Abdul said it had not been intentional and his opponent had elbowed him, among other infractions, multiple times throughout the fight. He said it was a trend among English fighters.



He said his English opponent was given favour because he was on “home” soil and said he had landed heavy punches on Thomas that did not count. “Instead of counting, they deduct my points, they warn me,” he said. “I’m a black African, OK ... I know, he’s in his homeland.” He questioned why the officials were “scared about this fight”. “Why couldn’t they let the fight continue,” he said. “What was wrong in the fight?”





“Like I said, I got the job done … the job is done,” he said. Asked by this masthead what he had expected of the fight with Abdul, Thomas said “literally that. “I didn’t expect anything else.” Thomas also said he didn’t want the fight “to end like that” and it “was not how he wanted it to go”. World.title: ‘I’m not there to come second’: Before a hostile crowd, this Australian wants to change history
World.content:
SportAthleticsCommonwealth Games ‘I’m not there to come second’: Before a hostile crowd, this Australian wants to change history Michael Gleeson July 30, 2026 — 8:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Cameron Myers knows no one wants him to win. Not the Scots anyway. Actually, the English are not terribly keen on him winning either. Those in green and gold are obviously fully behind the middle-distance runner, but after Australia’s domination in the pool throughout the Commonwealth Games, and on the track on Tuesday night, people are getting a bit sick of all the winning. Australian Cameron Myers leads the pack in his men’s mile heat in Glasgow, which he won. Getty Images Myers has done nothing wrong, other than be quick and the threat to Scotland’s pin-up boy of the Games, Josh Kerr. “Everyone’s cheering for the Scots, and I’m sure they want to go one, two. I’m trying to spoil that,” the 20-year-old Australian, who is ranked No.2 in the world, said after winning his heat and going into the mile (1600 metres) final.



Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Australia wraps up record stint in the pool with emotional win and a dead heat for gold; Dictator’s grandson hits out after boxing disqualification Kerr broke the mile world record last week at the London Diamond League. In Glasgow, they have scrapped the 1500 metres in favour of a mile as a sentimental nod to one of the great events of the sport. Myers, too, has his eye on this history. “Given the story of Roger Bannister and John Landy – I think Bannister won gold and Landy was holding the world record [in the mile]. Hopefully, I can reverse the roles there, but we’ll see,” said Myers, who won his heat in 3:53.85 from England’s former world champion from three years ago Jake Wightman. “It’s a different ball game coming to a championships. You have to deal with a lot more factors. I think we saw that at Paris 2024, Jakob [Ingebrigtsen] had run two seconds better than anyone else in the field, and he still wasn’t able to win. I think it shows you that championship racing is not about the time you have on paper; it’s how you execute. “I’m a competitor. I don’t want to lose, I’m not going there to come second. I’ll be cracking in as best I can.”



Kerr is clearly expected to win. He’s a world champion and a silver medallist, has just won the world record, and is running in front of his home crowd. Myers is a 20-year-old kid from Canberra who hasn’t won anything substantial yet other than the respect and fear of competitors who know he is the next big thing in the sport. At every age level, Myers has broken records, and he is the second-fastest man in the world this year over a mile behind Kerr. Mile world record holder Josh Kerr is Scotland’s poster boy of the Glasgow Games. Getty Images In drizzly, wet Glasgow, he wants to rain on the Scottish parade. “I have confidence, obviously, and I think it’s more about proving myself in a championship setting, I think that’s something that I’ve yet to do,” he said.



Related Article Analysis

Commonwealth Games Lachie Kennedy smashed the Australian 100m record. It shows he can win a medal at the Olympics “So for me, it’s actually still I would say a stepping stone to getting to becoming the sort of athlete that I want to be.” It’s a funny change to the mile from the 1500m for these Games. It is jarring because everything else is metric, but oddly enough, it makes more sense than the 1500m. It has history behind it – and the simple fact is that it is four laps of the track. Myers thinks the distance change should stick for the Olympics and world championships. “I think it’s a way that we can attract more people into the sport, holding the miles. I think obviously Americans still love it, so I think it’s just something that regular people can resonate a little bit more to.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Dictator’s grandson blasts ‘unfair’ result after disqualification in first fight “I think the 1500 is a weird one, you know. It’s not a [kilometre], which people know of. It’s not a 2K. I think it’s having those numbers that people don’t really understand the context behind it.” Earlier, Lachie Kennedy returned to the track for the 200m hearts with the sluggishness of a man who just became the fastest Australian man, won a silver medal and spent the night trying to comprehend it all. “I’m a bit cooked now, but yeah, no, it’s been an exciting couple of hours,” he said. “It’s still all sort of surreal. I guess I haven’t really grasped how big it is yet because I’ve still got races to run. Still got things to do. But I’m definitely coming around to it.”



After two days and six events, Tori West sat in third place in the heptathlon. The scenario for her last race, the 800m, was simple. Run a personal best, and stay in third to claim bronze, or let the English runner in fourth beat her across the line by more than five or so seconds and slip out of the medals. “That was the stupidest 800 I’ve ever run in my life,” West said after bolting to the front and nearly blowing up. But she hung on, ran her personal best and won bronze. Elsewhere, Sarah Billings was strong in her 800m semi-final, making it through to Friday’s final. World.title: ‘Very challenging’: Three dead after fire rips through Sydney granny flat
World.content:
A teenager is believed to be among the three people killed in a fire that tore through a granny flat in Sydney’s south-west on Wednesday night. Firefighters discovered the bodies of the people – who investigators believe are the usual occupants of the home – after being called to the Cornelia Street address in Wiley Park about 9.45pm on Wednesday. Investigators work to identify the three people killed in the fire. KATE GERAGHTY The property was decimated by the fire, which erupted only metres from a neighbouring apartment building. Nine First responders encountered a “very challenging scene”, according to Fire and Rescue NSW (FRNSW) Commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell, whose entry to the granny flat were slowed by a range of obstacles stacked across the property’s side path and garden.



“A lot of the material in the garden area of the granny flat was on fire as well, because there were flames coming out of all the windows and any opening in the building, and that had spread to the surrounding material,” Fewtrell told Nine on Thursday morning. A police officer watches on as detectives sweep through the Wiley Park granny flat on Thursday. KATE GERAGHTY The fire tore through the flat at the back of the property on Wednesday night. KATE GERAGHTY “They had to fight their way to get to the front door of the property, and then they had to sort of work their way in from there. So it was a very, very tough time for them.” Forensic officers have swept the scene overnight, as investigators work to confirm details of the people killed. Detectives are expected to continue their investigation at the scene for several hours on Thursday, as they work to understand the origins and circumstances of the fire.



A crime scene has been established by Campsie Police Area Command, ahead of a report being prepared for the coroner. FRNSW attended 480 residential fires in the first six weeks of winter, and more than 2000 this year. This included a fatal blaze in Randwick on July 7, when a woman in her late 70s was killed after a fire broke out in an Alison Road apartment. Five days later, another person in their 70s was found dead after a fire broke out in a Wollongong suburb. Fewtrell has encouraged residents to use the service’s free home fire safety visit program which includes smoke alarm checks.



Loading “Regularly check your smoke alarm, always keep looking when cooking, keep a fire blanket and extinguisher in your kitchen, keep flammable materials a metre from the heater, and don’t overload power board or power points,” he said. “Always check electric and heated blankets before turning them on, and look for frays, scorch marks, exposed wires or controller damage. If anything looks off, bin it.” More to come Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Oscar-winning Frames frontman Glen Hansard dies in motorcycle crash
World.content:
CultureMusicVale Oscar-winning Frames frontman Glen Hansard dies in motorcycle crash Padraic Halpin July 30, 2026 — 7:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dublin: Irish musician Glen Hansard, who won a Best Original Song Oscar in 2008 for the indie film Once and was lead singer for rock group The Frames, died in a motorcycle crash at the age of 56 early on Wednesday (Dublin time), his management company said. Bruce Springsteen, whom Hansard shared a stage with, said he and his band were heartbroken at the death of a “great musician, a good friend and a generous and gracious man”. Glen Hansard and Marketa Irglova in Once. Icon Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin described him as an artist “who made a significant contribution to Ireland’s cultural landscape.” The singer-songwriter began busking on the streets of his native Dublin at the age of 13 after dropping out of school, and formed The Frames in 1990. The band’s popularity at home helped make their lead singer a fixture on the Irish music scene for the next four decades.



Related Article Live music ‘We weren’t the next big thing’: Irish singer-songwriter’s unusual path to success U2 frontman Bono paid tribute to Hansard in a post on X, describing him as “a smiling rascal if you needed him to be ... this most musical and mischievous archangel of Ballymun.” Bono said Hansard “could never walk by a person living rough without checking they were OK,” and praised his work to help reduce homelessness. “Voice of the streets. A choir of angels in one man,” Bono said. Fight against homelessness



Hansard released a number of albums under his own name – receiving a Grammy nomination in 2016 – and as part of duo The Swell Season with fellow Oscar winner and Once co-star Marketa Irglova. The pair’s performances in the low-budget movie shot on handheld camcorders where a street musician falls in love with a young Czech immigrant, and their Oscar-winning duet Falling Slowly, brought Hansard’s music to a much wider audience. Irish singer-songwriter Glen Hansard with the Frames. He has died in a motorcycle crash. Daragh McDonagh The film, which featured a number of other songs composed and performed by Hansard and Irglova, was turned into a hit Broadway musical that won eight Tony Awards in 2012. Accepting his Oscar from presenter John Travolta, a stunned Hansard said: “What are we doing here? This is mad.”



His only acting experience prior to Once was as a band member in Alan Parker’s 1991 hit The Commitments. Related Article ★★★★★

Review Like cashmere and silk: These two singers turn this classic opera into a must-see Many tributes also focused on Hansard’s charity work and advocacy. A Christmas Eve busk he started at the depths of Ireland’s financial crisis in 2010 has raised over €2 million for the Dublin Simon Community charity, who described the singer on Wednesday as “a giant in the fight against homelessness”. The annual gathering in central Dublin has featured Bono, Sinead O’Connor and Shane MacGowan. Hansard led a rendition of The Pogues’ Christmas anthem Fairytale of New York at his friend MacGowan’s funeral in 2023. “With broken hearts we announce the passing of Glen Hansard who passed away, in the early hours of this morning, following a road-traffic accident in Dublin,” ATC Management said in a statement.



Irish police said a man in his 50s had died after a single-vehicle motorcycle collision in the west of Dublin. Emergency services were alerted shortly before 4.30am (Irish time) and the man was pronounced dead a short time after being treated at the scene. Hansard is survived by his wife, Maire Saaritsa, and their three-year-old son Christy. Reuters Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: ‘Never sexually assaulted anyone’: Jared Leto denies criminal allegations by four women
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCrime ‘Never sexually assaulted anyone’: Jared Leto denies criminal allegations by four women Emily Kaine and Kayla Olaya Updated July 30, 2026 — 8:48am ,first published 7:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oscar-winning actor Jared Leto has been accused of criminal sexual conduct by four women who alleged the offences occurred when they were teenagers. Leto has denied sexual misconduct allegations made by a total of ten women who detailed their encounters with the actor and Thirty Seconds to Mars frontman to the BBC in a new documentary titled Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret. Jared Leto pictured in 2025. Getty Images for Disney “I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life. These claims are absolutely and categorically false,” Leto said in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter. In the documentary, one woman alleged she was sexually assaulted inside a motel bathroom at the age of 17, while another said Leto threatened her with sexual assault when she was 19.



A third woman said she had under-age sex with the star in California when she was 17, and said he had “shrugged off” a conversation about the age of consent being 18 in the US state. The fourth woman claimed she was groomed by the star, and alleged he abused his celebrity status by repeatedly making sexually explicit phone calls to her when she was 16. She also said he suggested they should have sex on at least one occasion. Four more women also alleged they received odd and often very sexual phone calls from the star when they were younger. During these phone calls, the women alleged Leto asked them questions such as: “Are you a virgin? Do you have any kinks?” All the women allege their encounters with the actor took place between 2002 and 2016, when he was in his 30s and 40s. He is now 54.



One of his alleged victims told the BBC: “This was 25 years ago … He has gotten away with it.” Leto has been a prominent Hollywood figure since the 1990s. He won the 2014 Academy Award for best supporting actor for Dallas Buyers Club, and has appeared in hit films such as Fight Club, Blade Runner 2049, and Suicide Squad. Leto in Los Angeles in 2022. AP In June last year, Leto was accused by nine women of inappropriate behaviour – including claims his conduct was “predatory, terrifying and unacceptable” – in an Air Mail exposé. At the time, Leto “expressly denied” the accusations, including an allegation from one woman who said the actor approached her in 2006 when she was 16, and he was 35.



Another woman alleged that when she was 18, Leto “suddenly pulled his penis out and started masturbating”. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Anyone affected by sexual, domestic or family violence can also access 24/7, free and confidential trauma-specialist counselling through Full Stop Australia (1800 385 578).
